# fp tracker snapshot

**Generated by `data-raw/snapshot-tracker.sh` on 2026-11-18.**
273 issues. Do not hand-edit: the next run overwrites this file
wholesale.

`.fp/` is gitignored, so this file is the only copy of the tracker in
git. It is a backstop for the ROBO-* citations in
`NEWS.md`, the release audits under `design/` and the test suite, not a replacement for the tracker: `fp` remains
authoritative and `fp context <id>` remains the way to read an issue.

## ROBO-acoqvdfb: [PARKED] Validator: note when an Allow under a full block ends mid-segment

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

`Allow: /tc` under `Disallow: /` also matches `/tcfd-report`, `/tc-anything` and `/tcx`, and
can therefore allow them, unless a more specific Disallow wins. Patterns match by prefix, not by
path segment. An Allow ending without `/` or `$` may be intended to cover only that path and its
descendants, but it reaches every sibling that starts with the same characters.

Observed on https://www.bloomberg.com/robots.txt (fetched 2026-11-17), Google backend:
ClaudeBot `/tcfd-report` → allow (line 101), `/faqs-anything` → allow (100), `/companyx` →
allow (98). The file's own comment (lines 88-90) explains prefix matching for its `$` rules.

### Why it waits

Probably noisy: many sites write `Allow: /tc` to cover `/tc` and `/tc/…` and have no siblings.
It stays parked until a manually reviewed corpus run, with a defined false-positive measure,
shows it is worth a diagnostic. Matching alone cannot establish the author's intent.

### Scope

In: an info code for an Allow with no `*` anywhere in the pattern, whose last segment has no
trailing `/` or `$`, in a group that literally contains `Disallow: /` (first version; not
effective-rule analysis). Message: "also matches sibling paths starting with the same
characters". Exemptions for noise only, stated as such: a last segment containing a dot
(`/tc.html`).

Out: Disallow lines (`Disallow: /search` is usually deliberate); patterns with `*`; groups
blocked only by `Disallow: /*` or `Disallow: /$`.

### Acceptance criteria

- Fires on the Bloomberg shape.
- Silent on `/tc/`, `/tc$`, `/tc*`, `/foo*/tc`, `/tc.html`, and outside literal `Disallow: /`
  groups.
- Silent when a competing `Disallow: /tcx` covers the only sibling the file names.
- Repeated groups for the same agent are merged first.
- The corpus review is a prerequisite to implementation.

### Verification

Corpus review notes, then fixtures. Merge gate.

### Dependencies

None. Reviewed with GPT-6.1-Sol (medium) on 2026-11-17.


### Comments

#### 2026-11-17 — bartek@turczynski.pl

The maintainer asked on 2026-11-17 for bare (no trailing slash) rules to be flagged in general, not only Allows under a full block. That broader check is filed as ROBO-otomgbge, with this issue's noise concern carried over as a corpus measure before shipping. ROBO-otomgbge says this one is closed as absorbed or kept with a reason when it lands. Left open and parked here; the maintainer decides.




## ROBO-aeyefkgi: [PARKED] SF4 — Fetch-policy probes: status, redirect, and size behaviour against a local server

**Status:** todo | **Parent:** cbbyzfvflluniwyrplqtytozumblaeiu

### Description

Parked 2026-09-27 by the maintainer (fleet groom ROBO-lsbdefbm): a conformance study (analysis and vendor contact), not package code. Start only on an instruction naming this issue.

Independent of SF2/SF3 — can run on its own, and may be worth more than the matcher probes.

The local server exercises the L0 / §3 / §4 fetch-policy layer of `design/engine-profiles.md`, which **no static corpus can test**. This is where engines genuinely differ and where SEOs actually get burned.

Probes:
- `/robots.txt` → 404 (and other 4xx): does SF crawl freely, per Google's allow-all?
- `/robots.txt` → 503 / 500: does SF stop, per Google's disallow-all — or crawl the site anyway?
- redirect chains to `/robots.txt`: 1..5 hops, and >5 hops (RFC 9309 §2.3.1.2 requires at least five)
- cross-authority redirect: are the reached rules applied to the *initial* authority?
- redirect with no `Location`, and a redirect loop
- body >500KiB (Google's documented truncation point): is the tail honoured or dropped?
- slow response / timeout on `/robots.txt`

Record observed behaviour against what `design/engine-profiles.md` says Google does, in the same observational namespace as SF3. Same CI caveat: never runs in CI, snapshot with version + date provenance.

The server built here is the reusable piece — it generalises to any crawler, desktop or cloud.

### Comments

#### 2026-09-27 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Retitled by ROBO-lsbdefbm. Old title: SF4 — Fetch-policy probes: status, redirect, and size behaviour against a local server

## ROBO-ahqpndzq: Validator: recognize the RSL License directive and say its scope

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

https://www.theguardian.com/robots.txt (fetched 2026-11-17) ends with
`License: https://theguardian.com/license.xml` (line 104). This is the `License` directive of
Really Simple Licensing (RSL 1.0, RSL-SPEC-1.0, Recommendation, 2025-12-10,
https://rslstandard.org/rsl, §4.4). The validator reports it as `unknown_directive`, a warning
that says only "Directive is not recognized by this validation profile."

What RSL says, from §4.4:
- Syntax: `License: <absolute-URI>`. The value "MUST be an absolute URI".
- "The `License` directive does not modify the access permissions expressed by `Allow` or
  `Disallow` fields."
- Scope depends on placement. A `License` "within a User-agent group applies only to clients
  that select that group under RFC 9309". One "outside any User-agent group applies to all
  clients". A client whose group has its own `License` lines ignores the global ones.
- Example 1 puts a global `License` before the first `User-agent` line. Example 2 puts a
  group's `License` after its rules, followed by a blank line.

The Guardian line sits after the last group (37 stacked AI and other crawlers, `Disallow: /`)
and a blank line. RSL's example 2 places a group's `License` after its last rule, including the
final group at the end of the file, and treats it as group-scoped. RFC 9309 groups do not end at
blank lines, and §2.2.4 says other records must not interfere with parsing the defined ones. So
the trailing `License` is associated with the final group only. That discovery association
reaches only the 37 blocked crawlers; Googlebot, GPTBot and every other crawler on `*` find no
`License` in this file. The directive points to licensing information; it grants nothing itself.
The file's comments (lines 3-7) state licensing terms for LLM use, so the placement matters.
Putting the line before the first `User-agent` line would make it global.

Google's matcher ignores the line, and it ends no group.

### Scope

In: a specific code for a `License` line (working name `rsl_license_directive`), info, replacing
`unknown_directive` for it. Like `content_signal_directive`, the message says the line does not
change crawling permissions. It also states the line's scope:
- before the first `User-agent` line: global;
- anywhere after a group's `User-agent` lines and before the next group: group-scoped, naming
  the group's first line and its agents (bounded list). When no global `License` exists, the
  message adds that crawlers outside the group find no `License` here, and that placing it
  before the first `User-agent` line makes it global.

A value that is not an absolute URI gets a warning-level variant (same code, or a sibling code
decided in the MR). RFC 3986 absolute URIs include hostless ones (`urn:example:license`), so
reusing the sitemap URL parser is decided only after the URI fixtures below pass.

Out: fetching the license document; RSL's other discovery mechanisms (HTTP `Link`, HTML);
validating the license XML.

### Acceptance criteria

- A frozen copy of the Guardian file gets the info row on line 104, group-scoped to the final
  group with the "outside the group find no License" sentence, and no `unknown_directive`.
- Scope fixtures: global (before the first `User-agent`); group-scoped mid-group and after the
  last rule (with and without a blank line, before another group and at end of file); a group
  with no Allow/Disallow; `License` between stacked `User-agent` lines; global plus group-local
  lines (local overrides global, global is the fallback); several values; mixed valid and
  invalid lines.
- URI fixtures: a relative value (`/license.xml`), `urn:example:license`, a malformed escape,
  inner whitespace, a fragment, an empty value, and casing (`license:`).
- `content_signal_directive` and `unknown_directive` keep their meanings for other lines.
- Whether a `License` line between `User-agent` lines splits a stacked group follows the same
  rule as other unknown directives (`user_agent_joined_across_directive`) and is pinned by a
  test.
- Diagnostic table, `design/linter-set.md`, NEWS (one line).

### Verification

Fixtures above. Merge gate.

### Dependencies

None. Related: ROBO-fqkgreev (Content-Signal), ROBO-xepnhfgs.


### Comments

#### 2026-11-17 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Corrections and a severity rule, agreed with the maintainer 2026-11-17.

1. **Wrong comparison in Scope.** `content_signal_directive` is a **warning**, not info (`R/robots_validate.R:98`, `:942`). The new code is still info, for the reason in point 2. It is not "like" Content-Signal in severity.

2. **Severity rule for directives from other standards** (RSL, Content-Signal and later ones):
   - warning: the source standard is expired or superseded, or a better mechanism exists. Content-Signal stays a warning.
   - info: the source is a current standard and the line is well formed. RSL `License` with an absolute URI is info. A malformed value stays the warning-level variant already in Scope.
   Each message names the standard, says the line changes no access, and says whether any crawler operator documents reading it.

3. **Adoption, add it to the message.** As of 2026-11, no major crawler operator documents reading RSL. A 2026-08 check of OpenAI, Anthropic, Perplexity and Google crawler docs found no mention, and crawler-commons has only an open request (crawler-commons/crawler-commons#617, 2026-10-18). The message should say the scope applies under RSL 1.0 §4.4 and that no crawler is documented as reading the line, with the date kept in `design/linter-set.md` so it can be reviewed.

4. **Wording about the Guardian.** The final group is mostly AI crawlers blocked with `Disallow: /`, so a group-scoped `License` there may be deliberate ("you are blocked; license here"). The diagnostic states the scope and how to make the line global. It must not call the placement an error. Don't describe the Guardian file as a confirmed bug in the MR, tests or NEWS.

#### 2026-11-17 — bartek@turczynski.pl

A second candidate of the same kind: Yoast's `Schemamap:` directive. https://yoast.com/robots.txt (fetched 2026-11-18) line 19, `Schemamap: https://yoast.com/wp-json/yoast/v1/schema-aggregator/get-xml`, gets `unknown_directive` today. Needs a dated Yoast source for what it is and which consumer, if any, reads it, before it is recognized; if both land, one "recognized non-standard directive" mechanism should serve both.




## ROBO-ajcacryw: Pin redirects to an unzoned IPv6-literal Location through the real ssrf_prepare_hop() path

**Status:** done

### Description

Found in the pre-MR review of ROBO-atvfjuuw (2026-10-29). Pre-existing; not caused by that MR.

When a robots.txt fetch is redirected to a Location whose host is an IPv6 literal, zoned or not (`http://[::1%25lo0]/`, `http://[::1]/`), `httr2::url_modify_relative()` in the redirect loop (`R/fetch-policy.R`) throws "Failed to parse URL: Bad hostname". Nothing catches it, so the error escapes `robots_fetch()` instead of returning a `redirect_error` (or `ssrf_blocked`) source result. Reproduced by the reviewer.

No request is sent, so this is not an SSRF hole, but a hostile server can turn a fetch into an R error, and the SSRF guard never classifies an IPv6 redirect target: it only runs on the initial URL for these.

Fix direction: catch the resolve failure and return a `redirect_error` result with a reason (or classify the raw Location with the SSRF guard first, so a blocked target reports `ssrf_blocked`). Add a mocked-redirect test for both spellings. ROBO-jbralthm (move acquisition to ssrfr) would replace this loop; until then this needs its own fix.


### Comments

#### 2026-11-08 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Rescoped 2026-11-08 (burndown scout, verified by the lead). The defect is gone: a041a95 (ROBO-jbralthm) removed the httr2 url_modify_relative redirect loop. Today acquire_location_target() -> ssrfr::ssrf_prepare_hop() turns any Location parse failure into a parse / malformed-address refusal, mapped to ssrf_blocked (safety_refused), and nothing errors out of robots_fetch(). Zoned literals are already pinned (test-ssrf-atvfjuuw.R). Remaining scope, test-only: a loopback webfakes test redirecting to an unzoned IPv6 literal ([::1] with the server's port, since local_loopback_policy() sets allow_ports; and 2001:db8::1) through the real ssrf_prepare_hop(), not the fake's ssrf_inspect_url(). Expected: ssrf_blocked with the refusal reason ssrfr gives (loopback; reserved for 2001:db8::/32, which the test should confirm, not assume). No R/ change.

#### 2026-11-08 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Starting (burndown 2026-11-09, wave 1): implementer haiku/xhigh in a harness worktree, branch chore/ROBO-ajcacryw-ipv6-literal-redirect-pins, test-only. Lead gates and merges.

#### 2026-11-08 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Landed in !85 (merge 3ed19c4): tests/testthat/test-ssrf-ajcacryw.R pins redirects to unzoned IPv6-literal Locations ([::1], [2001:db8::1], relative, uppercase scheme, malformed brackets, non-ASCII) as ssrf_blocked with redirect_count 1 and no R error, plus a webfakes loopback test through the real ssrf_prepare_hop(). ## ROBO-aoslfvnx: Under crawler, 6to4, Teredo and ISATAP refusals are safety_refused, not unreachable_local

**Status:** done

### Description

### Why

ROBO-jqwukcog classed every ssrfr address-class code as `unreachable_local` under `safety_level = "crawler"`, which means "not dialed: the address is internal, so a public crawler could not reach it either". ADR 0001 §3 lists `6to4`, `teredo` and `isatap` as "IPv6 forms that embed one" (an internal address). But ssrfr 1.0.0.9001 refuses these whatever IPv4 they embed. `http://[2002:5db8:d822::1]/` (6to4 around public 93.184.216.34) gives `6to4`, `http://[2001:0:5db8:d822::1]/` gives `teredo`, and an ISATAP address around the same public IPv4 gives `isatap` (all tested 2026-11-11). Under crawler, such a target is therefore reported as internal and unreachable, which is a false statement about the site. The maintainer's goal 3 rules this out: ssrfr's safety behavior must not obscure the tool's diagnostics. NAT64 and IPv4-translated are refused only with a prohibited embedded address, so they stay address-class.

### Decision (settled 2026-11-11)

Settled by Claude and Codex (GPT-6.1-Sol), on the maintainer's delegation. `6to4`, `teredo` and `isatap` map to `safety_refused` at both levels: refused for safety, reachability unknown, no engine reading. robotstxtr does not extract the embedded IPv4 itself, because classification belongs to ssrfr. RFC 7526 §4 deprecates anycast 6to4 but keeps basic unicast 6to4, so deprecation does not make a destination unreachable.

### Scope

- `R/acquire-map.R`: give the three codes a class that maps to `safety_refused` at both levels (a third class, or url_shape-like handling; keep the walk test's "every admitted code is classed" guarantee).
- ADR 0001 §3 (and the slice 4 table), design/engine-profiles.md §3a and design/engine-contract-v1.md "Safety level": the address-class list loses the three; say why.
- Tests: the jqwukcog vocabulary walk moves the three codes to the safety_refused expectation; a test that a 6to4/Teredo/ISATAP target around a public IPv4 is `safety_refused` under crawler.
- NEWS bullet (the evidence mapping changes). The schema revision moves only if an enum or column changes (it does not); check the policy-table revision rule in design/engine-contract-v1.md.

### Acceptance

Under crawler, a 6to4, Teredo or ISATAP target gives `evidence_status = "safety_refused"` with `safety_block_reason` kept; every other address-class code is unchanged.


### Comments

#### 2026-11-11 — bartek@turczynski.pl

burndown-v2 run (2026-11-11). Starting: implementer dispatched in a harness worktree (.claude/worktrees/agent-*); branch feature/ROBO-aoslfvnx-transition-refusals; implementer opus/medium. RESCOPE by the orchestrator, verified against ssrfr verdict vectors: only `6to4` and `teredo` move to a new `transition` class (safety_refused at both levels). ssrfr refuses both whatever the embedded IPv4 (V0193, V0194, V0202). `isatap` stays in the address class: ssrfr admits ISATAP under a global prefix around a routable IPv4 (V0199) and refuses it only for a prohibited embedded address (R/vocabulary.R), so each isatap refusal is a true internal fact and unreachable_local is right. The settled decision's 'reachability unknown' rationale holds for 6to4/Teredo only.

#### 2026-11-11 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Review correction to the orchestrator's re-scope: ssrfr also refuses ISATAP with a GLOBAL prefix around a private IPv4 (`http://[2600::5efe:a00:1]/` -> code isatap, verified against ssrfr 1.0.0.9001), which is the standard RFC 5214 deployment a public crawler can reach; the fe80:: form gives the same code. robotstxtr cannot tell them apart without extracting the embedded IPv4, which the settled decision rules out. ## ROBO-aoyyhpdp: Retire the Claude auto-memory store: promote what is durable, delete the rest

**Status:** done | **Revisions:** `db465966`

### Description

Claude's auto-memory is now disabled globally (`autoMemoryEnabled: false` in
~/.claude/settings.json), so this project's store is inert and costs nothing while it sits.
This issue is to recover anything durable from it and then delete it.

### This store, measured

| | |
|---|---|
| Fact files | 6 |
| Size | 12 KB |
| MEMORY.md index | ~346 tokens, injected into every session while memory was on |
| Sessions in this project | 14 |
| Writes (Write/Edit on a memory file) | 22 |
| Explicit reads | 8 |
| Reads in a session that did NOT also write the file | **0** |

Store: `/Users/bartturczynski/.claude/projects/-Users-bartturczynski-Projects-robotstxtr/memory`

Fleet-wide the ratio was 774 writes to 60 genuine reads, and 93.7% of files were never
genuinely read. Small store — likely a short skim-and-delete rather than a promotion pass.

### Why this is not just a delete

Memories never expire and nothing reconciles them against the repo. In `rurl` several had gone
outright false — a file claiming `cran-comments.md` was untracked when it is tracked, memories
assuming a `Remotes:` field that no longer exists, one asserting `tools/verify.R` was absent from
main when it is present, and three superseded by ADRs that landed after the memory was written.
Skim for durable knowledge, but verify every claim against the tree before promoting it.

### Method (as used for rurl)

Sort every file into four buckets:

1. **Dead** — self-labels as HISTORICAL / CLOSED / RETIRED / FALSIFIED / "kept for the record".
   Delete; git and the tracker own it.
2. **Ephemeral state** — epic/phase status, "T4-T8 remain", "shipped in x.y.z". Delete; NEWS,
   git history and this tracker own it. In rurl these were the *largest* files and the most stale.
3. **Durable and project-specific** — promote into the real docs (AGENTS.md / ARCHITECTURE.md /
   CONTRIBUTING.md / an ADR / a design note). Check first whether the docs already say it; a lot
   of it was re-derived from what was already written down.
4. **Generic, not about this project** — do **not** write it to `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` or
   `~/.claude/fp-cli-notes.md`. Those load in every session in every project and the owner keeps
   them deliberately small. List such items in the closing comment (or propose them to the owner
   inline) and let the owner decide; otherwise delete them with the rest of the store.

Prefer consolidating many memories into one coherent doc over transcribing them one-to-one.
In rurl, 14 separate files became a single method note that is worth reading; 32 files were
deleted outright.

### Before deleting

Archive the store first:

```sh
tar -czf ~/Projects/_backups/claude-memory/robotstxtr-memory-$(date +%F).tar.gz \
    -C "$(dirname '/Users/bartturczynski/.claude/projects/-Users-bartturczynski-Projects-robotstxtr/memory')" memory
```

### Done when

- [ ] Every file triaged into one of the four buckets
- [ ] Durable items promoted into tracked docs, each claim verified against the tree
- [ ] Store archived to ~/Projects/_backups/claude-memory/
- [ ] Store deleted
- [ ] Any still-open question or live blocker found in it filed as its own issue here

### Precedent

`rurl` (MR !67, merged as d28ea6c): 104 files / 372 KB retired; 5 new design docs + an ADR,
1,076 lines added across 11 files; 32 files deleted as dead or ephemeral.


### Comments

#### 2026-09-13 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Bucket 4 revised 2026-09-13: generic items are no longer promoted to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md; list them for the owner instead. No code changed.

## ROBO-atkmqcov: Validator: a byte-order mark after the start of the file shows only as unknown_directive

**Status:** done

### Description

### Problem

A UTF-8 BOM that is not at byte 0 (mid-file, or before a later `User-agent` line) makes that line's key unreadable. The validator reports `unknown_directive` with no mention of the BOM, and when the hidden line is a `User-agent`, the group it opened is silently merged into the previous one with no report.

## ROBO-atvfjuuw: SSRF guard: IPv6 literal with a zone ID passes

**Status:** done

### Description

Found in the second review of ROBO-dxrljrde. Pre-existing; not caused by that fix.

An IPv6 literal with a zone ID gets past the structural SSRF guard: `http://[::1%25lo0]/`, `http://[fd00:ec2::254%25lo0]/`, `http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1%25lo0]/`, `http://[fe80::1%25eth0]/`. rurl yields no host for them (default and WHATWG views), and the guard allows a missing host. libcurl drops the zone and dials the bare address (reviewers saw libcurl 8.14.1 attempt ::1). Loopback and AWS IPv6 metadata reachable under the default `ssrf_guard = TRUE`: Critical in the OSS Scanner threat model.

Fix direction: fail closed, as ssrfr does (it returns `parse` for these). When the raw host is bracketed and rurl gives no host, strip a `%25zone`/`%zone` suffix and classify the bare address, or refuse the URL outright. Regression tests for the four spellings above.

Keep the details out of public text until the fix ships; a confidential GitLab issue tracks it.

## ROBO-bnvdmdjr: [USER] Evaluator: support explicit URL preprocessing before matching

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

The evaluator can match a supplied path that differs from the request target a client produces
by URL parsing or link resolution. The matchers take the path as given; RFC 9309 §2.2.2 defines
percent-encoding handling for comparison but says nothing about dot segments.

TESTED 2026-11-17 (`robots_evaluate_text_v1()`, Google, Bing and Yandex agree), with
`Disallow: /account/` and `Allow: /latam`:
- `/latam/../account/x` → allow (via `Allow: /latam`). curl, Node `fetch` and link resolution
  request `/account/x` → disallow.
- `/latam/%2e%2e/account/x` → allow. Node `fetch` (WHATWG) requests `/account/x`; curl sends it
  unchanged; Python `urllib` and Go `net/http` send both forms unchanged.

rurl already resolves URLs. `resolve_url(u, base, url_standard = "whatwg", output = "serialized")`
removes literal and encoded dot segments and leaves dots in the query alone, though WHATWG
serialization percent-encodes some query characters (a space becomes `%20`).
`url_standard = "rfc3986"` removes literal dots only and returns NA for spaces and backslashes.
`get_clean_url()` is a canonicalizer that rewrites the query (`/` → `%2F`), so it is the wrong
tool here.

### Why it waits

The maintainer decides, before implementation:
- the default mode (none, RFC 3986 §5.2.4 dot-segment removal, or full WHATWG parsing);
- whether WHATWG's other changes are in scope (percent-encoding spaces and non-ASCII, `\` → `/`,
  dropping default ports);
- whether this needs an ADR.

It changes evaluator answers for some inputs.

### Scope

In (proposed): an argument such as `url_normalization = c("rfc3986", "whatwg", "none")` on the
evaluate functions, where `"rfc3986"` means §5.2.4 dot-segment removal only. Normalization
happens before extracting the matcher's path-and-query input. Fragments are dropped, as the
matchers already ignore them. The matched path is recorded as evidence beside the input `url`.
A secondary flag marks inputs where the RFC 3986 and WHATWG forms give different decisions for
the selected matcher, or where one mode fails. Defined behavior for inputs a mode rejects (NA
from `"rfc3986"`).

Out: per-bot defaults (follow-up once the AI-bot class exists and lab evidence says what each
fetcher sends); query rewriting beyond the chosen standard; changes to the vendored matchers.

### Acceptance criteria

- The decision and exact mode semantics are recorded (ADR or `design/engine-profiles.md`),
  with the client evidence above.
- Each mode is tested on: literal dots; trailing `/..`; `..` above the root; mixed literal and
  encoded dots in either case; double encoding (`%252e`); encoded `/` (`%2F`); repeated
  slashes; names containing dots (`/a..b`, `/.well-known`); dots in the query (untouched);
  spaces; non-ASCII; a rejected input.
- An input already serialized for the selected mode is passed through byte-identical and gets
  the same decision as today.
- The disagreement flag is tested in both directions, and on forms that differ but decide alike.
- Existing result columns keep their meaning; the new evidence column is documented; NEWS one
  line.

### Verification

Focused evaluator tests per mode, an `allowed_by_robots_url()` mocked-fetch test, and the
`as_legacy_robots_decisions_v1()` path. Merge gate.

### Dependencies

Uses rurl's exported `resolve_url()`; no vendored-matcher change. Per-bot defaults are a
follow-up informed by the agent-view probe. Reviewed with GPT-6.1-Sol (medium) on 2026-11-17.


### Comments

#### 2026-11-17 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Per-bot defaults: agent-view AGEN-hsvkltop probes what AI fetchers request for dot segments. Validator side: ROBO-rnjfbhvn.

## ROBO-bpywsjwv: [USER] Bing and Yandex webmaster-tester checks for the unevidenced disagreement classes

**Status:** done

### Description

### Why

Bing and Yandex publish little; their backends rest on tester observations. The cross-engine triage leaves some disagreement classes with no evidence either way. Only the maintainer can run Bing Webmaster Tools' and Yandex Webmaster's robots.txt testers.

Gate: [USER] because it needs the maintainer's webmaster accounts and, where a live fetch is needed, a public host. Related: ROBO-ogwchglq (measuring fetch rules with served files), which stays parked.

### Scope

In: for each unevidenced class, the prepared synthesized file, URLs and token (listed in this issue's comments by the triage), run in the tester; record result, date and tool. Then update the tester corpora and engine-profiles.md tags (a normal code issue per change).
Out: anything the triage already settled.

### Acceptance criteria

Each listed class has an observed result with date, or is marked "not testable" with the reason.

### Dependencies

Cross-engine triage.


### Comments

#### 2026-11-10 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Tester questions from the cross-engine triage (ROBO-glssaxva, merged in !104; source: design/engine-disagreements.md "Tester questions"). One checklist item per question; record result, date and tool.


Each body is entered in the tester's editor for `https://example.com`; paths are
checked one per line. "Ours" is what our backend answers today.

**B1, Bing, class 2 (BOM).** Body: the bytes `EF BB BF`, then
`User-agent: *` / `Disallow: /b1/`. Profile Bingbot; path `/b1/x`. Disallow:
Bing skips a leading BOM, as Google does, and our scanner should too. Allow
(ours): the BOM spoils line 1. The editor may drop or keep the BOM, so record
whether it kept it; if it cannot carry one, the case needs a served file
(ROBO-ogwchglq) and is "not testable" in the editor.

**B2, Bing, class 3 (suffix).** Body: `User-agent: bingbot/2.0` /
`Disallow: /b2/slash/` / blank / `User-agent: bingbot 2.0` /
`Disallow: /b2/space/` / blank / `User-agent: bingbot*` / `Disallow: /b2/star/`
/ blank / `User-agent: *` / `Disallow: /b2/wild/`. Profile Bingbot; paths
`/b2/slash/x`, `/b2/space/x`, `/b2/star/x`, `/b2/wild/x`. Ours: only
`/b2/wild/x` disallowed. A disallowed suffix path means Bing reads that form as
`bingbot`, as Google does (and then `/b2/wild/x` becomes allowed).

**B3, Bing, class 6 (raw non-ASCII).** Body: `User-agent: bingbot` /
`Disallow: /b3/café`. Paths `/b3/caf%C3%A9` and `/b3/café` typed raw. Ours:
the escaped path allowed, the raw one disallowed. Escaped disallowed means
Bing escapes the rule, as Google does. Record the target the tester displays,
since it may escape a raw path itself.

**B4, Bing, classes 7 and 8 (CR).** Body with CR CR LF after each line:
`User-agent: bingbot` / `Disallow: /b4/`; a second body with lone CR. Path
`/b4/x`. Ours: allowed for both. Disallowed means Bing ends a line at CR. As
with B1, record whether the editor kept the bytes; if it normalizes line
endings, the case needs a served file.

**Y1, Yandex, class 2 (BOM).** Body: `EF BB BF`, then `User-agent: Yandex` /
`Disallow: /y1/`. Crawler Yandex; path `/y1/x`. Ours: allowed. Prohibited
means Yandex skips a leading BOM. Same editor caveat as B1.

**Y2, Yandex, class 3 (suffix).** Body: `User-agent: Yandex/1.0` /
`Disallow: /y2/slash/` / blank / `User-agent: Yandex*` / `Disallow: /y2/star/`
/ blank / `User-agent: Yandex, Other` / `Disallow: /y2/list/`. Crawler Yandex;
paths `/y2/slash/x`, `/y2/star/x`, `/y2/list/x`. Ours: all allowed. A
prohibited path means Yandex reads that form as `Yandex`. (The space form is
already observed: not matched.)

**Y3, Yandex, class 4 (whitespace before the colon).** Body:
`User-agent: Yandex` / `Disallow : /y3/space` / `Disallow\t: /y3/tab` (a tab) /
`Disallow: /y3/control`. Paths `/y3/space`, `/y3/tab`, `/y3/control`. Ours:
only `/y3/control` prohibited. Prohibited space or tab paths mean Yandex trims
the field name, as Google and Bing do. Record the analyzer's diagnostics.

**Y4, Yandex, class 6 (raw non-ASCII).** Body: `User-agent: Yandex` /
`Disallow: /y4/каталог` / `Disallow: /y4/café`. Paths
`/y4/%D0%BA%D0%B0%D1%82%D0%B0%D0%BB%D0%BE%D0%B3`, `/y4/каталог`,
`/y4/caf%C3%A9`, `/y4/café`. Ours: only the raw paths prohibited. Escaped
paths prohibited means Yandex escapes the rule; all allowed, with an analyzer
error, means Yandex drops the rule as the docs' Cyrillic ban suggests.

**Y5, Yandex, class 1 (stacked run).** Body: `User-agent: Yandex` /
`Crawl-delay: 5` / `User-agent: Other` / `Disallow: /y5/cd` / blank /
`User-agent: Yandex` / `# note` / `User-agent: Other` / `Disallow: /y5/comment`
/ blank / `User-agent: Yandex` / blank / `User-agent: Other` /
`Disallow: /y5/blank`. Paths `/y5/cd/x`, `/y5/comment/x`, `/y5/blank/x`.
Ours: all three prohibited (the stack holds). An allowed path means that line
ends the stack for Yandex, as `design/robotstxtbing-v2-spec.md` §9.3 claims, and
our Yandex backend would then contradict Yandex.

**Y6, Yandex, classes 7 and 8 (CR).** As B4, with `User-agent: Yandex` and
path `/y6/x`. Ours: allowed for both.

**Y7, Yandex, class 11 (escape case).** Body: `User-agent: Yandex` /
`Disallow: /y7/a%3cb`. Paths `/y7/a%3cb`, `/y7/a%3Cb`. Ours: the lower-case
path prohibited, the upper-case one allowed. The reverse means Yandex
upper-cases the rule's escape, as Google and Bing do; both prohibited means it
ignores escape case.

**Y8, Yandex, class 12 (empty value).** Body: `User-agent: Yandex` /
`User-agent:` / `Disallow: /y8/`. Path `/y8/x`. Ours: allowed. Prohibited means
Yandex skips the empty value and keeps the group.

`Allow: /b5/a%3cb` / `Disallow: /b5/a%3Cb`. Path `/b5/a%3Cb`. Ours: allowed
(Bing upper-cases the Allow's escape, both rules are 9 bytes and Allow wins a
tie). Disallowed means Bing does not compose its escape upper-casing with its
tie rule.

**B6, Bing, precedence ties: wildcards.** Four bodies, each
`User-agent: bingbot` and one pair: `Allow: /b6/a*` / `Disallow: /b6/ab`, path

`Allow: /b6/c$` / `Disallow: /b6/c*`, path `/b6/c`; `Allow: /b6/d$e` /
`Disallow: /b6/d*ex`, path `/b6/d$ex`. Ours: the first three allowed (a tie,
since Bing ranks by the rule's raw byte length, `*` and `$` included), the last
disallowed (8 bytes against 7). A disallowed `/b6/ab` means Bing drops `*`
from the length. A disallowed `/b6/xyb` means it drops `*` or a final `$`. A
disallowed `/b6/c` means it drops a final `$` but counts `*` (dropping both
still ties). An allowed `/b6/d$ex` means it drops `*` but counts an inner `$`,
as Yandex does (7 against 7). Record the target the tester displays for
`/b6/d$ex`, since it may escape `$`.

**B7, Bing, precedence ties: two groups.** Body: `User-agent: bingbot` /
`Allow: /b7/` / blank / `User-agent: bingbot` / `Disallow: /b7/`; a second
body with the two rules swapped. Path `/b7/x`. Ours: allowed for both (the
groups merge, and Allow wins the tie). Disallowed for one body only means Bing
breaks a tie across groups by group order.

**Y9, Yandex, precedence ties: two groups.** As B7, with `User-agent: Yandex`
and `/y9/`; path `/y9/x`. Ours: allowed for both.

**Y10, Yandex, precedence ties: an inner `$`.** Two bodies, each
`User-agent: Yandex` and one pair: `Allow: /y10/a$b` / `Disallow: /y10/a*bx`,
path `/y10/a$bx`; `Disallow: /y10/c$d$` / `Allow: /y10/c$d`, path `/y10/c$d`.
Ours: allowed for both (an inner `$` counts as one byte, `*` and a final `$`
none, so each pair counts 8 and 8). Prohibited means Yandex reads an inner `$`
otherwise. Record the target the tester displays, since it may escape `$`.

## ROBO-bsloeclp: Validator: explain redirect, transport and safety outcomes per engine (robots frame gains terminal_redirect_reason)

**Status:** done

### Description

Why: ROBO-ybzbxfml (settled 2026-11-09) gives each HTTP status class its own validator diagnostic and crawl explanation, but leaves transport, SSRF and redirect outcomes on `acquisition_failed`. Explaining a redirect outcome per engine needs the terminal redirect reason: over_budget reads as 404 for Google, loop and no_location are documentation gaps, and downgrade is a safety refusal. The public `robots_fetch()` robots frame does not carry it, and parsing `error_message` would be fragile.

Scope:
- In: add `terminal_redirect_reason` (and, if needed, `safety_block_reason`) to the robots frame of `robots_fetch()` and `allowed_by_robots_*()`, as an additive column with a NEWS line. Then give redirect, transport and safety outcomes their own validator codes and engine explanations, in the same way as ROBO-ybzbxfml.
- Out: changing fetch behavior.

Acceptance criteria: the columns exist and are documented, each redirect/transport/safety outcome class has its own code and explanation, and tests cover each class.

Dependencies: ROBO-ybzbxfml.

## ROBO-bukqpjli: Matcher seam slice A: one batch interface, generic dispatch, Google adapter

**Status:** done | **Parent:** tlvrxtvbuezxgyuierfybahgvjojrcpi

### Description

Why
Slice A of candidate 1 in ROBO-tlvrxtvb. `evaluate_rows_v1` (`R/engine-contract-v1.R`) dispatches on the engine name in several places, and Google is called per row through `match_backend_v1`, which re-validates the registry on every row. `design/engine-contract-v1.md` says a new backend needs only a registry entry; today it does not. The owner's rulings on Q1-Q7 (2026-10-21) apply.

Gate: [USER] only because of the robotstxtr hold (SEOR-ajvckndx, seor tracker): nothing that ships lands on robotstxtr main until CRAN decides on 0.3.1. Branch work before that is fine; the merge waits. Drop the gate when SEOR-ajvckndx closes.

Scope (in)
- One batch interface for every matcher backend: `match(bodies, urls, tokens) -> decision frame`.
- Generic grouping, dispatch and scattering in `evaluate_rows_v1`, with no dispatch on engine names.
- A Google adapter behind the interface, still matching row by row inside. It keeps row order, truncates before grouping, keeps each row's own truncation flag, and leaves `matched_rule_value_raw` NULL for Google rows.
- The registry passed in as an internal argument to `evaluate_rows_v1`, defaulting to the validated production registry (Q3). Not on the public functions.
- A runtime check of adapter output: row count and the 12 required columns, failing loudly like `validate_matcher_status_v2` (Q6).
- A root `CONTEXT.md` glossary (matcher backend, matcher adapter, decision frame, ...) and `^CONTEXT\.md$` in `.Rbuildignore` (Q7).
- `design/engine-contract-v1.md` ("Registering another matcher backend") corrected to match.

Scope (out)
- The shared Yandex/Bing batch module (slice B).
- Any behavior change. Google parse-once and populated raw values come later as separate changes (Q2). Candidates 3 and 7 stay deferred.

Contract (Q4, Q5)
- An adapter returns one row per input, in order, with `matcher_status`, `url_decision`, `reason`, `matched_line`, `matched_rule_type`, `matched_rule_value`, `matcher_input_bytes`, `matcher_body_truncated`, `error_stage`, `error_class`, `error_message` and `matched_rule_value_raw` (list column). Extras (`native_*` columns, the `n_parse_calls` attribute) are allowed and ignored.
- Per-row outcomes are always rows. An adapter aborts only on an internal invariant violation, and the evaluator does not catch it.

Acceptance criteria
- v1 output is byte-identical to main for every engine on the existing test corpus.
- No engine-name dispatch is left in `evaluate_rows_v1`.
- Tests swap engines with a fake registry, not `local_mocked_bindings(match_google_v1=...)`.
- A shared test helper runs the adapter-output check on Google, Yandex, Bing and the fake.
- New test files are named after this issue's id.

Verification
- The pre-push verify gate passes.
- A before/after identical() comparison of `robots_evaluate_*_v1` output over the test fixtures, recorded in the MR.

Dependencies
- SEOR-ajvckndx (seor tracker): CRAN's decision on robotstxtr 0.3.1. Cross-project, so this gate holds it.
- Shares no files with the ssrfr switch (candidate 4): it may run alongside the switch and never holds it up. If 0.4.0's scope grows, it moves to the following release.

## ROBO-bwpacxtq: wildcard_rules_not_inherited under a named full block reports only lost Allow exceptions

**Status:** done

### Description

### Why

The validator check on the corpus (ROBO-uhutmvlr) found `wildcard_rules_not_inherited` far noisier than the 2026-11-09 prediction. A large share of its firings lose nothing in effect: a named group that blocks everything (`Disallow: /`) is flagged for the `*` group's Disallows, which a full block makes moot.

Reproduction (synthesized):

```
User-agent: *
Disallow: /admin/
User-agent: ExampleBot
Disallow: /
```

`robots_validate_text()` reports `wildcard_rules_not_inherited` listing `/admin/` for ExampleBot. ExampleBot is already blocked from `/admin/`.

### Decision needed

A `*` Allow exception, e.g. `Allow: /public/` in the `*` group, is still lost under a named full block, and the crawler then cannot reach a path the site may have meant to open. Options:

1. Suppress the diagnostic entirely when the named group is a full block.
2. Under a full block, report only the `*` group's Allow rules that are lost, never its Disallows. **(Recommended: it keeps the one case that changes access and drops the moot ones.)**
3. Keep the current behavior and document the noise.

### Acceptance criteria

- The chosen option is implemented and pinned with the reproduction above plus an Allow-exception variant.
- design/ text describing the diagnostic is updated to match.

### Decision (settled)

Option 2. Under a named full block, report only the `*` group's lost Allow rules and drop its lost Disallows (they cannot strengthen a full block). Define 'full block' conservatively from the effective named group (including any groups the engine merges): a root-wide Disallow (`/`, or an engine-equivalent form such as `/*` on google) and no non-empty Allow the parser keeps. An empty Allow counts only if the parser ignores it. Any valid non-empty Allow of the group's own disables the shortcut. Describe the retained Allows as possibly lost exceptions, not mistakes, since a stricter named policy may be deliberate. RFC 9309's implicit /robots.txt allowance means 'full block' describes the explicit rules only. Defer broader subsumption filtering (a named Disallow covering a lost path). Precedence and Allows make it unsafe for now. The diagnostic output changes, so add a NEWS bullet.

Settled 2026-11-11: the maintainer delegated this decision to Claude and Codex (GPT-6.1-Sol, high effort) and accepted their agreement as the answer.

### Comments

## ROBO-cbbyzfvf: [PARKED] Screaming Frog robots.txt conformance study (client, not an engine)

**Status:** todo

### Description

Parked 2026-09-27 by the maintainer (fleet groom ROBO-lsbdefbm): a conformance study (analysis and vendor contact), not package code. Start only on an instruction naming this issue.

Idea captured 2026-07-24; not scheduled. Pick up after the Bing release verification (ROBO-xgjvnfii).

### Motivation

robotstxtr's audience is SEOs, and the crawler most of them actually run is Screaming Frog SEO Spider.
Google/Bing/Yandex answer "what will the search engine do"; Screaming Frog answers "what will my audit
tool tell me the search engine does". Where those two disagree, an SEO ships a wrong recommendation.
That gap is the deliverable.

### Framing decision (settled up front)

**Screaming Frog is NOT an engine. It is a client.** It must never become a value in
`matcher_backend` or `robots_policy_ruleset`.

Rationale, grounded in `design/engine-profiles.md` §1: that document already refuses to synthesise a
Bing status policy because no primary source publishes one — every cell is `documentation_gap`, and
explicitly *not* synthesised from RFC. Screaming Frog is strictly worse off than Bing: closed source,
no spec, no published conformance claim, and behaviour that can change silently on any release. Under
ADR-009 §0 tagging, every cell of a hypothetical `sf` profile would be `inferred` from black-box
observation. That is a standard the project has already declined to meet.

So the output is an **observational dataset in its own namespace**, with its own provenance manifest
(SF version, capture date, config hash) — never an engine profile, no schema revision, no
`matcher_backend` addition, no availability change.

Deliverable, stated as the sentence it should support:

> "Here are the N robots.txt constructs where Screaming Frog's verdict differs from Googlebot's, so
> your audit reports the wrong thing."

A null result ("SF agrees with Google everywhere we probed") is equally publishable and is reached
cheaply.

### Path 1 — source code: NO

Screaming Frog is closed-source Java and its EULA prohibits reverse engineering. Decompiling is off
the table, and it would poison the evidence chain anyway — nothing derived that way could be cited in
a `PROVENANCE.dcf`.

Two legitimate substitutes, both cheap, both worth doing before any harness work:

1. **Just ask them.** "Which robots.txt parser does the Spider use?" is a normal support question and
   the team is approachable. A one-line answer can collapse this entire project.
2. **Fingerprint the parser family rather than read it.** SF is Java. The dominant open Java
   implementation is `crawler-commons` `SimpleRobotRulesParser` (Apache-2.0, used by Nutch and
   StormCrawler), whose divergences from Google's C++ matcher are known and enumerable. This is a
   HYPOTHESIS, not a fact — but it is testable with ~10 probes. If it lands, we get an open reference
   implementation to diff against for free, with zero black-box inference.

### Path 2 — probes: YES

Reuse the shape of the Yandex corpus work (`inst/yandex-corpus/`: byte-pinned bodies, `cases.json`
with `expected.decision` / `expected.source` / `expected.matched_rule`, `PROVENANCE.dcf`). Same
discipline, separate namespace.

Discriminating cases that separate Google's matcher from typical alternatives:

- longest-match vs first-match precedence
- Allow / Disallow tie-break at equal length (Google: least restrictive)
- `$` end-anchor and `*` wildcard support
- empty `Disallow:` = allow all
- missing leading slash on a path value
- user-agent group selection: token match vs substring match; case sensitivity
- multiple groups with the same UA — merged or first-wins
- percent-encoding / UTF-8 path normalisation (historically the richest divergence area)
- malformed input recovery: missing colon, typo'd directive name, orphan directive before any
  `User-agent`, BOM, CRLF, mid-line comments
- >500KiB truncation (Google's documented limit)

### Path 3 — harness design

A robots.txt applies per origin, so **one fixture = one origin**. Simplest robust approach: a single
small local server binding N ports on `127.0.0.1`, one fixture per port, then drive SF in **list mode**
with a URL list spanning all origins — no link graph to construct.

Two complementary modes:

- **GUI Custom robots.txt tester** — reports the *matched line*, not just allow/deny. This is the only
  way to check rule attribution, which is what our corpora record in `matched_rule`. Use for the
  discriminator spike and for anything surprising.
- **Headless CLI** (`--headless`, `--crawl-list`, `--export-tabs`, `--config`) — bulk sweep producing
  CSV. Blocked URLs surface as `Blocked by Robots.txt` in Internal / Response Codes.

Gotchas that will produce wrong data if missed:

- **`Show internal URLs blocked by robots.txt` must be enabled** in the robots.txt config, or blocked
  URLs never appear in the export at all — and absence reads as "allow". This is the single most
  likely way to silently corrupt the dataset.
- **SF's User-Agent setting selects the robots group.** The default UA obeys `Screaming Frog SEO
  Spider` groups; set it to Googlebot and it obeys Googlebot groups. Minimum two runs. The
  UA-selection probes are among the most interesting cases and are meaningless without this.
- **Menu paths and CLI flags shift between releases** — verify against the installed version rather
  than trusting the notes above.
- **This can never run in CI.** Licensed desktop app, needs a machine with a GUI install. The artifact
  is a committed snapshot with version + capture-date provenance, plus a drift-detection test that is
  skipped on CRAN and on CI.

### Path 4 — fetch policy probes (possibly the higher-value half)

A local server also exercises the L0 / §3 / §4 fetch-policy layer of `design/engine-profiles.md`,
which **no static corpus can test**: 4xx → allow-all, 5xx → disallow-all, redirect chains including
cross-authority, >500KiB truncation, timeouts. Serve a 503 for `/robots.txt` and observe whether SF
crawls the site anyway.

This is where engines genuinely differ and where SEOs actually get burned, so it may be worth more
than the matcher probes. It also generalises: the same server harness works for any desktop or cloud
crawler (Sitebulb, JetOctopus, Ahrefs, Semrush, Botify), so build it tool-agnostic — probe corpus in,
"what did the tool say" CSV out.

### Sequencing

Do NOT build infrastructure first. Sequence is: ask them → 1-hour discriminator spike in the GUI
tester → only then decide whether the full harness is worth building. The spike alone tells us whether
SF is Google-equivalent, crawler-commons-shaped, or its own thing.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-24 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Filed 2026-07-24 from a design conversation; parked, not scheduled.

Entry point when picking this up: **SF1 (ask them) and SF2 (1-hour GUI spike) run in parallel — nothing else starts until SF2 returns a verdict.** SF3 depends on SF2; SF5 depends on SF3+SF4. SF4 is independent and can be pulled forward if the fetch-policy angle looks more interesting than the matcher angle.

The one framing commitment not to relitigate: Screaming Frog is a client, not an engine. No `matcher_backend` value, no `robots_policy_ruleset` value, no schema revision. Rationale in the parent description.

#### 2026-09-27 — bartek@turczynski.pl

## ROBO-cbzemsnq: No CI check for roxygen/Rd drift — stale generated docs can land silently

**Status:** done

### Description

Found during the ROBO-iithclei / ROBO-xmtazvxg orchestrate run (PR #55).

man/robots_engine_contract_v2.Rd had been stale in main since c29b9f0 (#51): the roxygen comment in R/engine-contract-v1.R was reflowed to satisfy the 80-char linter, but devtools::document() was never re-run, so the generated Rd kept the old prose. It sat undetected until the next docs change ran document() and the diff appeared out of nowhere.

Root cause: nothing in the verify chain compares man/ and NAMESPACE against what roxygen2 would generate from R/. dev/verify.sh runs lintr::lint_package() + R CMD check --as-cran; neither detects generated-doc drift, because a stale Rd is still perfectly valid Rd.

Suggested fix: add a drift check to dev/verify.sh (and therefore CI) — run devtools::document() against a clean export and fail if git reports any diff in man/ or NAMESPACE. Cheap, deterministic, and catches the whole class. Needs the roxygen2 version pinned to Config/roxygen2/version (currently 8.0.0) so a local version skew does not produce false failures.

Low priority: the drift is cosmetic when it happens, but it silently erodes the accuracy of published docs and creates confusing diffs in unrelated PRs.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-24 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Implemented on branch chore/docs-drift-gate; PR #59 open, CI running.

dev/check-docs-drift.R regenerates man/ + NAMESPACE and diffs them against what is committed, reporting changed / missing / stale files plus a unified diff, and exiting 1 on drift.

Two design decisions worth recording:

1. Roxygen runs through its DEFAULT pkgload loader — the same one devtools::document() uses — so what the gate demands is exactly what the documented fix produces. I measured the cheaper load_code='source' path: byte-identical output today and ~24x faster (0.75s vs 17.8s, no compile). Rejected anyway, because it evaluates package code differently, so a future dynamic doc could make the gate reject a tree that document() considers clean — an unfixable failure, the worst kind for a gate. Verified both loaders produce output byte-identical to committed HEAD.

2. roxygen2 version checked for EXACT equality against Config/roxygen2/version up front (the issue called for this). Output formatting shifts between releases, so an unpinned runner reports version skew as drift; roxygen2 also silently rewrites that DESCRIPTION field when it is the newer one. The CI job reads the pin from DESCRIPTION and installs that exact version, so the pin has one source of truth.

Wiring: peer 'docs' job in verify.yml (no needs:, runs in parallel, independently attributable) + dev/verify.sh ahead of the check (cheaper, so it fails fast) + CONTRIBUTING.md. The local gate gives the drift check its OWN git-archive export — verified empirically that pkgload leaves 30 .o files and a .so in src/, which would contaminate the R CMD build the check runs from.

Verified: clean tree passes; reflowed roxygen title detected with correct diff; deleted .Rd reported missing; orphan generated .Rd reported stale; version-skew branch refuses with actionable instructions. Full dev/verify.sh end-to-end exit 0, R CMD check clean apart from the pre-existing CRAN-incoming-feasibility NOTE.

#### 2026-07-24 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

CI caught a real gap in the first version of the docs job: it died with 'The decor package(s) are required for this functionality' before diffing anything.

Cause: pkgload runs cpp11::cpp_register() for a LinkingTo: cpp11 package before compiling, and that helper needs brio, cli, decor, desc, glue, tibble, vctrs. Those are Suggests of *cpp11*, not dependencies of robotstxtr, so setup-r-dependencies never installed them. Nothing else in CI needs them either — R CMD check builds from the committed src/cpp11.cpp rather than regenerating it — so no existing job would ever have surfaced this. It passed locally because a machine set up to run devtools::document() already has them.

Fixed by installing exactly cpp11:::get_cpp_register_needs() in the docs job, recorded as the source of truth, and noting the same requirement in CONTRIBUTING (it applies to running devtools::document() at all, not just to the gate).

Worth noting this validates rather than undermines the pkgload choice: the gate demands the same toolchain the documented fix demands, so a contributor who can fix drift can also run the gate. Had it used the cheaper source loader, CI would have been green while needing a strictly smaller environment than the fix instruction it prints.

Separately, an unrelated transient: one pre-push verify run failed with 'no package called punycoder'. Not a robotstxtr defect — punycoder 1.2.1.9000 (a dev build) was being reinstalled locally mid-session; the library dir is timestamped inside the session window and everything went green after, with no code change.

#### 2026-07-24 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Merged as 4f985f1 (PR #59, squash). All 12 checks green, including the new 'man/ and NAMESPACE in sync with roxygen comments' job (1m59s). Branch deleted local+remote. Closing.

## ROBO-cdsyatry: Attribute robots.txt blocks to versioned upstream lists and generator templates

**Status:** todo | **Parent:** qxalfvpbilkbedprrvlckauitwbujhgc

### Description

### Why

Bot-name counts are strongly affected by reusable lists. In the study, 2,486 of 4,464 interpreted tokens occur only in files naming at least 100 agents. Four publishers explicitly credit Mitchell Krog's Ultimate Bot Blocker with retained versions from 2021 through 2024; three link Perishable Press's Ultimate AI Block List. Whole files may layer Cloudflare-labelled content, a shared blocker and a separate WordPress plugin block. Attribution must be block-level.

### Scope

In: deterministic extraction of explicit source URLs, generator/plugin markers, begin/end boundaries and version labels; block fingerprints for exact bytes, normalized directive sequences, ordered agent runs and unordered token sets. Match frozen historical upstream versions and identify edited-descendant candidates with stated deterministic similarity rules. Use long shared sequences and unusual spellings as evidence; similarity or common popular bots alone do not establish an origin.

Initial candidate sources: Mitchell Krog's apache-ultimate-bad-bot-blocker robots.txt and Perishable Press's Ultimate AI Block List; source plugins/CMS templates and Cloudflare-managed sections when their exact templates and reuse terms can be pinned. Store source revision/hash, licence/reuse disposition, compared span, matched evidence and match coverage. All ordinary analysis is offline. Upstream refresh is explicit maintenance work, never automatic URL dereferencing from input files.

Out: saying identical blocks prove a publisher copied another publisher; treating a marker as proof of a currently installed product; assigning one source to an entire layered file; treating an upstream version date as an installation date; or inferring intent from template membership. Unknown must remain possible.

### Acceptance criteria

- Output distinguishes explicit credit, verified content/version match, inferred shared ancestry and unknown. Credits that disagree with content are visible.
- Several sources/versions can be attached to disjoint or overlapping spans in one file, with additions and unmatched material retained.
- Explain normalization, thresholds and their limitations. Changing effective directives is not hidden by a coarse fingerprint.
- Reproduce the credited samples and uncredited/edited variants using frozen distributable fixtures; quantify false matches with small common blocks and sorted-list counterexamples.
- Historical observations may constrain first-seen dates but do not claim the original author or copying direction. Output schema is reusable outside this corpus.

### Verification

Positive fixtures for exact and credited-but-edited blocks, mixed-source files, renamed markers and old versions; negative fixtures for common bot subsets and misleading credits. Stable reruns from pinned inputs and package gate.

### Dependencies

ROBO-lfxjkycf, public declaration inventory. Registry enrichment is complementary but not a prerequisite for literal-block attribution.

### Sources

https://github.com/mitchellkrogza/apache-ultimate-bad-bot-blocker
https://perishablepress.com/ultimate-ai-block-list/
Study evidence: news-ai-access/design/specs/robots-inventory.md; www.creators.com, www.xronos.gr, coastalvirginiamag.com, www.tremblantexpress.com; correiocidadania.com.br, www.latribuna.hn and www.thezimbabwedaily.com.

## ROBO-ctdkqawi: Validator misses rules a NUL hides when other rules parse

**Status:** done

### Description

Found in the review of ROBO-igrkabdb, at the boundary of its approach (B): the NUL-free count runs only when the raw parse finds no rule.

When the raw parse already reads at least one rule, the validator does not report rules that Google's matcher reads only once the NULs are dropped. Two synthesized cases:
- `User-agent: *\nDisallow: /private\n\0Disallow: /\n`: Google blocks the whole site, yet only `nul_byte@3` is reported.
- `User-\0agent: *\nDisallow: /x\n`: the result is `rule_without_user_agent@2` and `missing_user_agent`, although Google disallows /x.

Both cases behave the same on main before ROBO-igrkabdb.

Done when: the validator reports a rule or group that only the NUL-free read gives Google's matcher (per line, or one lineless summary), pinned on example.com fixtures. Bing and Yandex read raw bytes, so the wording must stay Google-specific.

## ROBO-cthdyvlk: robots_fetch(): keep Retry-After (and decide on other response headers) in the fetch row

**Status:** done

### Description

Why: `robots_fetch()` returns status, `fetch_outcome` and the body, but no
response headers. A caller that gets a 429 or 503 for robots.txt cannot honor
`Retry-After` (RFC 9110 §10.2.3), and RFC 9309 §2.3.1.3/2.3.1.4 handling of
unreachable or rate-limited robots.txt needs to know when to come back. For a
robots.txt diagnostic tool this is a gap: the answer that says "wait" is lost.

Found in news-ai-access (fp NEWS-xngvdyzi, 2026-11-04): its fetch queue honors
`Retry-After` for homepage GETs but has to leave robots.txt 429s to a
second-day re-probe because `robots_fetch()` drops the header.

Scope:
- In:
  - [ ] Keep `Retry-After` from the final response of a robots.txt fetch, as
    a new column on `robots_fetch()$robots` (raw field value), plus a parsed
    delay in seconds (delta-seconds or HTTP-date; NA when absent or invalid).
  - [ ] Decide whether to keep more of the final response's headers (for
    example `content-type`, which the HTML-shell rule also needs) as a list
    column; record the decision.
  - [ ] Same fields reachable from `robots_validate_url()` /
    `allowed_by_robots_url()` evidence where they carry the fetch row.
  - [ ] Tests with mocked responses: 429 and 503 with delta-seconds, with an
    HTTP-date, with an invalid value, and without the header.
- Out: retrying inside robotstxtr (the caller owns its queue).

Relation: ROBO-jbralthm moves acquisition to ssrfr; ssrfr's response carries
headers, so whichever lands second keeps the field. Not a dependency.

Acceptance criteria: a 429 with `Retry-After: 120` yields the raw value and
120 seconds in the fetch row; the engine-contract schema notes the new
columns.

Verification: the mocked tests; `R CMD check` clean.


### Comments

#### 2026-11-05 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Starting (burndown 2026-11-05 afternoon, wave 1): sub-agent keeps Retry-After in the fetch row. Branch feature/ROBO-cthdyvlk-retry-after, worktree /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-bartturczynski-Projects-news-ai-access/82c54f93-1ce2-4a4c-bfda-900089d55243/scratchpad/wt/ROBO-cthdyvlk. ## ROBO-cufxicmz: Validator: warn when a named group's Allow reopens a path that User-agent: * disallows

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

Under a full block (`Disallow: /`), sites list Allow prefixes for the sections a named crawler
may read. When `User-agent: *` disallows a narrower path under one of those prefixes, the named
crawler does not inherit that Disallow (RFC 9309 §2.2.1), so the Allow reopens it. The file reads
as "search stays blocked for everyone" and does the opposite for the named crawlers.

Observed on https://www.bloomberg.com/robots.txt (fetched 2026-11-17): the `*` group disallows
`/company/search/`, `/professional/search/`, `/latam/search/`, `/faq/search/` and `/tc/search/`
(lines 12-25). Six named groups (lines 34, 73, 94, 107, 216, 250) hold `Disallow: /` plus
`Allow: /company`, `/professional`, `/latam`, `/faq` and `/tc`. Tested with the Google backend:
ClaudeBot `/company/search/foo` → allow (line 98); Claude-SearchBot `/tc/search/q` → allow
(line 116). Today the only signal is one of 21 `wildcard_rules_not_inherited` info rows, where
these Disallows sit in a truncated list ("…and 15 more").

### Scope

In: a new warning code (working name `allow_reopens_wildcard_disallow`), one row per named
group (after merging repeated groups), anchored on its first User-agent line. It fires when a
concrete witness path exists that is:
- effectively disallowed under the `*` group, after resolving all of that group's rules
  (a `*` Allow can cancel a `*` Disallow);
- effectively allowed under the named group, after resolving all of its rules; and
- blocked for the named group if its Allow rules were removed (the Allow causes the opening,
  so an already permissive group is the other issue's case, not this one).

Decisions use the selected profile's longest-match and Allow-wins-ties rules. The message names
the reopening Allow line(s) and the `*` Disallow line(s), bounded like
`wildcard_rules_not_inherited`.

Out: matcher changes; inferring intent beyond the witness; any candidate where a `*` or `$`
pattern, in either group, could change either decision and the overlap cannot be decided
exactly (skip, never approximate).

### Acceptance criteria

- Fires on the Bloomberg shape: full block + Allow prefix + narrower `*` Disallow under it.
- Fires when the named group restates the Disallow but adds a more specific Allow under it.
- Silent when: the named group's effective rules block every witness; a `*` Allow cancels the
  `*` Disallow; the `*` Disallow is under none of the group's Allows; the group has no Allow;
  the group allows the path without any Allow (no full block).
- Fixtures for prefix boundaries (`/tc` vs `/tcx/search/`), case, a query in the witness, and
  percent-encoded `/`, using the selected profile's matching.
- Uses the group model of `wildcard_inheritance_diagnostics()`, including merged repeated
  groups and stacked User-agent lines.
- `wildcard_rules_not_inherited` keeps its severity and detection condition; its listed rules
  exclude those this warning reports for the same group.
- Docs table in `R/robots_validate.R`, `design/linter-set.md`, NEWS one line.

### Verification

Focused `robots_validate_text()` fixtures for each case above, the Bloomberg shape reduced to
about 10 lines. Each positive fixture is cross-checked with `robots_evaluate_text_v1()` on the
Google backend: the witness is allowed for the named token and disallowed for an unnamed one.
Merge gate.

### Dependencies

None. Shares `wildcard_inheritance_diagnostics()` with the wildcard-split issue. Related:
ROBO-bwpacxtq, ROBO-gkuuwbgc. Reviewed with GPT-6.1-Sol (medium) on 2026-11-17.


### Comments

#### 2026-11-17 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Shares wildcard_inheritance_diagnostics() with ROBO-pbwijkdq (loosening groups, row merging); coordinate the two.

#### 2026-11-17 — bartek@turczynski.pl

A second real file with this shape: https://www.washingtonpost.com/robots.txt (fetched 2026-11-17, Google backend, 188c0a6). Fifteen named groups have `Disallow: /` plus `Allow: /creativegroup/` and `Allow: /advertising/` (ClaudeBot at lines 177-180). `*` disallows `/*_print.html` (line 2) and 22 other `/*_…` suffix patterns.

Example path: `/creativegroup/a_print.html` → ClaudeBot allow L179, Claude-SearchBot (on `*`) disallow L2.

The `*` Disallow here is a wildcard suffix pattern, not a literal prefix under the Allow. The example-path condition in the scope covers it, so add it to the fixtures.




## ROBO-cvpkzckn: Validator: identify UTF-16/32 files without conflating encoding with UTF-8 byte validity

**Status:** done

### Description

### Why

BOM-less UTF-16LE ASCII content can currently report documents$encoding as utf-8 while NUL errors and rules_after_nul_removal flag its hazards. This is byte validity, not reliable identification of the source encoding.

### Scope

In: recognize UTF-16LE/BE and UTF-32LE/BE BOM signatures and conservatively identify likely BOM-less UTF-16/32 where byte structure supports it. Give actionable re-save-as-UTF-8 advice, with explicit certainty and raw evidence. Keep UTF-8 validity separate from inferred source encoding.
Out: general charset detection, automatic decoding/repair, matcher changes, identifying arbitrary binary data as text with certainty.

### Acceptance criteria

- Detect full BOM signatures with correct precedence, especially UTF-32LE versus its UTF-16LE prefix; handle short/partial signatures safely.
- Pin LE/BE fixtures, with/without BOM, short ambiguous bodies, valid UTF-8 and unrelated NUL-bearing/binary data.
- A likely-encoding finding is labelled heuristic and does not assert certainty or intent. Valid UTF-8 is not alone sufficient evidence of the intended encoding.
- Preserve existing NUL, invalid_utf8, BOM and hidden-rule evidence. Choose and document a backward-compatible representation of byte validity versus inferred encoding.
- Both raw text validation and URL-fetched bytes expose the diagnostic; character inputs already transcoded by R do not claim original file identification.

### Verification

Focused byte fixtures, regression for the ASCII UTF-16LE reproduction, existing encoding/NUL tests and merge gate. Update help, catalog and NEWS.

### Dependencies

None. Related completed issues: ROBO-igrkabdb and ROBO-xuusttbp; preserve their current semantics.


### Delivery

Requested by the owner on 2026-11-16 following the robots.txt validator audit. Standalone outcome; no parent or artificial ordering dependency. Do not make this a new 0.4.0 release blocker without an explicit release-scope decision. Preserve raw evidence and distinguish standards conformance, observed crawler behavior and heuristics.

## ROBO-dbvmxcfw: Validator: bind diagnostics once instead of per line (superlinear on many warnings)

**Status:** done

### Description

### Why

The ROBO-kormmfyg review measured validate_document_bytes() on files that draw one warning per line. Each per-line diagnostic goes through add_diagnostic() and a do.call(rbind) of data frames, which grows superlinearly. Two synthetic files show it:
- 20,000 lines with a lower-case escape: 18.6 s, against 2.7 s with the new check stubbed out.
- 20,000 lines missing a leading slash: 23 s, with no new code involved.

robots_validate_url() reads untrusted bodies of up to 500 KB, so a file with tens of thousands of short rule lines reaches this path.

### Scope

Collect diagnostics in a list, or in preallocated column vectors, and bind them once at the end, so validation time is linear in the number of diagnostics. Diagnostic order and content must not change: pin them on a synthetic file before the change.

### Acceptance

- 20,000 per-line warnings validate in time roughly linear in their number. Pin it with a structural or loose bound, not a tight wall-clock bound.
- Identical diagnostics on the existing test suite.

## ROBO-deehqhlc: Google fidelity: robotstxtr's Google paths match the pristine upstream engine on corpus and synthetic inputs

**Status:** done | **Parent:** fbbwepsvxhuarzilvvkeuamqiaswhohw

### Description

### Why

The Google backend wraps Google's open-source matcher, but robotstxtr adds layers around it: body truncation and complete-line windows, URL target extraction, empty-path normalization, metadata correlation, and three entry points (v1 facade, `allowed_by_robots_text()`, `allowed_by_robots_url()` with a supplied body). Any of these can drift from Google's engine.

### Scope

In:
- Reference: the pristine upstream Google engine at robotstxt-cpp's pinned SHA, built by its maintainer-only differential harness (lead builds it before dispatch and gives the agent the binary path).
- Feed identical inputs (harness `evaluate` path sets, all tokens) to the reference and to each Google path; compare decision and matched line.
- Group differences into classes; for each, a minimal synthesized fixture, a pinned test (current behavior, or a known-gap test naming its fp issue), and a verdict: our bug, or a deliberate robotstxtr choice already documented (cite it).
- Out: fixing bugs (the lead files one issue per class).

Privacy rule: see the corpus harness issue.

### Acceptance criteria

- The v1 google/google path shows no unexplained difference from the reference.
- Every difference class has a synthesized fixture, a test, and a verdict; bugs have fp issues.
- A short committed note in design/engine-profiles.md (or a linked design doc) records the method and the classes, with fixtures, no corpus figures.

### Verification

Pre-push gate; the reviewer reruns one class's fixture through the reference.

### Dependencies

The corpus harness; matcher seam slice B (ROBO-iwmtdutk), so the audit tests the refactored code.


### Comments

### Measured 2026-09-09

CRAN's complete rurl history, read from CRAN's own indexes:

    current  : 3.0.1   (published 2026-09-09)
    archived : 1.2.0

2.2.1 exists only as a git tag on `gitlab.com/bart-turczynski/rurl`. With no
`Remotes:` entry, a clean-environment install resolves rurl from CRAN, gets
3.0.1, and satisfies the floor by accident — the declared minimum itself is
unreachable. Any resolver asked for exactly 2.2.1 fails.

This is the same defect class as pagerankr's PAGE-tsbkxhoz (a floor naming a
version nobody can install), which was fixed there on 2026-09-09.

### Do

- Determine the real minimum rurl that robotstxtr passes against, running the
  suite against installable candidates, not against a version that cannot be
  fetched from CRAN. The CRAN candidate set is exactly `{1.2.0, 3.0.1}`.
- Correct `Imports:` to the lowest version that actually passes.

### Note on the likely answer

rurl 3.0.0 changed node identity and argument surface. In pagerankr, moving from
a local 3.0.0 build to CRAN 3.0.1 surfaced a NEW `get_clean_url` argument
(`credential_handling`). Whatever robotstxtr uses of rurl should be re-checked
against 3.0.1 rather than assumed compatible.

### Acceptance

- The declared rurl floor names a version CRAN has published.
- The suite has been run against that exact version, and passes.

## ROBO-dhwinnii: Document the Google v1 empty-value match (default_allow, no line)

**Status:** done

### Description

Why
The Google fidelity audit (ROBO-deehqhlc, class C1) found that when the matching Google rule has an empty value (`Disallow:` or `Allow:` with nothing after the colon), every robotstxtr Google path reports `reason = "default_allow"`, `matched_line = NA` and `matched_rule_type = "none"`. Google's own engine reports that line as the match. The decision is the same.

This is deliberate for the legacy paths: PRD §6.6 (the empty-path bullet of "Match metadata rules") and `normalize_ignored_empty_path()` in R/correlate_matches.R. On the v1 contract it is undocumented for Google rows. design/engine-contract-v1.md describes only the Yandex case, which reports `effective_empty_disallow` with the line, as does the v1 roxygen.

Scope
- State the Google rule in design/engine-contract-v1.md (next to the Yandex `effective_empty_disallow` paragraph) and in the v1 roxygen for `robots_evaluate_text_v1()` / `robots_evaluate_url_v1()` reason values.
- Docs only. Making Google v1 rows mirror Yandex's `effective_empty_disallow` would change a documented result and needs its own maintainer decision; it is not in scope here.

Acceptance
- The v1 contract and roxygen say what a Google row reports for an empty-value match, citing PRD §6.6.
- The pinned C1 test in tests/testthat/test-google-fidelity-deehqhlc.R is unchanged and still passes.

## ROBO-dwywkpes: Validator: advise investigating rendering dependencies when JavaScript is blocked

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

The owner requested an informational advisory for JavaScript blocking on 2026-11-16. Blocking scripts required to render page content can affect what Google sees; intentional restrictions on tracking or API endpoints may be appropriate. A .js suffix alone does not establish a rendering failure.

Live example: https://natu.shop/robots.txt, fetched 2026-11-16 through robotstxtr (HTTP 200, UTF-8 text/plain), blocks /cdn/wpm/*.js, /cart.js and /*/cart.js in the wildcard group, and /cdn/wpm/*.js in adsbot-google. Current validator provides no rendering advisory. This is a candidate pattern observation, not evidence that those endpoints are required for rendering or that this site's rendering is broken.

### Scope

In: a stable, bounded info-level advisory identifying Disallow patterns that can restrict JavaScript resources and inviting inspection of rendering dependencies. Account for applicable crawler groups and Allow exceptions; clearly distinguish static detection from confirmed resource denial or actual rendering impact.
Out: automatic removal of blocks; classifying tracking from filenames; crawling pages or fetching assets by default; running a browser/render audit; claiming every .js endpoint is a script; assuming all crawlers render JavaScript or inherit the wildcard group.

### Acceptance criteria

- Name relevant line(s), pattern(s) and the crawler scope established by the analysis, without applying AdsBot-only restrictions to Googlebot or restrictions for unrelated bots to Google rendering.
- Explain conditionally that blocking required scripts may impair rendering/indexing and suggest rendered-page/resource inspection. Acknowledge intentional tracking/API restrictions.
- Define conservative recognition for explicit .js paths and wildcard forms, including query suffix and end-anchor cases; avoid substring-only false positives such as unrelated path/query text.
- Respect comment cuts, active values, repeated-group merging, named/wildcard selection and known Allow overrides. Where effective blockage cannot be proven statically, call the finding a candidate restriction rather than invent a URL decision.
- Do not repeat one advisory per identical rule/group or produce an avalanche for broad blocks. Bound/group output and document its limits; no need to flag every Disallow: / as a JavaScript-specific concern.
- Pin synthesized fixtures for the natu.shop shapes, known overrides, wildcard/named crawler separation, tracking-like and endpoint-like names without invented classification, comments and ineffective full-URL rules. Both text and mocked URL validation behave consistently.
- Info never changes valid document status. Update code table, examples and NEWS. No new 0.4.0 release blocker without an explicit scope decision.

### Verification

Focused rule/group/exception fixtures and existing matching/validation regression tests, followed by repository merge gate. Tests use frozen synthetic bytes, not a live site or rendering service.

### Dependencies

None; standalone outcome. Related parameter-blocking advisory has no ordering dependency.

### Source

https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/javascript/javascript-seo-basics


### Comments

#### 2026-11-17 — bartek@turczynski.pl

A second shape for this advisory: directory blocks with extension-limited Allow exceptions. On https://sklep.kfd.pl/robots.txt (PrestaShop, fetched 2026-11-17, Google backend, 188c0a6), `Disallow: /modules/` (line 62) and `Disallow: /js/` (line 58) are opened only by `Allow: */modules/*.css`, `*.js`, `*.png`, `*.jpg` (lines 4-7) and `Allow: /js/jquery/*` (line 8):

- `/modules/ps_x/views/a.css` → allow L4
- `/modules/ps_x/views/a.svg` → disallow L62
- `/modules/ps_x/views/font.woff2` → disallow L62
- `/js/jquery/jquery.min.js` → allow L8
- `/js/theme.js` → disallow L58

The validator reports nothing for the whole file. A check keyed to explicit-extension patterns may miss `/js/theme.js`, whose blocking rule is `/js/`. It's worth deciding whether the scope extends to directory blocks and to other render resources (CSS, fonts, SVG), or stays JS-pattern only and says so.




## ROBO-dxrljrde: SSRF guard: metadata hostname with a trailing dot passes

**Status:** done

### Description

The structural SSRF guard blocks the metadata hostname `metadata.google.internal` only on an exact, case-folded match (`R/ssrf.R`, `ssrf_classify_literal()`). The fully qualified spelling with a trailing dot (`metadata.google.internal.`, any case, with or without a port) passes under the default `ssrf_guard = TRUE`; DNS on GCP resolves it to the metadata server like the undotted name. Reproduced offline against `main`.

Fix: drop trailing dots from the host before the blocked-name comparison; regression tests for the dotted, upper-case, double-dot and `:port` spellings. robotstxtr and sitemapr share this guard code, so both get the same fix.

Scope checked: IP literals with a trailing dot (`127.0.0.1.`) are already classified; `0x7f.1.` and `127.1.` are names libcurl 8.5 sends to DNS (DNS-dependent, out of scope); `[::1].` is rejected by libcurl.

Confidential GitLab issue: bart-turczynski/robotstxtr#1.
