## ROBO-eslcxgfc: Pre-push verify chokes on live browser socket under _scratch/ (R CMD build copies tree before .Rbuildignore)

**Status:** done

### Description

### Symptom
`git push` is blocked whenever a browser profile is live under `_scratch/` (e.g. `_scratch/yandex-browser`). The pre-push `verify` hook runs `rcmdcheck::rcmdcheck(--as-cran)`, which invokes R CMD build. R CMD build copies the **entire** package working tree to a temp dir *before* applying `.Rbuildignore`, and the recursive copy chokes on the live Chrome/Yandex Unix-domain socket (a non-regular file). `_scratch/` being Rbuildignored does not help — the failure happens during the copy, before filtering.

### Impact
Recurs on every push while any browser using a profile under `_scratch/` is open — forces closing the browser to push.

### Root cause
R CMD build's copy-then-prune order + non-regular files in the working tree.

### Fix
Run the pre-push build/check against a clean `git archive HEAD` export in a temp dir instead of the working tree. That export contains only committed, tracked files — exactly what gets pushed and what CI checks out — so `_scratch/` (untracked/gitignored) and any sockets under it are never copied. This makes the local gate a truer mirror of CI.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-15 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Fixed in PR #21 (squash-merged to main, commit on main). Pre-push verify now builds/checks a clean 'git archive HEAD' export in a temp dir instead of the working tree, so live browser sockets under _scratch/ can no longer break R CMD build's copy step. Verified green end-to-end with a live Unix socket present under _scratch/yandex-browser/; also confirmed raw 'R CMD build .' reproduces the 'is a socket (not copied)' copy against the working tree. Added ^dev$ to .Rbuildignore.

## ROBO-fabvezjc: PRD §6.6 and body-decode.R misdescribe how Google's matcher reads a NUL

**Status:** done

### Description

Why
design/PRD.md §6.6 (the NUL paragraph) and the header comment of R/body-decode.R describe the upstream Google matcher as "byte-transparent". They say it reads `"\0Disallow: /x"` as the unknown directive `"\0disallow"`. The Google fidelity audit (ROBO-deehqhlc, class 5 in design/engine-profiles.md §5b) found otherwise. The vendored src/robots.cc copies each line into a buffer and parses it as a NUL-terminated C string (strchr, strlen). So:

- a NUL before a key makes the line read as empty;
- a NUL inside a value cuts the value at the NUL (`Disallow: /a\0b` becomes the rule `/a`).

The pristine reference build confirms both. robotstxtr's own behavior (remove every NUL, never truncate) is unchanged and stays a deliberate divergence. Only the description of the reference is wrong.

Scope
- Correct the reference's mechanism in PRD §6.6 and in the R/body-decode.R header comment, and cite §5b class 5.
- Docs and comments only; no behavior change.

Acceptance
- Neither passage calls the reference byte-transparent, and both describe the line-as-C-string reading, with the value cut as an example.


### Comments

Fixed in !103 (7b240f1): PRD §6.6, the R/body-decode.R header and the edge-case catalog now describe the reference as parsing each line as a C string, citing engine-profiles §5b class 5.




## ROBO-fbbmvbob: Google crawler-token fallback and the AdsBot `*` exemption, by default on the google ruleset

**Status:** done

### Description

### Decision needed (maintainer)

ROBO-mxsphtoo recorded (design/engine-profiles.md §5a, merged in !95) that Google's common-crawlers page lists a parent token for seven crawlers (Googlebot-Image, -Video, -News, Google-InspectionTool and Google-CloudVertexBot list `Googlebot`; GoogleOther-Image and -Video list `GoogleOther`), and says a crawler needs to match only one of its tokens. robotstxtr's `google` binding reads the caller's one token, so `Googlebot-Image` on a file with only a `Googlebot` group and a `*` group gets the `*` rules. Second divergence: AdsBot-Google, AdsBot-Google-Mobile, Mediapartners-Google and APIs-Google ignore `*` per Google, but the binding gives them `*` when they have no group; the vendored matcher ships `RobotsMatcher::disallow_ignore_global()` for that.

Options (§5a has the trade-offs):

1. Opt-in documented token map, default off: query the crawler's own token; when no specific group was seen, query the parent token; never merge the groups. The same opt-in could route the AdsBot family through `disallow_ignore_global()`. Changes matcher results and the published contract under the opt-in.
2. Leave it to the caller (docs only; the caller needs to know whether a specific group was seen, which the R API does not expose today).
3. Document only: add to the `allowed_by_robots_text()` roxygen that a token never reaches a parent token's group, and point to §5a.

Recommendation from the research: 3 now, plus 1 as an opt-in if crawler-level answers are wanted. The default must not change silently.

Why gated: choosing changes matcher behavior or the published contract, which is the maintainer's call (ROBO-mxsphtoo's planning comment, 2026-11-09).

### Decision (settled)

Option (b), the default for the `google` ruleset with a NEWS bullet, not an opt-in. (1) A crawler that lists a parent token in Google's common-crawlers documentation queries its own token first; when no group names it specifically, it queries the parent (Googlebot-Image, -Video, -News, Google-InspectionTool and Google-CloudVertexBot use `Googlebot`; GoogleOther-Image and -Video use `GoogleOther`). Groups are never merged. (2) AdsBot-Google, AdsBot-Google-Mobile, Mediapartners-Google and APIs-Google ignore `*` through the vendored `RobotsMatcher::disallow_ignore_global()`. Reason: the tool answers 'would this crawler be allowed', and Google documents this as its crawlers' behavior. Conditions: the token map is data citing Google's page (design/engine-profiles.md §5a); 'no specific group' is detected inside the binding, never inferred from an allow/deny result; the result records which token's group decided. Caveat: this makes `google` a crawler-aware layer above the matcher, which the contract must say explicitly. Policy or contract revision as design/engine-contract-v1.md requires.

Settled 2026-11-11: the maintainer delegated this decision to Claude and Codex (GPT-6.1-Sol, high effort) and accepted their agreement as the answer.

## ROBO-fdhmlvwm: Validator: warn when an identical Allow cancels a Disallow (Allow: / + Disallow: / is fully crawlable)

**Status:** done

### Description

### Problem

When an Allow rule and a Disallow rule in the same group match a path with patterns of equal length, Google's matcher picks the Allow (RFC 9309: "If an allow rule and a disallow rule are equivalent, then the allow rule SHOULD be used"). The Disallow can then never win for any path, so it is dead.

The common case is a template that starts with `Allow: /` and later gets `Disallow: /` added to block everything:

```
User-agent: *
Allow: /
Disallow: /
```

The author expects the site to be blocked. It is fully crawlable. Checked on 2026-10-07: `allowed_by_robots_text()` returns `/` and `/a/b` as allowed (`rule_allow`, line 2), and `robots_validate_text()` reports the file as `valid` with no diagnostics.

### Scope

- Add a validator diagnostic, severity `warning`, for a Disallow in a group that also has an Allow with an identical pattern. Name both lines and say the Disallow never takes effect because the Allow wins ties.
- Call out `Allow: /` + `Disallow: /` in the message or documentation as the case people actually hit.
- Decide whether the comparison normalizes patterns first, such as percent-encoding or a trailing `*`, and document the decision. Equal-length patterns that are not identical (`/a*` against `/ab`) are out of scope here; they belong with the general redundancy work in the sibling issue on potentially redundant rules.
- Tests: the block-all case above; an identical pair on a deeper path (`/x/`); an Allow and Disallow in different groups (no diagnostic); identical patterns of different lengths after normalization, if normalization is adopted.

### Non-goals

- Changing matcher behavior. The tie-break is correct for Google and RFC 9309.
- Tie behavior of other engines, beyond what the validator's stated Google-compatible profile covers.

### Done

The block-all file above validates with one `warning` naming lines 2 and 3, the cases above are tested, the behavior is documented, and the verify gate passes.


### Comments

#### 2026-11-08 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Behavior settled 2026-11-09 (burndown: maintainer delegated to lead + Codex consult; both agreed). Calibrated against a private sample of real robots.txt files (internal; figures kept out of the tracker). Code disallow_tied_by_allow, warning, on the Disallow line, message names the Allow line: "Disallow never takes effect: the Allow on line N has the identical pattern, and Allow wins ties (RFC 9309 section 2.2.2)." plus, for /, "With Allow: / this Disallow: / blocks nothing." Do not say the file is fully crawlable. Byte-identical canonical (parser) values only: no * or $ stripping. Same-agent groups merged as Google does; the "different groups" test uses different agents. Docs note Bing and Yandex also let Allow win identical-pattern ties. Reuses ROBO-gfjotdrr's group helper (lands after it). Rare in the sample, but every hit was a broken block-all.

## ROBO-fuhcwaom: Validator: note when a query-parameter rule misses the parameter in a later position

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

`Disallow: /recipes/*?q=` reads like "block recipe searches". It can miss URLs where `q` follows
another parameter, because `?q=` is a literal run: the `?` must sit right before `q`. (`*` can
also consume a real `?`, so `/recipes/x?a=?q=a` does match.) Tested on
2026-11-17 at 188c0a6, Google backend, https://www.washingtonpost.com/robots.txt line 112:

| path | decision |
|---|---|
| `/recipes/x?q=a` | disallow L112 |
| `/recipes/x?a=1&q=a` | allow |
| `/recipes?q=a` | allow (no `/` after `recipes`) |

More real files with the same shape, Google backend:
- https://www.theguardian.com/robots.txt line 18, `Disallow: /*?commentpage=`:
  `/a?commentpage=2` → disallow L18, `/a?page=1&commentpage=2` → allow.
- https://www.newyorker.com/robots.txt, the Allow direction under `Disallow: /*?` (line 10):
  `Allow: /*?id=` (line 22) gives `/x?id=5` → allow L22, but `/x?a=1&id=5` → disallow L10.

https://sklep.kfd.pl/robots.txt (lines 10-21) writes each parameter rule twice, as `/*?order=`
and `/*&order=`. That covers both positions: `/pl/kategoria?page=2&order=x` → disallow L16.

The WaPo file shows a different alternative at lines 76, 79 and 84: `/*?*outputType=comment` matches the
parameter in any position (`/a?b=c&outputType=comment` is a disallow), at the cost of also
matching `?xoutputType=comment`.

### Scope

In: an info code on a Disallow or Allow whose pattern contains `?` immediately followed by a
literal parameter name (`[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+`) and `=`. Only the first `?` in the pattern counts as
the query start; a later `?` (`/search?next=?q=`) is not a candidate. The message says the rule
may miss URLs where that parameter follows another one, and shows one nonmatching example built
from the pattern (`…?a=1&q=`). Any suffix after the `=` is kept (`/search?q=*&type=recipe` →
`/search?a=1&q=x&type=recipe`). For an Allow, the message says the gap can leave such URLs
restricted.

Out:
- Rules where `*` precedes the name after `?` (`?*q=`).
- Rules that block the whole query (`/*?`).
- `$`-anchored rules, as a scope choice for the first version (`/recipes/*?q=*$` has the same
  order sensitivity).
- Suggesting a rewrite. The two usual rewrites (`*q=` overreaches, `&q=` misses `;`-separated
  queries) each change meaning, so the message names the gap only.

### Acceptance criteria

- Fires on `/recipes/*?q=` and `/search?q=`.
- Silent when the crawler's effective merged rules hold the same type with the `&` form whose
  remaining pattern text is otherwise identical (prefix, value constraint, wildcards and any
  terminal `$`), as with `/*?order=` plus `/*&order=` in the kfd.pl file. Anything less
  than identical text keeps the row.
- Silent on `/*?*q=`, `/*?`, `/p?$`, `/p?q=1$` and a pattern whose `?` is the last character.
- One row per rule, with no group-level aggregation needed.
- Isolated fixtures, cross-checked with `robots_evaluate_text_v1()` on the Google backend:
  - Disallow: the matching control URL is disallowed and the generated example is allowed.
  - Allow, under a fixture-only `Disallow: /`: the control is allowed and the example is
    disallowed.
- The generated example is checked to miss the pattern, and the control to match it.
- May coexist with ROBO-jnnnkyat's advisory on the same line; they say different things.

### Verification

Fixtures as above. Merge gate.

### Dependencies

None. Related: ROBO-jnnnkyat.

## ROBO-gcnlckao: PT2 — Semantic conformance tests for both bounded_profiles backends

**Status:** done | **Parent:** pkpnvfzpkctwflmjbqxyfzsjqymkqhjv

### Description

Gate the published profile table with tests that assert SELECTION BEHAVIOUR, not
just `matcher_status`. Depends on PT1.

Parent: ROBO-pkpnvfzp.

### Why status-only is not enough

A test that only asserts every published token evaluates proves the table has no
false positives and nothing else. It cannot catch changed case-folding, a
changed `group_selection` while the status stays `evaluated`, or accidental
broadening. The behaviour is the contract, so the behaviour is what gets pinned.

### Work

For every published profile on both backends, assert:

- Its exact group is selected (`User-agent: <token>` group applies).
- The sibling profile's group is NOT selected.
- Wildcard fallback is applied or not applied exactly as `group_selection`
  declares — `Yandex`/`bingbot` honour `User-agent: *`;
  `YandexAdditionalBot`/`adidxbot` do not.
- Lowercase and uppercase spellings of the token resolve identically.
- Near misses stay unsupported, with the per-backend failure vocabulary asserted
  as-is (yandex: `not_evaluated` / `unsupported_product_token`; bing:
  `unsupported_profile` / `robots_unsupported_profile`) — do not normalize the
  two. Cover affixed (`Bingbot/2.0`, `Yandex/1.0`), whitespace-bearing,
  partial (`YandexAdditional`, `bing`), `*`, and real crawler identities
  (`YandexBot`, `YandexImages`, `msnbot`, `BingPreview`).
- The published table and the matcher agree: every `accepted_token` evaluates,
  and its `group_selection` value predicts the observed wildcard behaviour.

All of it through a supplied-body `use_rules` path. An `allow_all`, transport,
or other policy short-circuit never invokes the matcher and would make the test
vacuous.

Record the known limit in a comment in the test file: this direction catches
false positives only; an unpublished-but-accepted token is a conservative false
negative that these tests will not surface.

### Done when

- Flipping a `group_selection` value in the published table fails the suite.
- Changing a published token to `YandexBot` fails the suite.
- Tests pass on the current tree.

### Comments

#### 2026-08-25 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Landed as $(git log -1 --format=%h) on feature/bounded-profile-token-sets. 12 cases / 122 assertions in tests/testthat/test-bounded-profile-conformance-gcnlckao.R, driven from the published table rather than duplicated literals.

Covers everything the issue asked for: exact-group selection, sibling isolation, wildcard fallback matching the declared group_selection, total ASCII case folding, near-miss rejection in each backend's own vocabulary, and table-vs-matcher agreement in both directions. Added BP6 (an exact group beats a wildcard group in BOTH modes) because BP5 alone cannot distinguish the two modes' shared half from their differing half, and BP11 (a published selector is rejected by the OTHER vendor's backend) as a bounded-means-bounded check.

Every behavioural case goes through bp_eval_matched(), which asserts policy_action == 'use_rules' first. Without that the whole suite would be vacuously green under any policy short-circuit.

FOUND WHILE WRITING IT: the empty string is not an unsupported profile. It is rejected one layer earlier at input validation - reason 'input_invalid', error_class 'robots_invalid_product_token', error_stage 'input' - and both backends agree there, unlike their divergent unsupported vocabularies. Split into its own case (BP8b) so the two layers cannot be conflated; the near-miss lists no longer contain ''.

Known limit recorded in the file header per the issue: this catches false positives only, never a token newly accepted natively but missing from the table.

## ROBO-gfjotdrr: Validator: flag a named user-agent group that silently drops the * group's rules

**Status:** done

### Description

### Problem

Authors read robots.txt as rules that stack: the `User-agent: *` rules apply to everyone, and a named group adds a few more rules for that crawler. The Google algorithm (and Bing's, and RFC 9309) works differently. A crawler obeys exactly one group, the one that best matches its product token, and ignores every other group. A `*` group is only a fallback for crawlers that have no group of their own.

So adding a short named group silently takes every `*` rule away from that crawler. `robots_validate_text()` reports such a file as clean, because it is syntactically valid.

Seen on tidio.com's robots.txt (2026-10-07). The `*` group disallows `/wp-admin/*`, `/tickets/satisfaction/*`, `/conversations/satisfaction/*` and two others. A separate `User-agent: Bingbot` group holds only `Disallow: /blog/search/`. `allowed_by_robots_text()` correctly returns `/wp-admin/x` as disallowed for TestBot (line 8) but allowed for Bingbot (`default_allow`). The author almost certainly meant Bingbot to get those rules as well.

### Scope

- Add a validator diagnostic for a named group that drops rules present in the `*` group. Name the named group's line, the crawler token(s), and the `*` rules it no longer inherits.
- Severity `info`, not `warning`: a named group that is meant to be more permissive (for example, letting Googlebot into paths that `*` blocks) is a legitimate pattern. The diagnostic states a structural fact (this crawler ignores these rules) and does not judge intent, which keeps it inside the validator's existing non-goal ("inferring whether rules reflect webmaster intent", ROBO-htvtajbr).
- The message should say how the file actually behaves in plain terms: one group per crawler, the best match wins, groups do not merge.
- Decide how to compare rule sets (exact directive and value; whether to treat `/x` and `/x*` as equal) and record the choice in the diagnostic's documentation.
- Tests: the tidio-shaped case above; a named group that repeats every `*` rule (no diagnostic); a file with no `*` group (no diagnostic); several user-agents sharing one group.
- Document the group-selection behavior where the validator and the decision functions are described, so a user who sees the diagnostic can find the explanation.

### Non-goals

- Changing matcher behavior. The matcher is right; the gap is that nothing explains it.
- Engine-specific group selection beyond the Google-compatible profile the validator already states.

### Done

Validating the tidio-shaped file yields one `info` diagnostic on the Bingbot group, listing the five `*` Disallow rules Bingbot does not inherit. The cases above are tested, the behavior is documented, and the verify gate passes.


### Comments

#### 2026-11-08 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Behavior settled 2026-11-09 (burndown: maintainer delegated to lead + Codex consult; both agreed). Calibrated against a private sample of real robots.txt files (internal; figures kept out of the tracker). Code wildcard_rules_not_inherited, info, one per named group, anchored on its first User-agent line. Compares Allow and Disallow (type + canonical value, trailing * stripped for comparison only; $ not stripped), after merging same-agent groups as Google does; lists the * rules the agent's effective set lacks, first 10 by line then "and N more". A named group with no rules still fires. Exemption: an agent whose merged effective rules are only explicit allow-all (empty Disallow and/or Allow: /) gets no diagnostic: in the sample these were more than half of the losing agent/group pairs (Mediapartners-Google, Googlebot-News...), deliberate. Message states behavior only (obeys only this group; groups do not combine), never intent. Done line: the tidio-shaped fixture is defined with five Disallows and no Allow.

#### 2026-11-09 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Starting (burndown 2026-11-09, wave 3): implementer opus/medium in a harness worktree based on a0ea592, branch feature/ROBO-gfjotdrr-wildcard-not-inherited. ## ROBO-gokbvzcb: Validator: report a robots.txt that redirects to another host or site

**Status:** done

### Description

Why: a robots.txt URL that redirects to another host serves that host's file, or its homepage. RFC 9309 section 2.3.1.2 says to follow up to five redirects and use the file at the end; Google documents the same. A site owner rarely means this: the usual cause is a site-wide redirect (a domain move, a catch-all to the homepage, or a lapsed domain that now points elsewhere). The result is often an HTML page that yields no rules, or another site's rules applied to this one. The fetch layer already records `effective_url` and `redirect_count`, but the validator says nothing about a host change, so a caller has to compare URLs by hand.

Found from a consumer study (news-ai-access), stated here with synthetic cases only.

Scope:
- In:
  - [ ] A validator diagnostic when the robots.txt's `effective_url` host differs from the requested host, distinguishing at least: same host with another path (for example /robots.txt to /), www/apex or other subdomain of the same name, and a different site. Decide whether "same site" needs the Public Suffix List (a new dependency) or a documented host-label heuristic; record the choice.
  - [ ] Severity per case: the different-site case at least a warning, since the rules applied belong to another site; combined with content_flag "html", the message says the robots.txt is effectively missing.
  - [ ] Per-engine explanation where the engines differ (RFC 9309 and Google follow and use the final file; record Yandex and Bing as documented, or as a documentation gap).
  - [ ] Synthetic fixtures for each case, reusable by the edge-case catalog (ROBO-mxermwed).
- Out: changing fetch behavior (redirects stay followed as today); any classification of the target site's content.

Acceptance criteria: the diagnostic and its cases are documented, each has a synthetic test, and NEWS has a line.

Verification: pre-push gate.

Dependencies: none. Related: ROBO-bsloeclp (redirect failure reasons; this issue is about redirects that succeed).

#### 2026-11-10 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Either of the first two becomes a warning when the page reached is HTML. A scheme or port change that keeps /robots.txt stays silent, and a trailing root dot no longer splits a host. The edge-case catalog's redirect-cross-host-html gap is closed. ## ROBO-gqkhoogt: Blind-reader review: have Haiku read real robots.txt files and diff its answers against our tool

**Status:** todo

### Description

Why
Our checks so far come from parsers compared with parsers (design/engine-disagreements.md, design/library-comparison.md, design/edge-case-catalog.md). Nobody has asked a plain reader what a robots.txt says. Haiku, blind to this tool, reads real robots.txt files from the news-ai-access corpus; where its answers and the tool's differ, the tool may have a bug, lack a check, or behave in a way an owner would not expect. Or Haiku is wrong. The goal is the best tool, backed by evidence.

START HERE: this issue is the home for this work. Read it, pick the first unblocked todo child (fp issue list --parent <this id>), and read its description. Anything you find that is not a child goes in as a top-level issue that cites this id.

The method (revised after a Codex consult; start small, grow only if it pays)
- Haiku is a candidate-finding heuristic, not an oracle. Agreement with the tool proves nothing, and Haiku may have learned from the same Google docs the tool follows. A candidate becomes a finding only when we resolve it ourselves against the RFC text or observed engine behavior.
- One prompt and one response per file, with a fixed product token and path chosen so matching is actually exercised. Haiku answers under a plain RFC 9309 reading: allow | disallow | unspecified | cannot_tell. Keep "the RFC is silent" (unspecified) apart from "the model is unsure" (cannot_tell). There is no RFC matcher in this package (the rfc9309 backend is capability_unavailable; every ruleset sends a supplied body to the Google matcher), so the tool is not an RFC oracle. Compare the answer with the tool's Google, Bing and Yandex decisions, and on synthetic rows with the manifest's hand-derived rfc9309_decision; for a real file the RFC answer is one we derive ourselves from the RFC text. Before trusting Haiku as an RFC reader, check which way it leans where RFC and Google differ (7 manifest rows) or the RFC is silent (30 rows): paste the relevant RFC clauses into the prompt and require a clause citation. If it still answers Google's way, treat the probe as a naive-reader / owner-expectation probe, which is also useful, and say so.
- Haiku also lists concrete suspected issues, quoting the line text (not injected line numbers, which can change how it reads), and anything that would surprise the owner. No category map and no 3-phrasing majority vote at the start: repeated phrasings are correlated, and a self-consistency filter would hide the ambiguity that can be the finding. Read every response, agreements included. Repeat a case only when it is uncertain or looks valuable, and keep the variation as evidence.
- Haiku sees only the file and the question, never check names or tool output. API calls use no tools; the file is fenced as untrusted data; every result row records the model id.
- The 14 + 23 classes already in design/engine-disagreements.md and design/library-comparison.md are known. Rediscovering them is a recall check; do not re-triage them.
- Encoding questions are answered from the bytes, not from Haiku reading decoded text.

Working rules (deliberately light)
- No approval step, no spec or ADR for this work. Whoever sees a candidate classifies it in a line or two in an fp comment: tool bug | Haiku wrong | RFC silent | known engine quirk | new check candidate | bad question. Then act: file the issue, add the fixture, or drop it.
- Decide by evidence and by what is best for a user of the tool. Nobody depends on current behavior staying the same; backward compatibility is not a reason by itself.
- Real robots.txt bodies are never committed. A finding becomes a minimal synthetic fixture on example.com, in tests/testthat/fixtures/edge-cases/manifest.csv's shape, with an ordinary testthat expectation justified by the RFC or observed engine behavior. Frozen Haiku answers are not tests.
- NEWS.md only for a user-visible change, one terse line (AGENTS.md rules). Write a design doc only when a finding needs one to be understood later.
- Haiku API spend is expected to be a few dollars. If an estimate for one run exceeds about $25, stop and tell the maintainer. Read the API key from 1Password as the agent-workflow skill says; never from a paste or a .env.
- The harness lives in dev/blind-reader/, outside the test suite. The corpus (~/Projects/news-ai-access/data/raw, about 341k files) is read-only.

Scope
In: the two child outcomes. Out: fixing every finding inside this epic (fixes are their own top-level issues), live crawler/fetch behavior, anything that sends real corpus files anywhere but the Haiku API calls.

Acceptance criteria
All children done, and a closing comment says what the loop found: counts by class and the ids of the issues and fixtures it produced. Further rounds, if wanted, are new children.

Verification
fp issue list --parent <this id> shows every child done; the closing comment's ids resolve.

Dependencies
None.

### Comments

## ROBO-hcqrzikz: Bare rawToChar() on a fetched body raises simpleError on a NUL-bearing robots.txt

**Status:** done

### Description

### Defect

Every decode of a FETCHED robots.txt body uses a bare `rawToChar()`, which raises `embedded nul in string` whenever a NUL is followed by a non-NUL. A server returning a robots.txt with a stray NUL therefore aborts the call with an unclassed base R `simpleError`.

Three internal sites, all on live paths:

- `render_body_bytes()` (R/robots_body.R:131) - reached from the public `robots_body(source_id, raw = FALSE)` preview accessor.
- `matcher_string_v1()` (R/engine-contract-v1.R:461) - reached from `match_google_v1()` (:735), i.e. the actual matcher path.
- the per-source decode loop in `allowed_by_robots_url.R:166`.

`allowed_by_robots_text.R:79` is NOT affected: its input is already a character string, and an R string cannot contain a NUL.

### Verified 2026-07-29 against installed robotstxtr 0.2.0

Helpers, directly:

    render_body_bytes(as.raw(c(0x55,0x73,0x65,0x72,0x00,0x61)))
    #> Error: embedded nul in string: 'User\0a'   (simpleError)
    matcher_string_v1(<same bytes>)
    #> Error: embedded nul in string: 'User\0a'   (simpleError)

Publicly, with a mocked 200 text/plain serving `User-agent: *\n\0Disallow: /`:

    allowed_by_robots_url("https://ex.com/x", "TestBot")
    #> Error: embedded nul in string   (simpleError)

    robots_evaluate_url_v1("https://ex.com/x", robots_product_token = "TestBot",
      robots_policy_ruleset = "google", matcher_backend = "google",
      ssrf_guard = TRUE)
    #> Error: embedded nul in string   (simpleError)

### render_body_bytes() contradicts its own documented contract

Its comment reads "Render raw bytes to a length-one character string WITHOUT ERRORING on invalid encoding (PRD 6.6 body handling)", and it carefully marks the result `Encoding = "bytes"` when `validUTF8()` fails. But `rawToChar()` raises before `validUTF8()` is ever reached, so the no-error guarantee holds for invalid UTF-8 and fails for an embedded NUL. The intent is already correct; only the decode is.

### Downstream impact: it escapes sitemapr's public API

sitemapr Layer E calls `robots_evaluate_url_v1()` from `robots_evaluate_facts()` (R/robots-facts.R:195) with no tryCatch anywhere in the chain. Verified end to end in sitemapr:

    validate_sitemap("https://ex.com/sitemap.xml", check_robots = TRUE)
    #> Error: embedded nul in string: 'User-agent: *\n\0Disallow: /tmp\n'
    (class simpleError/error)

So one malformed robots.txt on a crawled origin aborts a whole sitemap validation run. This is the SAME defect class as sitemapr SITE-ctkdkuna (tar sniffer) and SITE-udiqjraa (sitemapr's own robots discovery), both already fixed there.

### Why it is reachable in the wild

A WAF challenge page, a CDN error body, a UTF-16-encoded robots.txt, or a truncated/padded file all produce NUL-bearing bytes at /robots.txt. Fetching is best-effort everywhere else in this package - a 404, an SSRF block and a transport failure all degrade - so a weird body should degrade too, not abort.

### Approach

Decode without erroring rather than guarding each call. `rawToChar()` has no NUL-tolerant mode, so either strip/truncate at the first NUL before decoding or decode via a helper that catches and falls back to `Encoding = "bytes"`.

Note the three sites want DIFFERENT fallbacks and should not be blindly unified:

- `render_body_bytes()` is a human-facing preview: it should render, marked `bytes`, never error.
- the matcher path feeds bytes to C++: dropping vs keeping the NUL changes what the matcher sees, so the choice needs a documented rule (Googles reference matcher treats robots.txt as bytes and does not stop at NUL).
- `allowed_by_robots_url()` should surface a per-row error rather than aborting the whole vectorised call, matching how it already reports other per-row failures.

### Cross-repo

Mirrors sitemapr SITE-udiqjraa. sitemapr additionally needs its own decision - defensive guard vs pinning a fixed robotstxtr - tracked separately on the sitemapr side.

### Done

- A NUL-bearing fetched body no longer raises from `robots_body()`, `allowed_by_robots_url()`, or `robots_evaluate_url_v1()`.
- `render_body_bytes()` honours its stated no-error contract, asserted by a test.
- The matcher fallback rule is documented, not incidental.
- Tests mock a NUL-bearing 200 at each of the three entry points.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-29 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

The fix is smaller than it looks: the package ALREADY has NUL-safe byte handling, on a different path.

robots_validate_text() accepts raw input and its own docs (R/robots_validate.R:23) advertise exactly this: 'Raw input is useful when validating acquisition bytes that contain malformed UTF-8, a byte-order mark, or NUL bytes.'

Verified against installed 0.2.0 with the SAME bytes that abort the matcher path:

    robots_validate_text(as.raw(c(0x55,0x73,0x65,0x72,0x2d,0x61,0x67,0x65,
      0x6e,0x74,0x3a,0x20,0x2a,0x0a,0x00,0x44,0x69,0x73,0x61,0x6c,0x6c,
      0x6f,0x77,0x3a,0x20,0x2f)))
    #> OK, no error

So the package is internally inconsistent rather than uniformly missing a capability: the VALIDATION path tolerates NUL bytes by contract and in fact, while the MATCHING path (matcher_string_v1) and the body PREVIEW path (render_body_bytes) abort on them. See robots_validate.R:311, which already works on bytes_without_nul - the NUL-stripping idiom exists in-tree.

Suggests reusing that existing handling rather than inventing new fallbacks, which also settles the 'three sites want different fallbacks' concern in the description: the validator's rule is already the documented house rule, so the matcher should follow it and only the per-row error surfacing in allowed_by_robots_url() remains a genuinely separate decision.

#### 2026-07-29 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Fixed on branch `fix/nul-bearing-body-decode` (commit 0c3a300). Local verify gate green: lintr clean, docs-drift clean, R CMD check --as-cran 0 errors / 0 warnings / 1 pre-existing URL note. 4250 tests pass.

**What changed.** New `R/body-decode.R` owns the single NUL rule and both decode helpers (`nul_free_bytes()`, `decode_matcher_body()`); `render_body_bytes()`, `matcher_string_v1()`, the `allowed_by_robots_url()` per-source decode loop, `allowed_by_robots_text()` and `robots_validate.R`'s `bytes_without_nul` all route through it, so the rule has one implementation instead of five.

**The rule chosen**, per your comment on this issue: reuse the validator's existing handling. NUL bytes are REMOVED; the document is not truncated at them and no other byte is rewritten. `robots$body` keeps the acquired bytes verbatim, so `robots_body(raw = TRUE)` still round-trips the NUL. Documented in `R/body-decode.R` and normatively in `design/PRD.md` §6.6 body handling, including the divergence from the byte-transparent reference matcher and why the byte-transparent option is unreachable.

**Two findings while implementing:**

1. The three sites did NOT need three different fallbacks, and the third one dissolved entirely. `allowed_by_robots_url()` needs no per-row error surfacing: once NULs are removed, `rawToChar()` has no remaining failure mode (invalid UTF-8 never raised), so there is no per-row error left to report. That closes the 'genuinely separate decision' you flagged.

2. The string wall is wider than the three sites in the description. `robotstxtr_collect_directives_` returns each directive value through `Rf_mkCharLenCE`, which rejects an embedded NUL exactly like `rawToChar()` does — so a byte-transparent matcher path would only have moved the error from the decode into match-metadata correlation (reached from all three entry points via `collect_directive_lookup()`). That is the concrete reason byte transparency is not cheaply reachable here: it would need raw-vector bindings for `allowed_text_`/`matching_line_text_`/`collect_directives_` AND a raw `matched_rule_value` channel, i.e. a public schema change. The in-tree precedent for raws bodies already exists (`robotstxtr_validation_parse_`, the Yandex/Bing batch bindings), so it is a coherent later slice if you ever want exact Google parity on NUL-bearing documents — worth filing separately rather than folding in here. Test `tests/testthat/test-nul-body-hcqrzikz.R` pins the current rule, so such a slice would have to deliberately update it.

## ROBO-hegmdbon: [USER] Yandex: say when a file's YandexBot group is read by none of our Yandex profiles

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

https://www.washingtonpost.com/robots.txt (fetched 2026-11-17) has `User-agent: YandexBot` /
`Disallow: /` / `Allow: /creativegroup/` / `Allow: /advertising/` at lines 252-255. It has no
`User-agent: Yandex` group. Yandex's documentation says `YandexBot` names the main indexing robot
and that a robot with its own group ignores `Yandex` and `*`.

The `yandex` backend accepts only the selectors `Yandex` and `YandexAdditionalBot`
(`yandex-0.1.0`). `YandexBot` is rejected on purpose (`resolve-matcher-profile-v1.R:77`). Tested
on 2026-11-17 at 188c0a6:

`robots_evaluate_text_v1(body, "https://e.com/x", token, "yandex", "yandex")`:

| file | `Yandex` | `YandexAdditionalBot` |
|---|---|---|
| `User-agent: YandexBot` / `Disallow: /`, then `User-agent: *` / `Disallow: /s` | allow, no matched line | allow |
| `User-agent: Yandex` / `Disallow: /`, same `*` group | disallow L2 | allow |

The validator reports nothing for the first file. A user asking "does this file block Yandex?"
therefore gets "allowed" from every Yandex selector we offer, while YandexBot is blocked
outside the two allowed path prefixes. Each answer is right for what its profile models; the gap is that nothing tells the user
the file has a group none of our Yandex profiles read.

### Why it waits

Two different fixes, and the choice is the maintainer's:

1. **Signal only.** The validator, or a per-row evaluator note, says that a group names a Yandex
   robot no supported profile selects. The bounded-profile boundary stays as it is.
2. **Profile.** Add a `YandexBot` profile. Yandex documents YandexBot's group selection; this
   needs conformance fixtures for it and an assessment of vendored matcher changes.

### Scope

In: decide between 1 and 2, then file the implementation issue. For 1, the likely shape is an
info code on the `User-agent` line that identifies the affected documented Yandex robot token. It
uses a pinned token list (source URL and read date) and an explicit definition of profile
coverage. The definition must say whether the signal is about an unsupported crawler identity or
an unread group, since a group shared by `Yandex` and `YandexBot` answers those differently.
Arbitrary unknown agents are never flagged.

Out: changing the `Yandex` profile's group selection.

### Acceptance criteria

The decision, its reason and its evidence are recorded here, and the linked follow-up issue
exists. That issue's fixtures cover the WaPo shape, separate and shared `Yandex`/`YandexBot`
groups, case variants, a `*`-only file, and both allowed and blocked paths.

### Verification

Decision record only.

### Dependencies

None. Related: ROBO-pkpnvfzp (published token set), ROBO-ogwchglq, ROBO-oxfpgdrx (live Yandex
evidence).




## ROBO-hfbdlevd: Validator add-on: fetch declared Sitemap URLs and check they resolve to valid sitemaps

**Status:** done

### Description

### Problem

The validator counts `Sitemap:` lines but never checks that the URLs they declare work. A robots.txt that points to a 404, a redirect chain, an HTML error page or a malformed XML file validates clean. ROBO-htvtajbr listed sitemap fetching as a non-goal "unless separately designed and scoped"; this issue is that design.

### Scope

- An opt-in check, either a new exported function or an argument on the validation functions, that fetches each declared sitemap URL and reports per URL: final HTTP status, redirects followed, content type, whether the body is well-formed XML, and whether its root element is `<urlset>` or `<sitemapindex>`. Gzipped sitemaps (`.xml.gz`) must be handled.
- Reuse the package's deterministic fetch policy and SSRF guard. Do not add a second HTTP path.
- Check documented limits: 50,000 URLs and 50 MB uncompressed per sitemap file (sitemaps.org; Google's documentation).
- Decide whether a sitemap index is followed into its child sitemaps, how deep and how many, and with what cap; record the decision.
- Report a sitemap URL on a different host than the robots.txt as `info`. sitemaps.org allows cross-host sitemaps only with proof of ownership, and Google accepts them when both sites are verified, so this is evidence, not an error.
- Tests with mocked responses only, matching the package rule that no test touches the network.

### Non-goals

- Fetching or checking the page URLs listed inside a sitemap.
- Validating sitemap extensions (image, video, news, hreflang).
- Syntax-only checks of the `Sitemap:` value, which belong to ROBO-xblfzkid.

### Done

The opt-in check reports per-sitemap results for supplied and fetched robots.txt documents, tested offline with mocked responses and documented, and the verify gate passes.


### Comments

#### 2026-11-08 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Superseded 2026-11-08: the maintainer placed this work in sitemapr, which already implements nearly all of it (sitemap_tree(from = 'root') + use_robots, ADR-006; probe_url(), ADR-007; fetch_source() redirect chains, ADR-003; the 50,000 URL / 50 MiB limits; index_limits()). Doing it here would add an xml2 Import to a CRAN package, stretch acquire_robots() to sitemaps, and break PRD §3 'Not a web crawler'; a robotstxtr -> sitemapr dependency would also be circular. The three remaining gaps are filed in sitemapr: SITE-zaerllaz (check the sitemaps declared in supplied robots.txt text), SITE-zczpxmow (info finding for a declared sitemap on another host), SITE-utjicjfu (a declared sitemap that fails during discovery becomes a finding). Sitemap value syntax checks stay here under ROBO-xblfzkid. No code changed under this id.

## ROBO-htvtajbr: Add a public robots.txt document validation API

**Status:** done

### Description

### Problem

The exported APIs fetch robots.txt documents and evaluate URL decisions, but none validates the document itself or returns syntax and structure diagnostics. The internal `validate_robots_txt()` only checks that an R input is a single non-missing character value. The internal directive collector exposes recognized callbacks, but callers cannot obtain a supported validation report.

This gap surfaced while testing the live LinkedIn robots.txt: confirming that all 4,660 active lines were recognized required a custom harness around internal callbacks plus separate encoding and structural checks.

### Scope

- Design and export a text-first validation API, with a URL-fetching counterpart or a documented composition with `robots_fetch()`.
- Return a stable typed result containing a document summary and per-line diagnostics with line number, severity, diagnostic code, directive or raw text, and message.
- Detect malformed or unrecognized active lines, missing or empty user-agent values, invalid group structure, relevant empty directive values, encoding hazards such as BOM or NUL bytes, and acquisition limits or truncation when validating a URL.
- Report recognized directive counts and basic document evidence such as byte size, line count, encoding status, and final newline status where useful.
- State the validation profile explicitly. Initial support may be Google-parser-compatible, but must not claim universal crawler or RFC 9309 validity.
- Reuse the existing deterministic fetch policy and stored raw body rather than introducing a second HTTP path.
- Add focused tests for valid files, ignored comments and blanks, malformed directives, unknown directives, group errors, byte-level hazards, and live-fetch outcomes through mocked responses.
- Document the distinction between file validation, URL allow/disallow evaluation, webmaster-intent review, and remote sitemap availability.

### Non-goals

- Inferring whether rules reflect webmaster intent.
- Claiming behavior for unavailable matcher backends.
- Fetching and validating declared sitemap resources unless separately designed and scoped.

### Done

A documented exported API validates supplied and fetched robots.txt documents, returns stable machine-readable line diagnostics and document evidence, identifies its parser or standards profile without overclaiming, includes representative tests and examples, and passes the project verify gate.

### Comments

## ROBO-huimrcbm: C5 - Maintainer-only differential harness (>=10k cases)

## ROBO-hzcnolhe: Pin RURL_GIT to v3.0.1 — CI installs rurl's dev head, as the file's own header warns

**Status:** done

### Description

`.gitlab-ci.yml` installs rurl from its **default branch**, not from a release
tag. Observed in the check job of pipeline 2838356532 (2026-09-10):

    ✔ Installed rurl 3.0.1.9000 (git::https://gitlab.com/bart-turczynski/rurl.git@0315c7d)

So every robotstxtr CI run tests against rurl's development head. The file says
so itself, in the DEPENDENCY RESOLUTION header:

    # rurl has no v3.0.0 tag yet, so this tracks its default branch. That is a
    # moving target: if rurl's main breaks, this pipeline goes red on a
    # robotstxtr tree nobody touched. Pin to a tag as soon as rurl cuts one.

**That condition is now met.** rurl cut `v3.0.1` at commit `0ca8f09` and is live
on CRAN (`src/contrib` serves 3.0.1; published 2026-09-09 07:40:02 UTC).

### What to do

Pin `RURL_GIT` in `variables:` to the tag:

    RURL_GIT: "git::https://gitlab.com/bart-turczynski/rurl.git@v3.0.1"

### Why this is worth doing rather than waiting for CRAN

Two independent reasons, both measured:

1. **The moving target is real.** Testing against `3.0.1.9000` means a rurl
   development commit can turn robotstxtr red with no robotstxtr change. It also
   means CI is *not* exercising what a user would install.
2. **p3m lags CRAN, so "just use CRAN" does not work yet.** Recorded on
   `SEOR-eqpdrqnl`: ~38 h after publication, p3m still served rurl 1.2.0 on
   every snapshot including `__linux__/noble/latest`, which is this pipeline's
   exact path. The CI file already appends CRAN behind P3M in `.r-binaries`, so
   the source is available; the pin is what makes the version deterministic.

### Related, and deliberately kept separate

`ROBO-depmsgpz` — the declared floor is `rurl (>= 2.2.1)`, a git-tag-only
version that was never on CRAN. pagerankr and sitemapr both moved to
`>= 3.0.1`; robotstxtr should follow. That is a DESCRIPTION change and a release
decision, whereas this issue is a one-line CI change with no effect on the
submitted tarball. They pair naturally but do not have to land together.

**Not blocked** by the rurl Windows binary (`SEOR-tjihigug`) — this touches CI
only, not submission.

### Acceptance

- `RURL_GIT` names `@v3.0.1`.
- A pipeline on `main` is green with the pin in place.
- The now-stale "Pin to a tag as soon as rurl cuts one" instruction in the
  header comment is updated to describe the pin instead.

## ROBO-igrkabdb: Validator: a UTF-16 body without a BOM is reported no_rules while the matcher enforces its rules

**Status:** done

### Description

### Problem

A UTF-16LE body with no BOM decodes, after robotstxtr drops the NUL bytes (R/body-decode.R, deliberate), to plain ASCII rules that the matcher enforces (`Disallow: /a` disallows). The validator reports `nul_byte` per line, `malformed_line` and `no_rules` ("places no restrictions"), which contradicts the matcher's decision.

Found by the edge-case catalog (ROBO-mxermwed, 2026-11-09). Fixture(s): `enc-utf16le-no-bom`, in tests/testthat/fixtures/edge-cases/ (manifest.csv) and design/edge-case-catalog.md; the current behavior is pinned in tests/testthat/test-edge-cases-mxermwed.R under a `# known gap:` comment, so a fix turns that block red and updates it.

### Scope

In: make the validator's reading agree with the matcher's NUL handling (validate the same decoded text, or replace `no_rules` with a diagnostic that says the body looks like UTF-16 and its rules are enforced after NUL removal).

Out: matcher behavior changes. A fix that would change a documented engine policy goes to the maintainer as a [USER] decision first.

### Acceptance criteria

The fixture's known-gap block is replaced by an assertion of the new diagnostic, the catalog row is updated, and the validator code table (roxygen of robots_validate_text) documents any new code.

## ROBO-iooslxvj: Matcher seam slice C: Google adapter parses each body once

**Status:** done | **Parent:** tlvrxtvbuezxgyuierfybahgvjojrcpi

### Description

### Why

Slice A (ROBO-bukqpjli) put the Google matcher behind the batch adapter interface but kept it row by row inside (Q2: parse-once comes later as a separate change). Every (URL, token) row re-parses the whole body, so a row's cost grows with body size. On large inputs this dominates: the corpus harness's evaluate runs take hours, and the harness needs a narrow tier for large bodies just to finish. Every matcher-touching unit pays for that in its equivalence runs.

### Scope

In:
- The Google adapter parses each distinct (readable) body once and answers all of its rows: the same grouping-by-body the Yandex and Bing adapters do.
- The vendored upstream matcher has no parsed-model API. It parses in a stream, with a match handler per query. So this needs either a native entry point that runs one parse with a handler answering many (URL, token) pairs, or a recorded parse replayed per query. It must not edit the vendored upstream sources. If it needs a change there, stop and file a `[USER]` decision.
- Row order, each row's own cut flag, the 512,000-byte window and `matched_rule_value_raw` stay as slice A defines them.
- Measure before and after: a synthesized large-body benchmark committed as a dev script, plus the private corpus evaluate run's wall time (kept private).

Out: populating `matched_rule_value_raw` for Google rows (separate change), and any behavior change.

### Acceptance criteria

- v1 output is identical to main on the test fixtures (the bukqpjli pin) and on the private corpus baseline (the harness compare).
- Results stay identical to the pristine upstream engine on the Google fidelity inputs (ROBO-deehqhlc's method).
- Measured speedup on the large-body benchmark, recorded in the MR.

### Dependencies

Matcher seam slice B (ROBO-iwmtdutk), so the batch module shapes are settled.

## ROBO-irdjzbay: Assert fragment convergence across all robotstxtr entry points

**Status:** done

### Description

### What

Assert that every robotstxtr entry point resolves a fragment-bearing URL to the
same matched path.

### Why

Three independent fragment code paths exist in the package:

- `src/bing_binding.cpp:344-346` — the adapter finds the first `#` and keeps
  everything before it, so the byte-transparent core never sees a fragment and
  never returns `invalid_request_target`.
- `src/yandex_target_binding.cpp:46-48` — same shape, separate implementation.
- `R/allowed_by_robots_url.R` — passes the URL verbatim and lets Google's
  `GetPathParamsQuery` strip internally. `tests/testthat/test-allowed_by_robots_url-r8.R:180`
  asserts "fragment kept in url; not in matched path".

They should all agree. The edge where they might not: Google returns `/`
outright when the `#` precedes the path start
(`~/Projects/robotstxt-cpp/robots.cc:205`), rather than the truncation result.
So `http://example.com#foo` resolves to `/` there. The package-owned extractors
take everything before the first `#` and then derive the path, which should also
yield `/` — but that is inference from reading the code, not an assertion.

### Scope

A table-driven test over fragment URL shapes, asserting every entry point agrees
on the matched path:

- `#` after a path — `http://a/plain#secret`
- `#` before path start — `http://example.com#foo`
- `#` immediately after the authority with a trailing slash
- empty fragment — `http://a/p#`
- `#` inside a query — `http://a/p?q=1#frag`
- multiple `#` — `http://a/p#one#two`
- `%23` in the path — `http://a/p%23name`, which must NOT be treated as a
  fragment on any path, and must reach the matcher intact

### Why it matters

An R user calling three functions on one URL and getting three answers is a
real-life failure the current tests would not catch. The convergence is
deliberate design — `design/robotstxtbing-integration-v2-spec.md:623`
(BI-V2-TARGET, APPROVED) puts URL→origin-form conversion in the adapter so the
byte-transparent core stays source-preserving — so it deserves an assertion
rather than three parallel implementations that happen to match today.

The `%23` row is shared with the Bing-side differential filed separately; if
that work finds a cross-library divergence, this test is where it surfaces for R
users.

## ROBO-isbpzgqn: content_flag's anywhere-marker rule flags SVG, feeds and comment-led robots.txt as html

**Status:** done

### Description

### Why

Found in the review of ROBO-qquftxcx. That change made `robots_content_flag()` call a body "html" when it opens with `<` and has `<!doctype html`, `<html`, `<head`, `<body`, `<script` or `<style` anywhere in its first 4096 bytes. The review found where that rule still misreads bodies.

Bodies wrongly flagged "html" (they were "xml" before):

- XML that holds those tags by design: SVG `<svg><style>`, `<!DOCTYPE svg><svg><style/>`, KML `<Style>`, an S3 `<Error><Message>x <style> y</Message>`.
- Feeds with embedded markup: RSS `<![CDATA[<script>]]>`, Atom xhtml content with `<style>`.
- A real robots.txt that opens with a markup comment and mentions a marker. Both `<!-- generated -->\nUser-agent: *\nDisallow: /*<script\n` and `<!-- <script> -->\nUser-agent: *...` draw `html_body`. This is the case that costs a user something: a working robots.txt gets an HTML warning.

Bodies still missed: minified HTML after leading text, as in `Warning: x<br />\n<script>a()</script><!DOCTYPE html><html></html>\n`, gives NA. This was already the case before ROBO-qquftxcx.

For XML and feeds the impact is low: such a body is not a robots.txt either way. The comment-led robots.txt is the one to fix first.

### Scope

In:
- Narrow the anywhere rule so a markup comment, or XML whose root is not `html` (svg, kml, rss, feed, Error), does not count as HTML.
- Decide whether leading text before the first `<` should still allow the anywhere rule.
- Tests for each example above.

Out: changing the line-start `content_html_pattern`.

### Acceptance criteria

The comment-led robots.txt examples draw no `html_body`. SVG, KML, the S3 error and feeds with CDATA flag "xml". Every ROBO-qquftxcx pin stays green.


### Comments

## ROBO-jbralthm: Acquire robots.txt through ssrfr: one acquisition module around ssrf_prepare_hop()/ssrf_fetch()

**Status:** done

### Description

Gate lifted by the maintainer, 2026-11-05. It used to wait on CRAN serving ssrfr 1.0.0 (seor SEOR-wbrcseui; ssrfr SSRF-nagyezau). ssrfr 1.0.0 was submitted on 2026-11-03 (SHA ddb3389) and is in CRAN's queue; SSRF-hotiouqk (G1) is done. The switch lands on main now so the news-ai-access study can pin robotstxtr from GitLab (that repo's ADR 0001). The next robotstxtr CRAN release still waits for ssrfr's acceptance: no submitted DESCRIPTION may carry `Remotes:` (SEOR-eqpdrqnl acceptance), so until then ssrfr reaches CI and dev installs the way ssrfr reached pslr before pslr was on CRAN (SSRF-mspjpegk's CI pin).

Owner, 2026-10-21 (ROBO-tlvrxtvb): this switch also carries the architecture review's candidate 4, one acquisition module built around `ssrf_prepare_hop()`/`ssrf_fetch()` as separate reviewable commits, and settles the `body_truncated` meaning. Candidates 5 and 6 are retired; their testing goals survive as a fake at the ssrfr boundary and explicit redirect-loop tests. robotstxtr keeps translating ssrfr's refusals into its own published reason codes.

**Order:** this goes in the release after 0.3.1. It depends on ssrfr 1.0.0 on
CRAN with G1. It adds `ssrfr` to Imports, and `httr2` leaves Imports unless
another path still needs it.

**Calls to replace:**
- `R/fetch-policy.R:perform_fetch`, `build_fetch_request`,
  `read_body_within_limit`, `accumulate_within_limit`,
  `close_stream_response` and `classify_transport_condition`.
- All of `R/ssrf.R` (`robots_ssrf_check`, `ssrf_check`,
  `ssrf_whatwg_second_look`, the classifiers and the raw-host helpers).
- The `httr2::url_modify_relative`/`url_parse` redirect checks.

**Candidate-4 acquisition module.** Use one internal module, say
`R/acquire.R`, as the only caller of ssrfr. `robots_fetch()`,
`robots_validate_url()`, `allowed_by_robots_url()` and
`robots_evaluate_url_v1()`/`fetch_evidence_v1()` all reach it through the
existing `make_source_result()` shape. The module:
1. Builds one `ssrf_policy()` per call, with these fields:
   - `user_agent = fetch_ua`
   - `max_redirects = 6`: five followed redirects, with the 6th 3xx returned
     as a response so `over_budget` keeps `location_header`
   - `total_timeout = max(1, ceiling(timeout))`
   - `connect_timeout = min(3, that)`
   - `max_response_size = max_bytes`
   - `allow_ports = 1:65535`, which keeps today's any-port behavior and keeps
     `port` out of the enum; or adopt 80/443 and add `port`
2. Runs the hop loop. Prepare, branch on class, fetch, branch on class, then
   handle the response: an empty or missing Location, the loop check on
   `binding$url`, the 6th redirect, then `classify_status()`. It appends
   `redirect_hops` from `b$url`, `b$state$status` and the next URL.
3. Holds the two translation tables in 1b, refusal code to
   (`fetch_outcome`, `terminal_redirect_reason`, `safety_block_reason`) and
   cause to `transport_error_kind`, as data with a test that walks
   `ssrf_vocabulary("reason_codes")$code` and `ssrf_vocabulary("causes")$cause`
   in full. A new ssrfr code then fails a test instead of falling through.
4. Catches `ssrfr_error` conditions. A bad `fetch_user_agent` (CR/LF) raises
   `ssrfr_error_invalid_policy`. Pre-validate it in
   `validate_fetch_user_agent`, so the call-level error keeps robotstxtr's
   class.

**Reason-code mapping:**
- The 17 shared codes pass through unchanged.
- `downgrade` becomes `https_downgrade` with `redirect_error`/`downgrade`.
- `scheme` at `hop > 1` becomes `redirect_error`/`non_http_target`/`scheme`.
- `userinfo`, `parse`, `multicast` and `reserved` (plus `port`,
  `host-denied` and `range-denied` if adopted) are admitted to
  `safety_block_reason` by a versioned engine-contract schema revision
  (`engine_schema_revision_v1/v2`, `design/engine-profiles.md` §2).
- `redirect-limit` does not occur under the N+1 budget. If it does, map it to
  `over_budget`.
- Causes map as follows: `timeout` gives `timeout`; `tls-failed` gives
  `tls_error`; `unresolvable`, `connect-failed`, `pin-mismatch` and
  `protocol-error` give `network_error`; `response-too-large` with
  `check == "decoded-bytes"` gives `body_too_large` (with `check == "header"`,
  `network_error`). `detail$step == 12` on a `timeout` may set
  `termination_reason = "deadline"`.
- NEWS records each relabel: ULA becomes `private`, malformed literals become
  `parse`, the bare `metadata` becomes `network_error`, and names now resolve.

**`body_truncated`.** ssrfr never returns a partial body: on overflow, "none
of it is returned" (§5.3; `R/fetch.R:attempt_address`). What it exposes is the
cause, `detail$check == "decoded-bytes"` and `detail$limit ==
"max_response_size"`, and after G1 also the status and the observed byte
count. No truncated body can exist, so the honest single meaning is
`body_truncated = FALSE` everywhere, which is what `R/robots_validate.R`
already hard-codes. The overflow fact lives in `fetch_outcome =
"body_too_large"`, `termination_reason = "ceiling"` and `limit_exceeded =
TRUE`. The module should set `body_truncated = FALSE` and change
`make_source_result()`'s `body_too_large` branch, which says `TRUE` today,
with a NEWS line. The other choice is to define the field as "the transfer was
cut short" and set it `TRUE` in both places. Either way the two files must
agree.

**Timeouts.** robotstxtr documents "a total timeout per origin including
redirects" (`robots_fetch()` roxygen) but sets `httr2::req_timeout()` per hop
(`build_fetch_request`). ssrfr's `total_timeout` is chain-scoped, fixed by hop
1 and inherited through `from`, which is exactly one origin's chain. The switch
therefore makes the documented behavior true. Two caveats belong in the docs:
- The time between hops in robotstxtr's own code is not counted.
- `curl::nslookup()` cannot be preempted, so a slow resolver can overrun, and
  elapsed time is re-checked only after resolution (§5.3).

Fractional `timeout` is rounded up (N1).

**`ssrf_guard = FALSE`.** ssrfr has no off switch. Choose one:
- (a) Deprecate the argument and keep it as a permissive policy
  (`allow_ranges = c("0.0.0.0/0", "::/0")`, all ports, `allow_hosts` = the
  gate-5 names). Tier 1 (6to4, Teredo, NA, embedded) and exact provider
  endpoints stay refused. This is recommended because it keeps one module.
- (b) Keep a second, unguarded httr2 path for `FALSE`. This defeats the
  single module.

**Tests and examples.** `httr2::with_mocked_responses()` no longer intercepts
anything. The examples move to `\dontrun{}` or to `allowed_by_robots_text()`.
The tests use a local fixture server under a loopback-allow policy. Refusal
mapping tests use literal hosts offline.

**Closes:**
- ROBO-atvfjuuw: a zone ID refuses as `parse`.
- ROBO-pvntbjlb: there is no second look; WHATWG plus libcurl agreement fails
  closed as `parse`.
- ROBO-xzbyxipg: `fd20:ce::254` is gate 2 `cloud-metadata`; `instance-data`
  names are covered by resolution and gate 2, except the unresolvable bare
  name (N4).
- ROBO-tyhouhua: the total timeout per origin.
- It also removes the hand-kept matcher sync with sitemapr (ROBO-mgumaoyf
  follow-through).

## ROBO-jdnluzbb: Validator: name the path to write when a rule value is a full URL

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

https://natu.shop/robots.txt (fetched 2026-11-17) has 22 lines such as
`Disallow: https://natu.shop/collections/produkty-bialko` (lines 97-119). Each one gets
`rule_missing_leading_slash` (warning), with the message "Pattern does not start with '/' or
'*'; URL paths always start with '/', so this rule never matches."

That is correct but doesn't tell the author the fix. The author wrote a full URL; the rule
needs the path, `/collections/produkty-bialko`. Every one of the file's 22 such warnings has
this shape.

Fixing it naively has a trap the message should mention. `Disallow: /collections/produkty`
(line 105 with the host removed) is a prefix rule, so it would also block
`/collections/produkty-bialko`, `/collections/produkty-ebooki` and every other
`produkty-…` collection.

### Scope

In: when a `rule_missing_leading_slash` value starts with `http://` or `https://` (ASCII
case-insensitive) and parses as an absolute URL, the message variant:
- names the pattern to write instead: path plus query exactly as spelled (case, escapes and
  query kept). An empty path suggests `/`, and the message says that `/` matches everything;
- says: "Without wildcards or an end anchor, this pattern matches any path and query beginning
  with it. A trailing `$` requires matching through the end of the path and query." The
  sentence is omitted when the extracted pattern already holds `*` or ends in `$`;
- under `robots_validate_url()`, when the value's origin (scheme, host, effective port)
  differs from the robots.txt origin, says that removing the authority makes the rule apply on
  the origin served by this robots.txt, not the one written in the value.

The same code and severity apply. One row per line, as today.

Out: other non-slash values (`private/`, `$`), which keep today's message; a message variant
for a `*`-led value.

### Acceptance criteria

- The natu.shop lines get the variant, naming `/collections/produkty-bialko` and so on.
- Fixtures: `http://`, `HTTPS://`, host only (`https://e.com`), host plus query, a query,
  a port, literal `*` and a terminal `$` in the URL, percent-encoded characters, a different
  origin under `robots_validate_url()`, `https://` alone, and `https:/x`. A fragment goes
  through the real parser, where `#` starts a comment. Values that don't parse keep today's
  message.
- Code, severity and row count are unchanged.
- The suggested pattern, written as a rule, is checked through `robots_evaluate_text_v1()` to
  match the original URL, query included.
- NEWS: one terse bullet for the new message.

### Verification

Fixtures above. Merge gate.

None. Related: ROBO-xblfzkid (introduced the code).




## ROBO-jnnnkyat: Validator: explain crawl-versus-index implications of parameter-blocking rules

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

The owner requested an informational advisory for query-parameter blocking on 2026-11-16. Companies may use robots.txt intending to prevent indexing, but blocked URLs can still appear in Google Search, and Google cannot read a page-level noindex when crawling is blocked. Blocking faceted URLs can also be intentional crawl control, so this must not be presented as an automatic error.

Live example: https://natu.shop/robots.txt, fetched 2026-11-16 through robotstxtr: HTTP 200, 3658 bytes, UTF-8 text/plain. Patterns include /collections/*sort_by*, /collections/*filter*&*filter*, /*?*ls=*&ls=*, /*?*oseid=* and preview parameters. Current validator provides no indexing-intent advisory. The repeated wildcard group and full-URL patterns are already separately diagnosed; they are not the purpose of this issue.

### Scope

In: a bounded, informational note for active Disallow patterns that demonstrably or plausibly target query parameters. Name relevant lines/patterns and invite investigation of crawl control versus indexing exclusion versus duplicate consolidation. Define a conservative detection rule, including broad query delimiters and common parameter-like patterns without asserting that a substring always denotes a query parameter.
Out: automatic edits; unblocking recommendations regardless of intent; fetching target pages, GSC access or an assertion that any URL is indexed; treating every query restriction as wrong; canonical/noindex implementation.

### Acceptance criteria

- Stable info code and useful line evidence, with grouped/bounded output rather than repeating a tutorial on every rule.
- Explain that robots.txt restricts crawling, not guaranteed indexing; Google may index a blocked URL without its content.
- For intended exclusion, explain that meta robots noindex or X-Robots-Tag noindex must be accessible to the crawler. Never suggest adding noindex to robots.txt or promise a blocked page's tag will be read.
- For equivalent/duplicate URLs, distinguish canonicalization from exclusion: canonical is a consolidation signal, not a guaranteed exclusion directive. Do not recommend noindex as a blanket canonicalization fix.
- Acknowledge legitimate crawl-budget/faceted-navigation restrictions and avoid advising users to expose infinite URL spaces merely to apply noindex.
- Respect parser comment boundaries, ineffective rules, group selection/repeated groups and known exceptions; avoid claiming a sampled query is effectively blocked from pattern text alone. Explicitly document heuristic scope and engine attribution.
- Cover actual query patterns, parameter-like path text, comments, Allow-only cases, repeated groups, ineffective full-URL rules and the natu.shop shapes with synthesized minimal fixtures. Text and mocked URL paths agree; info does not change valid document status.
- Update diagnostic help, examples and NEWS; no new 0.4.0 release blocker without an explicit scope decision.

### Verification

Focused positive/negative/advisory-deduplication fixtures, existing group/escaping diagnostics and repository merge gate. No live site dependency in tests.

### Dependencies

None; standalone outcome. Related independent JavaScript rendering advisory and completed repeated-group checks.

### Sources

https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/block-indexing
https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/faceted-navigation
https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls

**Status:** done

### Description

Waits on the maintainer: should the structural guard block `localhost`, `localhost.` and `*.localhost`?

RFC 6761 reserves them for loopback and libcurl resolves them locally without DNS, so they reach loopback under the default `ssrf_guard = TRUE`. ## ROBO-juatemlg: Harden mid-stream transport failures in perform_fetch to network_error

**Status:** done | **Parent:** bfkdfhmsrpzvgqzjrycvlxamglvfrpyr

### Description

Introduced by R7 (ROBO-bowvkbks). perform_fetch() switched body reading to httr2::resp_stream_raw() inside read_body_within_limit(), which is OUTSIDE the outer tryCatch that wraps req_perform_connection(). A transport failure that occurs DURING body streaming (connection drop mid-body against a real server) therefore escapes as an uncaught error and aborts the whole robots_fetch() call, instead of being classified as network_error per PRD §6.4. Connection-OPEN failures are still caught/classified correctly; only mid-stream drops regress. Not covered by acceptance tests (rare, real-server only). Fix: wrap the streaming read in tryCatch and route conditions through classify_transport_condition(). Low priority; consider during R8/R9.

## ROBO-kormmfyg: Validator: flag a lower-case percent-escape in a rule, which Google matches only in upper case

**Status:** done

### Description

### Problem

A rule written with a lower-case percent-escape, such as `Disallow: /a%3cb`, does not block the exact path the site owner wrote under Google's matcher: the matcher upper-cases escapes in rule values (`MaybeEscapePattern`) but not in the URL, so `/a%3cb` is allowed while `/a%3Cb` is disallowed. Under RFC 9309 §2.2.2 the literal URL `/a%3cb` matches the rule octet for octet. No validator diagnostic tells the site owner.

Found by the edge-case catalog's review (ROBO-mxermwed, 2026-11-09). Fixture: `esc-lower-hex-rule` in tests/testthat/fixtures/edge-cases/ (manifest.csv) and design/edge-case-catalog.md; current behavior pinned in tests/testthat/test-edge-cases-mxermwed.R under a known-gap comment.

### Scope

In: a warning when a rule value holds a lower-case percent-escape, saying Google matches it only against the upper-case form. Out: matcher behavior changes (matcher fidelity; a change goes to the maintainer as a [USER] decision first).

### Acceptance criteria

The fixture's known-gap block is replaced by an assertion of the new diagnostic, the catalog row is updated, and the validator code table documents the code.

## ROBO-kzyfejcv: Validator: recognize the aipref __usage_ai-training preference token

**Status:** done

### Description

### Why

draft-kelley-aipref-training-preference-signal-00 (aipref WG, 2026-10-30, expires 2027-05-03) expresses an AI-training preference with ordinary robots.txt groups keyed by the policy token `__usage_ai-training` in a User-Agent line. It adds no directive and no grammar:

```
User-Agent: __usage_ai-training
Disallow: /
Allow: /press-kit/
```

Disallowed means a preference against training on that path, allowed means a preference in favor, and no such group means no preference. Two rules differ from crawler lookup (§4.2): a `User-Agent: *` group MUST NOT be read as matching the policy token, and the token is matched exactly, apart from case (no prefix or flexible matching). The token says nothing about crawling (§4.3, §4.4).

Adoption, as the maintainer reports: Anthropic says it has been rolling this out since 2026-10-30, and OpenAI support said it committed on the 30th and will implement it. Google is also reported to have agreed. Before the docs claim any adoption, check it against each vendor's own documentation and cite it.

Today the validator treats the token as just another agent. It even reports `wildcard_rules_not_inherited` for a `__usage_ai-training` group, which is noise, since the draft says `*` never applies to that token.

### Scope

In (validator, `robots_validate_text()` / `robots_validate_url()`):
- Recognize `__usage_ai-training` groups. Never report `wildcard_rules_not_inherited` for the policy token.
- Info: a training preference is expressed, naming the group's line. The checks run on the token's group alone, without `*`.
- Warning: a near-miss token that would not match exactly, e.g. `__usage_ai_training`, `usage_ai-training` or `__usage-ai-training`.
- Warning: a group that names only the policy token but carries lines other than Allow and Disallow, such as Crawl-delay. Those lines mean nothing there (Sitemap lines are file-level and fine).
- Cross-reference: ROBO-xglcoagv's `DisallowAITraining:`-style keys, which Google reads as `Disallow` and which therefore block all crawling. The message should point to the policy-token form.
- design/ diagnostic catalog and engine-profiles.md: a short section citing the draft and its status, and saying it is a draft.

Out, for now: a public API that answers "is training on this path opted out?" (a separate issue once the draft stabilizes), and any matcher change.

### Acceptance criteria

- Synthesized fixtures pin each diagnostic, plus a file without the token (no new diagnostics).
- No `wildcard_rules_not_inherited` for a policy-token group.
- The docs cite the draft by name and version.


### Comments

#### 2026-11-10 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Seen in the cross-engine triage (ROBO-glssaxva), synthesized shape: 'User-agent: *' followed only by non-rule lines (e.g. Content-Signal:, Sitemap:), then 'User-agent: __usage_ai-training' / 'Disallow: /'. Google's open-source engine stacks the two User-agent lines into one group, because the lines between are not rules. So the training opt-out's Disallow applies to every crawler under Google, while our Bing backend ends the * group at the unknown field. The draft says a * group must not match the token, but here the stacking makes the token's rules apply to *. The parser check should warn when a __usage_* User-agent line stacks onto another agent's group (no Allow/Disallow line between them).

## ROBO-laydgesq: SSRF matcher: IPv6 transition embeddings 6to4/Teredo/ISATAP are not decoded

**Status:** done

### Description

The matcher in R/ssrf.R decodes five IPv6->IPv4 embedding forms and re-classifies the embedded address. Three further RFC-defined embedding mechanisms are not decoded, so a blocked IPv4 address wrapped in any of them reaches the default allow.

Verified against the shipped matcher on 2026-07-25 (source R/ssrf.R; ssrf_check(host, scheme = 'https')):

  2002:7f00:1::             6to4 -> 127.0.0.1                    allowed=TRUE
  2002:a9fe:a9fe::          6to4 -> 169.254.169.254 (metadata)   allowed=TRUE
  2002:a00:1::              6to4 -> 10.0.0.1                     allowed=TRUE
  2002:c0a8:1::             6to4 -> 192.168.0.1                  allowed=TRUE
  2001:0:0:0:0:0:f5ff:fffe  Teredo -> 10.0.0.1                   allowed=TRUE
  2001:0:0:0:0:0:5601:5601  Teredo -> 169.254.169.254            allowed=TRUE
  2001:db8::5efe:a00:1      ISATAP (global prefix) -> 10.0.0.1   allowed=TRUE

Controls behave correctly: ::ffff:127.0.0.1 -> ipv4-mapped, 64:ff9b::7f00:1 -> nat64, ::ffff:0:7f00:1 -> ipv4-translated, ::7f00:1 -> ipv4-compatible. Bracketed input ([2002:7f00:1::], the form rurl emits) is also allowed.

WHY THE EXISTING DECODERS MISS THESE

All five implemented decoders read the IPv4 address from the low 32 bits (ssrf_embedded_ipv4() computes tail32 <- h[7] * 65536 + h[8]), except the NAT64 local-use case. The three missing mechanisms pack the IPv4 elsewhere:

- 6to4 (RFC 3056, 2002::/16) puts V4ADDR in bits 16-47, i.e. hextets 2-3.
- Teredo (RFC 4380, 2001::/32) puts the client IPv4 in the low 32 bits but XOR-obfuscated with 0xffffffff, so the raw value never matches a blocked range.
- ISATAP (RFC 5214) puts the IPv4 in the interface identifier after a 0000:5efe or 0200:5efe marker, under an arbitrary outer prefix.

ISATAP under a link-local prefix (fe80::5efe:a00:1) IS blocked today, but incidentally — by the outer fe80::/10 rule, not by decoding the embedded address. Under a global site prefix nothing catches it.

EXPLOITABILITY

Deployment-dependent: reaching one of these addresses requires the host to actually route that transition mechanism, and 6to4 anycast was deprecated by RFC 7526. Where it is not routed the connection simply fails, which is fail-closed by accident rather than by design. This is filed as a classification-correctness defect, not a confirmed live bypass.

That framing is deliberate. This is the same defect class as pydantic-ai's three CVEs against one blocklist in ~4 months (CVE-2025-25580 -> -46678 -> -48782), each a different IPv6-transition wrapper of the same metadata address. Adding 2002::/16 and 2001::/32 to a range list does NOT fix it: those prefixes are legitimately globally reachable, and what matters is the value they wrap.

RELATION TO ssrfr

ssrfr's ADR-001 §2.3 records this and makes the general rule normative (INV-13 embedded-address corollary): every form that embeds an address must have the embedded value extracted and classified independently, and the set of such forms is a decoder inventory, not a range table. ssrfr will ship decoders plus conformance vectors for all three.

DECISION NEEDED

Whether to patch the vendored matcher in place now, or wait for the ssrfr extraction (ROBO-mgumaoyf). Patching in place means writing it twice more (here and sitemapr) in the same shape that ROBO-pjvypcjk already shipped twice. Waiting means the gap stays open for however long the extraction takes.

Mirrored in sitemapr.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-25 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Mirror created in sitemapr as SITE-uxxdadsa. Decide once, in whichever repo acts first, and keep the two matchers in sync — or fold both into the ssrfr extraction.

#### 2026-07-25 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Fixed on fix/ssrf-transition-embeddings. Hand-mirrored from sitemapr SITE-uxxdadsa per the ROBO-mgumaoyf decision to keep independent copies until ssrfr can own the matcher.

ssrf_transition_ipv4() decodes 6to4 (hextets 2-3), Teredo (low 32 bits, XOR-undone as 4294967295 - tail32), and ISATAP (*:5efe marker, arbitrary outer prefix), handing each wrapped address to the existing IPv4 classifier. Called last from ssrf_embedded_ipv4() so the RFC 6052/4291 forms win any spelling both could claim.

All vectors from this issue verified: the four 6to4 and two Teredo forms and 2001:db8::5efe:a00:1 all moved from allowed to blocked with the new codes 6to4 / teredo / isatap. Public-wrapped controls stay allowed and are tested.

fe80::5efe:a00:1 now reports isatap rather than link-local (embedding decoder runs before the prefix block, so it names the reason that actually applies); fe80::5efe:808:808 with a public wrapped address still reports link-local via the outer prefix. Blocked either way, only the reason moved.

Note for ssrfr: ssrf_l0_reason_codes does not yet carry 6to4/teredo/isatap; it will need them when it absorbs this matcher.
