## ROBO-ldpahknv: Read the first max_bytes of an oversized robots.txt (RFC 9309 2.5)

**Status:** done

### Description

Why: RFC 9309 section 2.5: a crawler may impose a parsing limit, which must be at least 500 KiB, and parses what it read. robotstxtr today records a robots.txt over max_bytes as body_too_large with no body, which governs nothing (and news-ai-access then treats the site as unreachable). The body_truncated field exists but is always FALSE (R/fetch-policy.R comment). Decided by the maintainer 2026-11-05 (news-ai-access overnight choice 1): follow the RFC.

Scope:
- In: fetch with ssrfr's truncation option (ssrfr SSRF-pnzhhlve); parse the first max_bytes; set body_truncated = TRUE; keep a fetch_outcome that says the file was cut off, distinct from a whole file. Keep max_bytes >= 500 KiB as the documented floor for RFC mode.
- Out: per-engine limits (Google's 500 KiB and others): part of the per-engine redirect and SSRF policy discussion, not this issue.

Acceptance: an oversized 2xx robots.txt yields rules from its first max_bytes and body_truncated = TRUE.

## ROBO-lfxjkycf: Expose a public agent inventory separating literal names, RFC syntax and matcher interpretation

**Status:** todo | **Parent:** qxalfvpbilkbedprrvlckauitwbujhgc

### Description

### Why

Downstream callers currently use private collect_directive_lookup() and reimplement token extraction. A public inventory must distinguish what was written, RFC syntax, what a selected matcher reads, and what entity the author may have intended.

### Scope

In: expose a documented offline inspection API for User-agent declarations, with source/body identifier, line and group context, original bytes or an explicitly documented byte-safe representation, literal value, RFC syntax flags, selected-backend interpretation/support status, and parser diagnostics. Preserve empty, malformed, non-UTF-8, multiword and full-header values. Keep '*' and policy/control tokens distinguishable from verified crawler identities.

Offer transparent views/flags for: a leading slash, a slash anywhere, internal whitespace after delimiter/comment trimming, a version/header-like suffix, no leading product token, and full RFC product-token syntax. The RFC identifier is [A-Za-z_-]+, with '*' a separate special value. A full HTTP User-Agent header has different syntax. Filtering and candidate suffix stripping are named operations with an audit trail; neither deletes evidence or changes evaluation. Keep case-folded spellings, suffix candidates, identity candidates and actual matcher tokens separate.

A count diagnostic should compare the user's proposed exclusion of slash-led/space-containing values, optional cut-at-slash-or-whitespace candidates, and the full RFC-valid view. State the exact operation and denominator. Current study baseline: 6,822 raw values; zero start with '/', 1,239 contain whitespace, 5,583 survive that exclusion; 4,514 are literal [A-Za-z_-]+ or '*', reducing to 3,809 after case folding. These are corpus checks, not hardcoded package constants.

Out: bot identity inference, population counts, altering permissions, silently repairing files or treating malformed spellings as necessarily ineffective. Reuse existing validator information; ROBO-txnzyugl owns changes to user_agent_cut wording and written names in diagnostics.

### Acceptance criteria

- Downstream code needs no private namespace access or duplicated product-token regex to obtain the supported public inventory.
- RFC conformance, Google acceptance/interpretation and inferred identity are separate fields/concepts. Other backend claims are profile-specific; unsupported interpretation is explicit rather than guessed from Google's parser.
- Examples include Googlebot, Googlebot/1.2, Googlebot 1.2, a multiword name, /Bot, 360Spider, MJ12bot, URL/header-like values, '*', __usage_ai-training, tabs/comments and invalid bytes.
- Every filter retains a reason and permits reconstruction of all included/excluded source rows. Public output schema and byte/truncation policy are documented.

### Verification

Fixtures assert RFC syntax separately from pinned evaluator behavior. Google documents accepting googlebot/1.2 and googlebot* as googlebot; test version suffixes rather than assuming strict RFC rejection. Confirm all existing evaluator results are unchanged; package gate.

### Dependencies

None. Related: ROBO-txnzyugl (diagnostic wording), ROBO-mtmkpwuf (caller-supplied evaluator token validation); neither is replaced by this inventory.

### Sources

https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html#section-2.2
https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec#order-of-precedence-for-user-agents
Study seed: news-ai-access/design/specs/robots-inventory.md and its hashed inventories.

## ROBO-lhwpffij: Idea: spin out `indexationr` — indexation-signals library (<head> + headers + robots.txt + GSC API)

**Status:** done

### Description

### Idea: spin out `indexationr` — a dedicated indexation-signals library

Surfaced while scoping sitemapr's Layer E (per-URL page inspection, SITE-ihycidfl). Rather than growing Layer E indefinitely, a separate R library — `indexationr` — could own the full indexation picture in greater detail:

- **Page `<head>` directives:** meta robots, `rel=canonical`, `rel=alternate` hreflang.
- **HTTP headers:** `X-Robots-Tag`, `Link` (canonical / hreflang).
- **robots.txt allow/disallow:** via `robotstxtr` (engine-aware matcher already built here).
- **Ground truth from the Google Search Console API:** integrate an R GSC client (cf. the `google-searchconsole` project) to check the **actual** index status / coverage state from Google's API — not just what on-page signals *infer*.

### Why it's compelling
sitemapr's Layer E infers "effective indexability" from an **unrendered** snapshot: it can't see JS-injected markup and can't see Google's *actual* decision. The GSC API gives ground truth (indexed / crawled-not-indexed / excluded-by-noindex / blocked-by-robots, etc.). `indexationr` could reconcile the inferred signal against the real one — the single most valuable thing missing from a static inspector. sitemapr's Layer E could then consume or defer to it.

### Status
Idea / proposal for discussion — **not scheduled**. Relates to sitemapr Layer E (SITE-ihycidfl) and the meta-vs-header empirical-test issue filed in sitemapr.

## ROBO-lovclcex: [USER] Measure whether Claude's web fetch refuses a page whose robots.txt is over 500 KiB (or HTML)

**Status:** done

### Description

Why: the news-ai-access redirect study (news-ai-access design/specs/claude-redirect-checks.md, round 5; agent-view fp AGEN-adlmdztl) found that Anthropic's API web_fetch tool (web_fetch_20260318) returns url_not_allowed for some sites where every host is allowed. Each live case it saw in round 5 had a robots.txt request that ended on an HTML page over 500 KiB: charlestonchronicle.net (a 301 to another host's homepage, 638,059 bytes) and two other spam chains (714,516 and 663,273 bytes). Every fetch that succeeded had a small robots.txt. A robots.txt that redirects to another host's HTML did not cause a refusal on its own: one such site fetched fine. This is inferred, not tested. Google, by contrast, parses the first 500 KiB of a robots.txt and does not refuse (RFC 9309 §2.5). If Claude's fetcher refuses when a robots.txt is too large, robotstxtr's rulesets and validator cannot show that today.

Approach:
- On a host we control, serve one test page under several robots.txt variants, one at a time or on separate subdomains:
  (a) plain-text robots.txt with a valid allow-all group, padded with comments to just under 500 KiB (512,000 bytes) and to just over it;
  (b) the same sizes as HTML (Content-Type text/html);
  (c) a small HTML robots.txt, to separate the effect of HTML from the effect of size;
  (d) a rule that applies to Claude-User placed after the 500 KiB mark, to see whether the bytes after the cut are read.
- Fetch the page with the API web_fetch tool (with a query string, since `use_cache: false` still serves stored copies) and with Claude Code WebFetch. Record the error code each one returns and the server logs: which robots.txt was requested, the user agent, and how many bytes were read.
- Run each variant at least twice. The runner and API notes are in agent-view-lab 2026-11-11/redirect-control-5/ (api-run-env.py).

Done when: Claude's robots.txt size rule and its HTML rule are recorded as observed, with the date, in the research record (agent-view research/claude-blocklist.md and news-ai-access design/specs/claude-redirect-checks.md). The maintainer then decides whether robotstxtr models them: a validator note on an oversized or HTML robots.txt for AI fetchers, or a Claude fetch profile next to the engine rulesets. Related: ROBO-uwveumyp (Google's entry points disagree past the 500 KiB window).


### Hold (2026-11-11, burndown-v2 scout)

Waits on the maintainer. The deliverable is a live measurement with no robotstxtr code target: its results belong in agent-view (research/claude-blocklist.md) and news-ai-access (design/specs/claude-redirect-checks.md). Running it needs a public host serving variants (a)–(d) with server logs, an Anthropic API key for the web_fetch tool, and Claude Code WebFetch — none of which a burndown unit has. Question for the maintainer: run it yourself (or in a session with network and API access), and should the ticket move to agent-view, leaving a robotstxtr follow-up ("decide whether to model Claude's size/HTML rule") that depends on it? Also: the "(RFC 9309 §2.5)" citation is off — §2.5 sets only a ≥500 KiB floor; Google's prefix parsing comes from Google's own docs.


### Comments

#### 2026-11-12 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Superseded by agent-view AGEN-ubefccfc, which absorbed this work and widens it (HTML with rules, empty text/html, cross-host redirect, ChatGPT as well as Claude), as the 2026-11-11 hold suggested: a live measurement belongs in agent-view. When it reports, the maintainer decides whether robotstxtr models the result; that becomes a new robotstxtr issue. Also noted there: RFC 9309 2.5 sets only a >=500 KiB floor; Google's prefix parsing comes from Google's docs. No code changed under this id.

## ROBO-mgtngbpm: Validator: summarize XML and JSON bodies served in place of robots.txt

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

The content sniffer already exposes xml/json flags, but only HTML gets a dedicated validator summary. A JSON access-denied response currently yields unknown_directive plus no_rules; XML yields generic line errors. These obscure the deployment problem.

### Scope

In: clear document-level diagnostics for bodies that the existing bounded sniffer classifies as XML or JSON, available for raw text and fetched URL validation. Reuse the content flag rather than introduce a second parser/sniffer.
Out: asserting every XML/JSON body is an error page; remote API inspection; changing matching or discarding embedded recognized directives; an unbounded content scan.

### Acceptance criteria

- Stable code(s) and severity explain that the body appears to be XML/JSON rather than ordinary robots.txt; say access-denied only when supported, not merely because it is JSON.
- Preserve raw evidence, recognized directive parsing and per-line diagnostics as html_body does.
- Cover JSON object/array, XML error/feed, ordinary robots text, comment-contained markup and truncated bodies; avoid adding warnings to absent/unacquired bodies.
- Keep binary/HTML precedence and the sniffer's bounded-window limitations explicit. Update diagnostic docs, catalog and NEWS.

### Verification

Focused text and mocked URL examples; content-flag regression tests; merge gate.

### Dependencies

None. Builds on completed ROBO-nhuirvrd and ROBO-ccfsanhq.


### Delivery

Requested by the owner on 2026-11-16 following the robots.txt validator audit. Standalone outcome; no parent or artificial ordering dependency. Do not make this a new 0.4.0 release blocker without an explicit release-scope decision. Preserve raw evidence and distinguish standards conformance, observed crawler behavior and heuristics.




## ROBO-mgumaoyf: Extract the SSRF guard into a standalone ssrfr package

**Status:** done

### Description

Cross-repo mirror of sitemapr SITE-yeozymry. Settles the open question left by
ROBO-pjvypcjk ("should this guard become shared code rather than two
copies?").

### Decision (2026-07-25, user)

**Keep each repo's own copy for now.** robotstxtr and sitemapr each continue to
carry an independent SSRF matcher; no shared dependency is introduced, and no
CI parity job is added. Later, extract the guard into **ssrfr**, a standalone
library both packages depend on.

This unblocks the instruction ROBO-pjvypcjk left behind — "settle that before
writing a third mirrored patch". It is settled: a third mirrored patch is fine.
Mirror it by hand as before, and note it here.

### Why not shared code yet

Extracting now would put a new hard dependency on the critical path of a
package heading for CRAN submission, and an uncertain dependency chain is
already what blocks ROBO-ufxrxxga (R-universe staging cannot be retired until
rurl and its pslr/punycoder chain reach CRAN). Adding ssrfr to that chain
before robotstxtr itself is on CRAN would make the release order worse, not
better.

### What ssrfr would own

The whole structural matcher, which is currently duplicated near-verbatim:

- the IPv4 CIDR matrix and `ssrf_classify_ipv4()`
- the IPv6 expander (`ssrf_ipv6_hextets()` and its helpers), which is the piece
  both parity bugs lived in
- `ssrf_ipv6_special()`, `ssrf_ipv6_prefix_block()`, `ssrf_embedded_ipv4()`,
  `ssrf_embedded_reason()`, `ssrf_classify_ipv6()`
- the numeric/hex/octal literal detector
- the stable reason-code vocabulary

What must NOT move: the per-package fetch-engine integration and the
`ssrf_guard` caller toggle. Those differ between the two packages and are not
part of the shared matcher.

### Prior art to carry over

Both parity bugs were in the same file and had the same shape — a rule matching
the LITERAL string instead of the expanded address:

- ROBO-pzgzxkoj / SITE-vovtwvuh — the `::1` and `::` specials
- ROBO-pjvypcjk / SITE-mhfmtdxa — `fe80::/10` and `fd00:ec2::/32`

ssrfr must keep the invariant those established: every IPv6 rule matches on the
expanded hextets, never on the literal. sitemapr's ADR-003 §1 now states this
explicitly and is the closest thing to a spec for the extracted package; the
policy stays in that ADR even after the implementation moves.

Also carry over the open posture question, ROBO-udnyuuwn / SITE-zgufvkks
(malformed IPv6 literals fail open) — better to decide it once inside ssrfr
than twice outside it.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-31 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Doing this at ~/Projects/ssrfr




## ROBO-mhzmembp: Make vendor-scoped matcher semantics and Google arbitrary-token capability explicit

**Status:** done

### Description

### Problem

The engine-aware contract separates matcher backend from robots product token, but the issue history does not state the capability boundary plainly enough. Accepting an arbitrary token must not be confused with modeling the named crawler.

### Decision

Each matcher backend is authoritative only for its owning vendor semantics. Google additionally accepts arbitrary valid robots product tokens; such a result means Google parsing and matching semantics applied to that token, not behavioral compatibility with the crawler named by the token. Yandex and Bing expose only their evidence-backed supported crawler profiles unless a separately named, non-vendor generic contract is approved later.

### Scope

- Document the distinction between matcher semantics and group-selection token.
- Publish or clarify the backend capability matrix: Google arbitrary valid token; Yandex supported Yandex profiles; Bing supported Bing profiles; RFC behavior only under an RFC backend.
- Ensure public result wording and capability metadata cannot imply that Google evaluation of `bingbot`, `Yandex`, or another token predicts that crawler.
- Reconcile examples and backend-registration guidance with this boundary.
- Add focused contract tests where the distinction is executable.

### Related

- ROBO-unowhvjx: engine-aware facade.
- ROBO-gndlytpm: faithful Google parser.
- YDX-sitzaopa: closed by owner decision; arbitrary-token evaluation is not a Yandex-engine requirement.
- BING-jeeycsyh: bounded Bingbot and AdIdxBot compatibility profiles.

### Done

Committed durable documentation, capability metadata, examples, and applicable tests state the boundary unambiguously; Google arbitrary-token evaluation is described as Google semantics rather than third-party crawler compatibility; Yandex and Bing remain bounded to their supported profiles; and the project verify gate passes.

### Comments

## ROBO-mtmkpwuf: Evaluator: refuse product tokens outside [A-Za-z_-] instead of silently using User-agent: *

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

`robots_evaluate_text_v1()` and `robots_evaluate_url_v1()` accept any non-empty
`robots_product_token`. A token that contains a character outside `[A-Za-z_-]` can never equal a
group's user-agent under Google's matcher. Google's matcher cuts each `User-agent` value in the
file at its first such character, then compares the cut value with the caller's token as given.
The caller's token is not cut. Such a token cannot match a named group: `*` rules apply if a `*`
group exists, and otherwise the URL is allowed by default. The row still reports
`matcher_status = "evaluated"`.

Tested on 2026-11-17 at 188c0a6, Google backend and `google` ruleset, against a file with
`User-agent: archive.org_bot` / `Disallow: /`, `User-agent: Googlebot/2.1` / `Disallow: /g` and
`User-agent: *` / `Disallow: /star`:

| token | `/g` | `/star` |
|---|---|---|
| `archive.org_bot` | allow `[*]` | disallow L8 `[*]` |
| `Googlebot/2.1` | allow `[*]` | disallow `[*]` |
| `Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Googlebot/2.1)` | allow `[*]` | disallow `[*]` |
| ` Googlebot` (leading space) | allow `[*]` | disallow `[*]` |
| `Googlebot` | disallow L5 `[Googlebot]` | allow |

The `rfc9309` ruleset gives the same results. A real file shows the cost:
https://www.washingtonpost.com/robots.txt (fetched 2026-11-17) has `User-agent: archive.org_bot`
/ `Disallow: /` at line 147. Passing that spelling returns allow.

The RFC grammar supports treating this as invalid input. RFC 9309 §2.2.1 says a product token
"MUST contain only uppercase and lowercase letters ('a-z' and 'A-Z'), underscores ('_'), and
hyphens ('-')". ROBO-mhzmembp's decision already says Google accepts arbitrary *valid* robots
product tokens. Returning an error is this package's policy: upstream Google ships
`RobotsMatcher::IsValidUserAgentToObey()` (vendored at `src/robots.cc:670`) for callers to use,
but neither `AllowedByRobots` nor upstream `robots_main.cc` applies it. The robots token and the
HTTP User-Agent string are easy to confuse, as `resolve-matcher-profile-v1.R` already notes, and
a full UA string is one of the inputs this catches.

### Scope

In:
- Rows on the `google` and `rfc9309` backends whose token does not match
  `^[A-Za-z_-]+$` (ASCII) come back `not_evaluated`, with error class
  `robots_invalid_product_token` (the class already exists).
- The message names the problem and, when present, the leading syntactically valid prefix
  (`archive`, `Googlebot`) as a hint. A prefix need not identify the intended crawler, so it is
  offered, never applied. An input with no valid leading run gets the message without a hint.
- This applies under both entry points, and before any fetch on the URL entry point, so no
  request is spent on a row that can't be answered.
- Bing and Yandex keep their current refusal paths.

Out:
- The legacy `allowed_by_robots_text()` and `allowed_by_robots_url()`. They keep today's
  behavior; an `@details` sentence warns about the case.
- Trimming or rewriting the token for the caller.
- Changing how User-agent values *in the file* are read (`user_agent_cut` covers that).

### Acceptance criteria

- The invalid tokens in the table are refused, one row each, with no throw for a vector input.
  `Googlebot`, `Googlebot-Image`, `google_extended` and `a-` stay evaluated.
- Also refused: digits only (`123`), a literal `*`, a trailing space or tab, and non-ASCII
  letters (`Gooģlebot`).
- A mixed vector of valid and invalid tokens gives the right per-row outcome, and the URL entry
  point makes no fetch that only an invalid row needs.
- Rulesets that decide without a matcher (`allow_all` and the like) are unaffected.
- The token grammar is published in the backend capability object that already carries
  `product_token_role` and `product_token_comparison` (`R/engine-contract-v1.R`, around line
  480), as a new field for `google` and `rfc9309`.
- The NEWS line names the change, since a caller that passed `Googlebot/2.1` gets a different
  result.

### Verification

Unit tests on both entry points, the URL one with a mocked fetch that asserts no request for a
refused row. Merge gate.

### Dependencies

None. Related: ROBO-mhzmembp (capability boundary), ROBO-txnzyugl (file-side cut wording).




## ROBO-mxermwed: Edge-case catalog: how odd robots.txt files behave in RFC 9309, Google's docs, our validator and our matcher

**Status:** done

### Description

### Why

Every validator gap found on 2026-10-07 was an edge case nobody had written down: a named group dropping the `*` rules (ROBO-gfjotdrr), `Allow: /` cancelling `Disallow: /` (ROBO-fdhmlvwm), dead patterns (ROBO-xblfzkid), rule-less documents reported as errors (ROBO-vxrzcqpe). Finding them one at a time, by accident, is slow. A deliberate pass over the odd files that real sites serve should find the rest in one go and give the package a fixture set that other work (the competitor deep dive) can reuse.

### Scope

In: a catalog of edge cases. For each case record the RFC 9309 rule, Google's documented behavior, Google's matcher result (through our matcher), our validator's diagnostics, and whether the outcome would surprise a site owner. Families to cover at least:

- **Encoding:** UTF-8 BOM, BOM in mid-file, UTF-16 with and without BOM, Latin-1 bytes, invalid UTF-8, NUL bytes, non-ASCII paths in rules.
- **Escaping:** percent-encoded against raw characters in rules and URLs (`%2F`, `%7E`, non-ASCII), letter case in percent-escapes and paths, `*` and `$` in odd positions.
- **Blank and empty:** 0 bytes, whitespace only, line endings (CRLF, CR only, mixed), no final newline.
- **Content-Type mismatches:** an empty body served as `text/plain`; a non-text body (HTML, an SPA catch-all page, gzip, an image) served as `text/plain`; a valid robots.txt served as `text/html` or `application/octet-stream`. The fetch layer does not record `Content-Type` today (no reference in `R/`), so part of this case is deciding whether it should.
- **Comments only, sitemaps only, and both**; ROBO-vxrzcqpe fixes the known part.
- **Grouping surprises:** a named group drops the `*` rules; several `User-agent` lines sharing one group; a `User-agent` after rules starting a new group; blank lines inside a group (Google ignores them); two groups for the same agent (merged); product-token matching (`Googlebot/2.1`, letter case, `Googlebot-Image` falling back to `Googlebot`); a `Sitemap:` line in the middle of a group.
- **Size and limits:** files over Google's 500 KiB limit, very long lines, very many groups.
- Anything else the pass turns up.

Out:
- Fixing what the catalog finds. Each gap becomes its own fp issue, created when the catalog is written.
- Engines other than Google, except where the engine contract already records a documented difference.

### Acceptance criteria

- A committed catalog in `design/` (`design/` holds committed design docs; `docs/` is the generated site and is gitignored), one row or section per case, with the columns above and sources for every documented-behavior claim.
- Each case has a fixture under `tests/` that the catalog points to, so the set can be rerun and reused.
- Every surprising or wrong outcome is either already covered by an fp issue (cited by id) or has a new one.

### Verification

The fixtures run in the test suite, pinning the current behavior or marked as known gaps tied to their fp issue. The verify gate passes.

### Dependencies

None. The competitor deep dive depends on this issue's fixture set.

## ROBO-mxsphtoo: Research Google crawler-token fallback (Googlebot-Image to Googlebot) against the single-agent matcher binding

**Status:** done

### Description

Why: found by the ROBO-mxermwed scout, 2026-11-08. src/matcher_binding.cpp calls Google's single-agent `OneAgentAllowedByRobots`, so a caller token such as `Googlebot-Image` obeys a `Googlebot-Image` group if one exists, and otherwise falls back to `*`, never to a `Googlebot` group. Google's crawler documentation describes some of its crawlers following Googlebot's rules when they have no group of their own. The C++ library also has a multi-agent entry point (`AllowedByRobots` with several user agents) for that case. Which crawlers fall back, and in which order, is not settled here. Nor is whether that fallback belongs in the matcher or with the caller.

Scope:
- In: research and record, citing sources, which Google crawler tokens fall back to which group, and in what order. Then decide whether robotstxtr should model the fallback (a documented token map passed to the multi-agent matcher), leave it to the caller, or only document it. Record the decision in design/engine-profiles.md.
- Out: implementing the change. That becomes its own issue once decided.

Acceptance criteria: the fallback table is recorded with sources, and a decision with its reasons, plus a follow-up issue if anything changes.

Dependencies: none.

## ROBO-nrnucnru: Validator calls a rule empty when a NUL after its colon hides the path Google's matcher reads

**Status:** done

### Description

### Why

Found in the review of ROBO-ctdkqawi. A NUL right after a rule's colon leaves the parser an empty value, so it reports `empty_rule_value` ("ignored by the matcher"), while robotstxtr's Google matcher, which drops NULs, reads and enforces the full path. The validator says the line does nothing when, as Google's matcher reads it, the line blocks a path.

Example: `User-agent: *\nDisallow: \0/private\n` gives `nul_byte@2` and `empty_rule_value@2`, and no `rules_after_nul_removal`. Behavior on main before ROBO-ctdkqawi is the same, so this is pre-existing.

ROBO-ctdkqawi keys hidden rules by line, type and group, not by value (a NUL that only shortens a value keeps its rule). An empty raw value is no rule at all, so it sits outside that boundary.

### Scope

In: decide how the validator reports a rule whose raw value is empty but whose NUL-free value is not: count it in `rules_after_nul_removal`, or reword `empty_rule_value` on such a line. Tests with test-local bytes.
Out: changing how the parser or the matchers read NULs.

### Acceptance criteria

The example above draws a row that says Google's matcher reads `/private` on that line. The existing pins (the `Disallow: /a\0b` "neither code" test, the no-raw-rule message) stay green.


### Comments

## ROBO-nvgtqdlu: Blind-reader pilot: 24 real files, one Haiku read each, every answer inspected

**Status:** todo | **Parent:** gqkhoogtukbnpwrgdnvsnxxswjodwsqm

### Description

Why
The cheapest experiment that tells us whether this whole approach is worth continuing. If 24 files do not produce findings we did not already have, we stop and have spent very little.

Scope (in)
- A small script in dev/blind-reader/ that sends one prompt per file to claude-haiku-5-5 (direct API calls; no batching at this size) and saves each response as JSONL with the model id. The prompt text lives in the repo.
- 24 real files from ~/Projects/news-ai-access/data/raw: 12 chosen at random from files robots_validate_text() calls clean, and 12 spanning existing validator diagnostics and the known disagreement classes. Prefer files outside whatever the earlier private runs sampled; look at what those used before choosing. Keep the sampling seed.
- Per file: a token and path chosen so matching is exercised; the RFC 9309 decision question (allow | disallow | unspecified | cannot_tell); suspected issues quoting the line text; what would surprise the owner.
- A handful of synthetic manifest rows as anchors, chosen from the rows where Google and rfc9309_decision differ (7 of 108) or the RFC is silent (30 of 108): they show which way Haiku leans, with the relevant RFC 9309 clauses pasted in the prompt and a clause citation required, and they catch a broken prompt or parser. If Haiku still answers Google's way, the decision question is a naive-reader probe, not an RFC probe; say so in the closing comment.
- Read every response, agreements and uncertain ones included. Classify each candidate in a line in a comment on this issue (the epic's list), and resolve it against the RFC text or engine behavior ourselves before calling it a finding.
Scope (out): batch plumbing, a validator category map, majority voting, a large sample, a baseline error rate (this is a pilot, not a measurement), fixes for what is found.

Acceptance criteria
24 responses saved; every candidate classified and resolved; actionable ones filed as top-level issues citing the epic or added as a synthetic fixture with an ordinary expectation. The closing comment gives: novel actionable findings, false alarms, Haiku cost, minutes spent reading, and one line on whether to continue (and what the pilot taught about the prompt). It makes no claim about how common anything is in the corpus.

Verification
The closing comment's ids resolve with fp issue show; the script reruns from the saved sample list.

Dependencies
None.

## ROBO-nvzzjubl: Validator: report a lower-case escape whose upper-case twin is already in the group as a duplicate

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

Shopify's default `robots.txt.liquid` writes every rule with an escaped `+` twice, once as `%2B`
and once as `%2b`. The validator gives each `%2b` line a `rule_lowercase_escape` warning that
says "write it as '%2B'", although the line above already does. https://www.gymshark.com/robots.txt
(fetched 2026-11-18), a Shopify store, gets 15 such warnings; every store that keeps the default
gets them too.

Checked with the Google backend on 2026-11-18: `Disallow: /c/*%2b*` and `Disallow: /c/*%2B*`
give the same answers. Both disallow `/c/a%2Bb`; neither disallows `/c/a%2bb` or `/c/a+b`.
Google upper-cases the escape in the pattern, so the `%2b` line is a duplicate of the `%2B` line,
and no Google rule can match a URL written with `%2b`.

### Scope

In: when a group already holds the rule a lower-case-escape line becomes after Google
upper-cases its escapes, report that line as a duplicate of the earlier one (info, naming its
line), and say that a URL written with the lower-case escape is matched by neither. The
`rule_lowercase_escape` warning stays for a lower-case escape with no upper-case twin. The same
holds for mixed lines such as Shopify's `ls%3d*%3fls%3d*` beside `ls%3D*%3Fls%3D*`.

Out: changing matching. Bing and Yandex: ROBO-polznjqh records that Yandex compares the rule as
written, so the twin is not a duplicate there; the wording is per engine profile.

### Acceptance criteria

- The Gymshark shape gives no `rule_lowercase_escape` warning on a line whose upper-case twin
  is in the same group; each such line gets one info row naming the twin.
- A lone `%2b` rule keeps today's warning. A twin in a different group is not a duplicate.
- `duplicate_rule` keeps its meaning (rules identical as written); the new row is distinguishable
  from it. Docs entry; NEWS one line.

### Verification

Synthetic fixtures: the twin pair, a lone lower-case rule, a twin in another group, a mixed
`%3d`/`%3f` line. Cross-check each with `robots_evaluate_text_v1()` on the Google backend.

## ROBO-ogwchglq: [PARKED] Measure Yandex's and Bing's robots.txt fetch rules with served test files

**Status:** todo

### Description

Why: Yandex documents no robots.txt redirect limit and no outcome past it (ADR 0001 open question 3, "Yandex over_budget -> allow_all", and the hop-cap gap in design/engine-fetch-rules-sources.md). Bing documents none of its robots.txt fetch rules (ADR 0001 open question 7): redirect count, size limit, https->http. Maintainer, 2026-11-05: the bing ruleset stays on RFC 9309 defaults labeled assumed_rfc9309, no recurring documentation search; measure instead. Maintainer, 2026-11-05: don't decide it on paper; measure it. An edge case, outside the news-ai-access study's focus (AI agents and their blocking), so parked: start only on an instruction naming it.

Until measured, the yandex ruleset's over_budget cell stays documentation_gap with the five-hop application_choice fallback; ADR 0001 does not adopt "over_budget -> allow_all".

Approach:
- On a host we control, serve robots.txt behind a redirect chain of N hops (each hop a distinct URL, then a 200 robots.txt with a distinctive rule), and let Yandex fetch it (YandexBot crawl, or Yandex Webmaster's robots.txt analysis tool, whichever reports what it read).
- Start at N = 20 (the WHATWG Fetch redirect limit) and work down (20, 10, 6, 5) to find the largest N Yandex follows, and what it does past it: rules read, file treated as open (allow all), as missing, or as unavailable.
- Bing (Bingbot, or Bing Webmaster Tools' robots.txt tester): the same redirect-chain series, plus an oversized robots.txt (rules placed before and after 500 KiB) and an https->http redirect to see whether it follows a downgrade.
- Record dates, the tool or bot, raw server logs, and what each engine reported.

Done when: the yandex ruleset's hop cap and over_budget meaning, and the bing ruleset's redirect, size and downgrade rules, are set from the measurements, labeled as observed (with date), in engine-profiles.md and the research record.


### Comments

#### 2026-11-09 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Related, 2026-11-09: ROBO-bpywsjwv ([USER]) collects webmaster-tester questions for matcher disagreement classes the engine audit (ROBO-fbbwepsv) cannot settle. This issue stays parked; it covers fetch rules, which need served files.

## ROBO-otomgbge: Validator: note bare-prefix rules that also match sibling paths (corpus-gated)

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

A literal rule (no `*`) without a trailing `/` or `$` matches every path that *starts with* it, not only the
path it names and its subpaths. Authors often expect it to stop at the segment boundary.
Observed on https://www.washingtonpost.com/robots.txt (fetched 2026-11-17), Google backend at
188c0a6, `*` group:

- `Disallow: /search` (line 88): `/searchlight` → disallow L88.
- `Disallow: /comments` (line 87): `/commentsx` → disallow L87.

https://natu.shop/robots.txt (fetched 2026-11-17) shows the trap from the other side. Its
lines 97-119 are full URLs that never match. Fixed by removing the host,
`Disallow: /collections/produkty` (line 105) would also block `/collections/produkty-bialko`,
`/collections/produkty-ebooki` and the other `produkty-…` collections the file lists
separately.

Under a full block, the same shape on an Allow opens siblings. Bloomberg's `Allow: /tc` allows
`/tcfd-report` (ROBO-acoqvdfb).

The maintainer asked on 2026-11-17 for "no trailing slash lines" to be flagged, since they are
implicit prefix matchers. ROBO-acoqvdfb (parked) covers only the Allow-under-full-block case and
waits on a corpus noise measure. That concern applies here more strongly, because this flags
ordinary literal Disallow lines file-wide.

### Scope

In: an info code, at most one row per group, on the group's first candidate line. A candidate
is a literal Allow or Disallow (no `*`, no `$`) whose last segment has no trailing `/` and no
`.`. The row lists up to five candidates plus a count, each with a generated sibling example
(`/search` → `/searchx`) that the pattern matches. The message says what the rule matches and
names `P/` and `P$` as narrower spellings. It does not call the rule wrong.

Out: patterns with `*` or `$`; a last segment with a dot; `/`; empty values; patterns with a
query (`?`) or percent-encoding; Allow lines already reported by
ROBO-acoqvdfb's code, if that ships first.

### Acceptance criteria

- Before implementation, run it on a pinned corpus sample and record rows per file and the share
  of files with a row in this issue. The maintainer then decides whether to ship it as info, put
  it behind an option, or drop it.
- If shipped: the WaPo reduction fires, with one row for the `*` group. Silent on `/x/`, `/x$`,
  `/x*`, `/x.html` and `/`. Each generated sibling is matched by the pattern, which is checked by
  a fixture.
- ROBO-acoqvdfb is closed as absorbed, or kept with the reason recorded.

### Verification

Corpus notes, then fixtures. Merge gate.

### Dependencies

None. Related: ROBO-acoqvdfb, ROBO-roypaoox (bare URL versus slash URL decisions), ROBO-xexjgecr.

## ROBO-ovgfyowt: Validator: warn when valid UTF-8 rules hit observed Yandex Unicode matching failures

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

Valid UTF-8 rules can be ineffective in Yandex's robots.txt analyzer even though the document passes encoding checks. The Y4 observations in ROBO-bpywsjwv (2026-11-13) found raw /café and /каталог rules did not restrict the tested raw or escaped targets and drew WARN_SUSPECT_SYMBOL; a percent-encoded café rule worked. July observations ydx-20/21 also concern this class. These findings need promotion/replication through YDX-vakiowhn and YDX-vgomfspr, not extrapolation from Bing.

Owner requested sibling-engine coverage on 2026-11-16 after ROBO-wrlaufai was filed for Bing.

### Scope

In: a stable, line-specific validator warning for raw Unicode Allow/Disallow patterns whose Yandex compatibility problem is established by accepted evidence. Distinguish well-formed UTF-8 from an engine-specific matching problem; explain the affected pattern and recommend UTF-8 percent-encoding only where paired accepted probes establish the repair. Cover text and URL validation, diagnostic documentation, edge-case catalog and NEWS.

Out: matcher changes; automatic rewriting/transcoding; HTTP charset inference; generic mojibake detection; copying Bing's affected-character set; blanket claims about every non-ASCII scalar or all WARN_SUSPECT_SYMBOL findings; crawler-confirmed claims based only on analyzer observations.

### Acceptance criteria

- Derive the warning's exact character/pattern scope from accepted Yandex observations adopted through ROBO-spssfbdo; record observation IDs and evidence tier. Supplement with the explicit Cyrillic guidance at https://www.yandex.com/support/webmaster/en/controlling-robot/robots-txt where applicable, while distinguishing documentation from observed matching effects.
- Emit a stable warning code on the affected rule line, naming Yandex and supplying useful pattern/character evidence. Keep the document encoding status UTF-8 when its bytes are valid UTF-8.
- Preserve actual parser comment/value boundaries. Comment-only occurrences, unaffected tested controls and tested encoded repairs do not draw the warning.
- Do not equate WARN_SUSPECT_SYMBOL with an inert rule: that analyzer warning also appears on other tested patterns that do match. Assert ineffectiveness only where paired matching observations establish it.
- Existing malformed-byte diagnostics remain unchanged. Keep Bing-specific detection independent, although byte-scanning helpers may be shared.
- Pin regression cases for affected raw literals, accepted encoded repairs, unaffected controls, comments and malformed bytes. Cover Allow as well as Disallow where evidence supports the same effect; do not invent unmeasured semantics.
- Include a Google control: literal UTF-8 rules remain supported without a Google-specific compatibility warning. Google documents raw UTF-8 support at https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec and tests/testthat/test-upstream-matcher-cases-r9.R already pins literal-Unicode rule matching against an escaped URL.

### Verification

Focused validator tests for raw/character input and a mocked URL path preserving fetched bytes, existing encoding diagnostics, documented observation provenance, and the repository merge gate.

### Dependencies

Depends on ROBO-spssfbdo for the adopted Yandex behavior and regression corpus, which waits on ROBO-jtsmzesl. Upstream: robotstxtyandex YDX-vakiowhn (fresh evidence) and YDX-vgomfspr (0.3.0 release). Related, not ordered: ROBO-wrlaufai (Bing warning). Standalone validator outcome; no new 0.4.0 release blocker is added without an explicit scope decision.




## ROBO-oxfpgdrx: Validate Bing, Yandex and Googlebot-Image robots.txt findings on turczynski.pl with live crawler evidence

**Status:** in-progress

### Description

### Why

Our Bing and Yandex compatibility findings came from probing the webmaster tools' admin panels and robots.txt testers. The maintainer has now identified turczynski.pl as a live site where we can test whether those findings hold for actual crawling. Validate the existing findings against served files and observed crawler requests, keeping tester observations distinct from production crawler evidence.

### Scope

In:
- Inventory the existing Bing and Yandex findings and unresolved questions from the engine profiles, source research and sibling-library corpora. Select synthesized fixtures that discriminate the competing interpretations, with ordinary allow/disallow controls.
- Use turczynski.pl, or isolated test origins under it, to serve versioned robots.txt bodies and harmless probe pages. Record exact body bytes and hashes, URLs, bot/profile, expected decisions and the basis of each expectation before each run.
- Compare webmaster tester results with verified Bing/Yandex crawler requests and server logs. Record robots.txt retrieval, fixture version, cache/refresh timing, redirects, response status, observation date and crawl window. Verify crawler identity rather than trusting the User-Agent alone.
- Exercise matcher disagreements first. Include fetch-policy questions only where the live setup supports an interpretable measurement; coordinate with ROBO-ogwchglq without starting its parked program implicitly.
- Preserve a reproducible evidence record and a per-finding verdict: confirmed, contradicted or inconclusive. Restore the site's original configuration after the experiment.

Out: changing matcher semantics or shipping new engine claims on the strength of a tester alone; publishing private corpus files, paths, examples or figures; restarting the full parked fetch-policy study. Any confirmed implementation correction is follow-up work in the owning repository.

### Google: Googlebot-Image parent-token fallback (ROBO-fbbmvbob)

Since ROBO-fbbmvbob, robotstxtr's v1 `google` ruleset follows Google's common-crawlers documentation: a crawler with a parent token (Googlebot-Image -> `Googlebot`) obeys its own group, else the parent's group, else `*`. Google's open-source matcher has no crawler-to-token map (`src/robots.cc` `HandleUserAgent()` compares the caller's tokens only), so for this case the documentation is the only evidence, and the legacy functions still give the matcher's literal answer (`*`). This probe tests the documented reading against the real crawler.

- Fixture: the catalog's `grp-googlebot-image-fallback` shape, on fresh probe paths: `User-agent: Googlebot` / `Disallow: /gi-x/` / blank / `User-agent: *` / `Disallow: /gi-y/`, plus the site's normal rules.
- Probes: one image under each of `/gi-x/` and `/gi-y/`, referenced from a page Googlebot already crawls, plus an allowed control image outside both.
- Predictions: documented fallback (v1 today): Googlebot-Image fetches `/gi-y/` images and never `/gi-x/`. Matcher literal (`*` group): the reverse.
- Controls: Search Console's robots.txt report shows the fixture version fetched; Googlebot-Image fetches the control image in the same window; crawler identity verified by reverse DNS and Google's published IP ranges, not the User-Agent. Only a positive fetch on the predicted-allowed side, repeated with fresh paths, counts; an absent fetch alone is inconclusive.
- Outcome: confirmed keeps the v1 behavior and records the evidence in design/engine-profiles.md §5a; contradicted is a follow-up issue to revert the fallback (ROBO-fbbmvbob's option 3).

### Gate

[USER] / maintainer-gated: execution needs the maintainer to provide or confirm access to the site's hosting/configuration, server logs and relevant webmaster accounts, and the isolated origins or paths available for the experiment. Filing this issue does not deploy anything or change the live site's robots.txt.

### Acceptance criteria

- A dated matrix maps every selected finding to the exact served fixture, tester observation, crawler evidence and verdict.
- Controls establish that each observed crawler fetched the intended robots.txt version and could reach allowed probe pages. A missing crawl alone never proves a disallow; cache uncertainty or insufficient crawl activity yields an inconclusive result.
- The record separates tester behavior, observed crawler behavior and any generalization. Contradictions and remaining gaps have explicit dispositions.
- Evidence is sanitized before committing; credentials, account information and unsanitized access logs stay outside git. Durable results belong under design/ and relevant sibling corpora receive separately scoped follow-ups.
- The original site configuration is restored and checked.

### Verification

Reproduce local matcher predictions from the saved fixture bytes and pinned library versions. Review timestamped server evidence against those predictions and the webmaster observations. Repeat discriminating cases with fresh probe URLs and a documented robots.txt refresh before promoting a finding.

### Dependencies

Maintainer access/setup gate above. Related: ROBO-bpywsjwv (unevidenced disagreement classes in webmaster testers), ROBO-glssaxva (cross-engine triage), ROBO-ogwchglq (parked fetch-rule measurements). Existing findings can be selected without waiting for the full triage; new classes can be added when it produces them. No hard issue dependencies.

## ROBO-oykjiyjj: Allow-list the two curl advisories the hard-dependency audit cannot clear

**Status:** done

### Description

Route **(a)** of `SEOR-feqgnbwt`, chosen by the owner on 2026-09-10: allow-list
the two `curl` advisories by ID, each with a written reason and a review date,
and add a stale-row check so the list cannot rot silently.

### Why this repo is different

Scoping the OSS Index audit to hard dependencies (`Depends` + `Imports`)
cleared five of the seven repos carrying `tests/testthat/test-security.R`.
It does **not** clear this one: `curl` is a genuine hard dependency here,
reached through httr2. Measured 2026-09-10 — hard scope audits the smaller set
and still reports `curl`.

CRAN's current `curl` is 8.0.0 (verified against `available.packages()` on
cloud.r-project.org, 2026-09-10) and both advisories name libcurl ranges that
include it. **There is no version to upgrade to**, so no local change makes the
audit clean.

- **CVE-2026-18924** — CWE-416 use-after-free, HTTP/2 server push over a shared
  connection handle. CVSS 9.1, published 2026-09-06 — that date is when this
  started blocking pushes.
- **CVE-2026-3783** — CWE-522, an OAuth2 bearer token leaked to a redirect
  target when `.netrc` carries a machine/default entry. CVSS 6.9.

### The three rules

- **A UNEXPECTED** — an advisory that is reported and not allow-listed FAILS.
  The gate keeps doing its job for httr2, xml2 and everything else.
- **B STALE** — an allow-listed advisory that is no longer reported FAILS. An
  allow-list may not over-permit; a row that has outlived its justification has
  to be deleted, not left to silently widen the exemption. Same rule as C0 in
  rurl's `tools/curl-zero-gate.R` (`RURL-cunfohwy`).
- **C DRIFT** — past its review date, or audited at a `curl` later than the
  version the row was written against, a row **warns**. Deliberately not a
  failure: a calendar date that turns every push red is how a gate teaches
  people to reach for `--no-verify`. The warning is visible in the testthat
  summary and in CI logs.

A separate offline test checks that every row is well-formed — all five fields
present, and a reason of real length rather than a placeholder.

### Measured reachability, recorded so it can be re-checked

`curl::curl_options()` exposes no option matching `push`, and
`curl::multi_set()` takes only `total_con`, `host_con`, `max_streams`,
`multiplex` and `pool` — no push callback. `CURLMOPT_PUSHFUNCTION` is therefore
not settable from R at all, so the HTTP/2 server-push path CVE-2026-18924
requires cannot be entered through the R `curl` package. Re-check with those
two calls before renewing the row.

Fleet epic: `SEOR-eqpdrqnl`. Decision: `SEOR-feqgnbwt`.


### Comments

#### 2026-09-10 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Verify gate PASS (lint clean, no generated-docs drift, R CMD check --as-cran against a clean git archive export: 0E/0W/1N) — the first green push in this repo since 2026-09-06. The remaining NOTE is the pre-existing GitHub-URL blocker ROBO-plzvdbjz, untouched. Branched from `main`, deliberately not from `feature/gitlab-ci-verify-pipeline` (MR !2, held): no file overlap, so this does not wait on that migration. ## ROBO-pbwijkdq: Validator: warn when a named group drops User-agent: * Disallows, and merge identical inheritance rows

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

A common mistake is to write a named group as if it added to `*`: a few extra Disallows, or a
single Allow. It replaces `*` for that crawler instead (RFC 9309 §2.2.1), so every `*` Disallow
is lost. Every named group gets the same `wildcard_rules_not_inherited` info today, so this
loosening case drowns among deliberately stricter groups.

Observed on https://www.bloomberg.com/robots.txt (fetched 2026-11-17), Google backend:
- `Googlebot-News` (line 55, three Disallows): `/account/settings` and `/search?q=x` allowed,
  though `*` disallows both.
- `Twitterbot` (line 60, only `Allow: /en/news/thp`): everything allowed; the group's only
  effect is to lift all `*` rules.
- `Mediapartners-Google` (line 42) and `Spinn3r` (line 50) have the same shape.

The same file gets 21 `wildcard_rules_not_inherited` rows; 12 carry the same content (full block
loses `Allow: /account/newsletters`) and differ only in their token list.

### Scope

In:
1. A new warning code (working name `wildcard_disallows_not_inherited`) for a named group
   (repeated groups merged) whose effective rules hold no full block and that lacks at least one
   `*` Disallow, by the existing lost-rule predicate of `wildcard_rules_not_inherited`, where a
   concrete witness path is disallowed under `*` and allowed under the named group. An
   allow-only group (no non-empty Disallow in its merged rules) says so in the message. The
   message lists only the lost `*` Disallows that have such a witness.
2. `wildcard_rules_not_inherited` keeps info severity and its detection condition. Rules the
   warning reports for a group are left out of that group's info row; a group can carry both
   codes when they describe different lost rules (e.g. lost Allows in the info).
3. After that suppression, info rows with identical remaining lost-rule content merge into one
   row, anchored on the earliest group's first User-agent line, naming every group with its
   line (bounded list, "and N more groups" past the bound). Warning rows never merge.

Out: changing the lost-rule predicate; consolidation suggestions (ROBO-rdxgnqhw); full-block
groups whose Allow reopens a `*` Disallow (ROBO-cufxicmz).

### Acceptance criteria

- Bloomberg shape: warnings for the Googlebot-News, Twitterbot, Mediapartners-Google and
  Spinn3r groups; the 12 identical full-block rows become one info row.
- A named group that restates every `*` Disallow gets no warning; the info still reports any
  lost `*` Allow.
- Pattern cases: `*` `Disallow: /private` vs named `Disallow: /private$` warns (witness
  `/private/x`); a `*` Allow that cancels the lost Disallow on every witness means no warning.
- Repeated named groups merge before the check; an empty `Disallow:` counts as no Disallow.
- An `Allow: /` group warns. https://wordpress.org/robots.txt (fetched 2026-11-18) gives GPTBot,
  ClaudeBot and seven others `Allow: /` groups under a `*` group that disallows `/wp-admin/`,
  `/search`, `/?s=` and `/plugins/search/`; today those groups get no row at all.
- AdsBot tokens (`AdsBot-Google`, `AdsBot-Google-Mobile`) get no warning: they ignore
  `User-agent: *` with or without a group of their own (ROBO-fbbmvbob), so the group loosens
  nothing. Their info row says the `*` group never applied to them.
- Severity of no existing code changes. Docs table, `design/linter-set.md`, NEWS one line each
  for the new code and the merge.

### Verification

Focused fixtures for: an additive group, an allow-only group, a restating group, a full-block
group, several full-block groups with identical loss (merged), several with different loss (not
merged), the pattern cases, a repeated group and an empty Disallow. Existing
`wildcard_rules_not_inherited` tests change only where rows merge. Merge gate.

### Dependencies

None. Shares `wildcard_inheritance_diagnostics()` with ROBO-cufxicmz
(`allow_reopens_wildcard_disallow`). Related: ROBO-bwpacxtq, ROBO-gkuuwbgc, ROBO-rdxgnqhw. Reviewed with GPT-6.1-Sol (medium)
on 2026-11-17.



### Comments

#### 2026-11-17 — bartek@turczynski.pl

More evidence from four files fetched 2026-11-17 (Google backend, 188c0a6), and two gaps in the scope as written.

- **WaPo** (https://www.washingtonpost.com/robots.txt): 34 `wildcard_rules_not_inherited` rows. 23 are the full-block variant, and each lists the same three `*` Allows (`/pb/resources/`, `/pb/gr/`, `/pb/resource/`). Those cut holes in `*`'s `Disallow: /pb/`. Repeated across full-block groups, the missing-Allow details add noise, which supports the merge in item 3.
- **Escalation signal.** Twitterbot (lines 119-121) holds `Allow: /posttv-beta/` and `Disallow: /amphtml/*`. That Allow does not change access within its own group, since nothing there disallows `/posttv-beta/`; it differs from `*` only because `*` has `Disallow: /posttv-beta/` (line 41). Meanwhile Twitterbot gets `/search` and `/subscribe/signin/`. The warning's message could name such an Allow as an effect fact (no change in-group; lifts a `*` Disallow), without claiming intent. SemrushBot (lines 123-125) adds one path and drops all 116 `*` rules.
- **Gap 1: allow-all named groups are skipped.** `wildcard_inheritance_diagnostics()` skips a crawler whose judged rules are all allow-all (`if (any(judged) && all(allow_all[judged])) next`). So "the existing lost-rule predicate" never sees `User-agent: OAI-SearchBot` / `Allow: /` on https://natu.shop/robots.txt (lines 121-122). That group lifts `/admin`, `/checkout`, `/cart/` and `/account`; for example, OAI-SearchBot gets `/checkout` → allow. The same holds for the New Yorker's `Allow: /` group for Google-InspectionTool, Storebot-Google, Twitterbot and others (lines 44-52): Google-InspectionTool gets `/account/x` → allow L52. Vendors' docs suggest exactly that snippet ("User-agent: OAI-SearchBot / Allow: /"). Decide whether an allow-all named group gets the warning, requiring a witness path its otherwise-applicable `*` group blocks. Intentional grants are common, so the message describes the changed coverage without calling it a mistake. Assign overlaps with ROBO-cufxicmz consistently. Exempt the tokens below either way.
- **Gap 2: crawlers that ignore `*` anyway.** `google_crawler_tokens_v1()` marks `AdsBot-Google`, `AdsBot-Google-Mobile` and `Mediapartners-Google` as `exact_only`, following Google's special-case crawler docs: they ignore rules addressed only to `*`, named or not (a group naming both `*` and the crawler still applies). Tested on the package: with only `User-agent: *` / `Disallow: /`, AdsBot-Google and Mediapartners-Google get `/x` → allow and Googlebot disallow. The acceptance criterion "warnings for … Mediapartners-Google" is therefore wrong for Google: that group loses nothing it would otherwise have had. Today's info row for natu.shop's `adsbot-google` group (line 70) also says "`User-agent: *` applies only to crawlers no group names", which is false for AdsBot. These tokens need no warning, and a reworded info row (or none).

#### 2026-11-17 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Evidence fetched 2026-11-18, Google backend; the description's acceptance criteria now also cover `Allow: /` groups and AdsBot.
- https://www.forbes.com/robots.txt line 380, `AmazonAdBot`: only Allow lines that copy most `*` Disallows (`/following/`, `/search/`, `/preview/` …) but not `/ajax/`, `/json/`, `/test/`, `*wp-admin*`, `/advisor/journey/` or `/research-survey`, so with no Disallow the bot may crawl everything. The author apparently expected the group to add to `*`.
- forbes.com line 26, `googlebot-news`: 21 Disallows for sponsored `/sites/…` paths; loses `/search/`, `/ajax/`, `/json/` and `*wp-admin*`.
- forbes.com line 372, `AhrefsBot` + `AhrefsSiteAudit`: only `Crawl-delay: 2` (then joined to `Claude-User`/`Claude-SearchBot` and their `Allow: /`).
- https://www.shopify.com/robots.txt, `AdIdxBot`, `Pinterestbot`, `AdsBot-Google`, `AdsBot-Google-Mobile`: only `Allow: */ppc/*` and `Allow: *utm_medium=cpc*`, meant to lift two `*` Disallows; they lift about 100.
- https://www.yahoo.com/robots.txt line 69, `Claude-SearchBot` + `OAI-SearchBot`: one Disallow, loses the 21 `*` Disallows.
- https://wordpress.org/robots.txt: the `Allow: /` groups, now an acceptance line.

## ROBO-phfbpfiy: Google's robots.txt window is 500 KiB = 512,000 bytes; robotstxtr uses 524,288

**Status:** done

### Description

Why: Google documents a robots.txt size limit of "500 kibibytes (KiB)", that is 500 × 1,024 = 512,000 bytes, and ignores content after it. robotstxtr uses 524,288 bytes (512 KiB) as Google's window in several places:

- `match_google_v1()` in R/engine-contract-v1.R (`limit <- 524288L`), and the `google` value of 524288L near line 1212. A body between 512,000 and 524,288 bytes is matched past Google's window, so a rule there can give a verdict Google would ignore (wrong results on a rare path).
- design/adr/0001-safety-level-vs-engine-ruleset.md §5 ("Google parses the first 500 KiB (524,288 bytes)"), its slice 9 acceptance, and its "Changes to engine-profiles.md" item 8 (`stored_bytes ≥ 524288`).
- ROBO-ptibdnvy's description (`stored_bytes >= 524288`).

robotstxtr's own R/fetch-policy.R:62 already reads 500 KiB as 512000 bytes. The default `max_bytes = 524288L` is fine: it is a fetch ceiling, above the window.

Found by the review of sitemapr ADR-011 (SITE-senkdjer), which permits the Google cut-file reading only on the documented 512,000-byte window.

Scope:
- In: the Google matcher window becomes 512,000 bytes; ADR 0001's figure and slice 9 threshold are corrected (an accepted ADR, so the maintainer approves the correction); ROBO-ptibdnvy's description follows; tests pin a rule at byte 512,000+ being ignored under `google`.
- Out: `max_bytes`'s default.

Acceptance: under `google`, a rule starting past byte 512,000 never affects the decision; ADR 0001 and ROBO-ptibdnvy say 512,000.

## ROBO-pjvypcjk: Harden the link-local and cloud-metadata IPv6 rules: they match the literal, not the expanded address

**Status:** done

### Description

Cross-repo mirror of sitemapr **SITE-mhfmtdxa**. Same defect, same file, same
lines — the two guards are copies of each other.

Deferred out of ROBO-pzgzxkoj / sitemapr SITE-vovtwvuh. That fix decided the two
all-zero-prefix specials (`::1`, `::`) on the **expanded** hextets. The remaining
two IPv6 rules in `ssrf_classify_ipv6()` (`R/ssrf.R:291` and `R/ssrf.R:295`)
still match **regex against the literal string**, and both fail — in opposite
directions.

### Confirmed empirically in the sitemapr copy (byte-identical rules)

```
fd00:ec2::254             -> cloud-metadata
fd00:0ec2::254            -> NA          <-- BYPASS: same address, allowed
fd00:0ec2:0:0:0:0:0:0254  -> NA          <-- BYPASS: same address, allowed

fe80::1                   -> link-local  (correct)
fe8::                     -> link-local  <-- OVER-BLOCK: hextet is 0x0fe8
fe8:0:0:0:0:0:0:1         -> link-local  <-- OVER-BLOCK
feb::                     -> link-local  <-- OVER-BLOCK
fea:                      -> link-local  <-- OVER-BLOCK
```

`ssrf_classify_literal()` returns `ssrf_result(is.na(reason), reason)`, so `NA`
means **allowed**. The cloud-metadata rows are a real SSRF bypass of the AWS
metadata block. Re-probe locally before fixing to confirm this copy behaves
identically (the rules are textually identical, so it should).

### Root cause

1. **cloud-metadata (under-blocks).** `low == "fd00:ec2::254" ||
   grepl("^fd00:ec2:", low)`. A hextet may carry leading zeros, so `0ec2` is the
   same 16 bits as `ec2` but misses the literal prefix.
2. **link-local (over-blocks).** `grepl("^fe[89ab][0-9a-f]?:", low)` — the 4th
   hex digit is optional, so a 3-digit first hextet `fe8` (`0x0fe8`) matches
   despite being nowhere near `fe80::/10` (`0xfe80`-`0xfebf`). No bypass in the
   other direction: `fe80` is already four significant digits, so it has no
   leading-zero spelling.

### Fix shape

Both rules should read the expanded hextets from `ssrf_ipv6_hextets()` — the
same expander `ssrf_ipv6_special()` and `ssrf_embedded_ipv4()` already use:

- link-local: `bitwAnd(h[1], 0xffc0) == 0xfe80`
- cloud-metadata: `h[1] == 0xfd00 && h[2] == 0x0ec2`, then the `::254` host part
  for the exact endpoint vs the `/64` prefix

Add tests for every spelling of both, mirroring the 12-spelling table that
ROBO-pzgzxkoj added for the specials.

### Land together

sitemapr and robotstxtr must land byte-for-byte identical patches. Shipping one
without the other reintroduces the drift ROBO-pzgzxkoj existed to remove.

### Open question, still unresolved

Should this guard become **shared code** rather than two copies? This is the
second parity fix in a row against the same file. Settle that before writing a
third mirrored patch.


### Comments

#### 2026-07-24 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Cross-repo mirror of sitemapr SITE-mhfmtdxa. Land the two patches together.

#### 2026-07-25 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Fixed and merged as 6777da2 (PR #60); all CI checks green, branch deleted local+remote.

Both rules now read the expanded hextets from ssrf_ipv6_hextets():
- link-local: bitwAnd(h[1], 0xffc0) == 0xfe80  (fe80::/10)
- cloud-metadata: h[1] == 0xfd00 && h[2] == 0x0ec2  (fd00:ec2::/32)

Reproduced the issue's table locally before fixing; this copy behaved identically to sitemapr's, as expected. The /32 breadth matches what the old literal '^fd00:ec2:' match already had, so nothing previously blocked became allowed. The 'low == "fd00:ec2::254"' clause was already dead code (that literal starts with fd00:ec2:) and is gone.

ssrf_classify_ipv6() now expands the literal ONCE and passes hextets to every rule, so no rule can disagree with another about which address it is looking at. ssrf_embedded_reason() takes hextets instead of a literal.

Landed byte-for-byte with sitemapr SITE-mhfmtdxa (ff1215d, sitemapr PR #175); ssrf_ipv6_prefix_block() and ssrf_classify_ipv6() are byte-identical across the two repos, verified by diff. sitemapr's ADR-003 §1 matrix already specified fe80::/10 and fd00:ec2::254 — only the code had drifted, so no ADR change was needed.

Open question (shared code vs. two copies) is NOT resolved by this patch — see the separate note below.

#### 2026-07-25 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

OPEN QUESTION NOW SETTLED (2026-07-25, user decision). This issue's 'Open question, still unresolved' section said to settle shared-code-vs-copies before writing a third mirrored patch.

Decision: keep each repo's own copy for now; extract into a standalone **ssrfr** library later. Tracked as ROBO-mgumaoyf (mirror: sitemapr SITE-yeozymry).

A third mirrored patch is therefore fine — mirror it by hand as before and note it on ROBO-mgumaoyf. No CI parity job was added.




## ROBO-pkpnvfzp: Publish the accepted product-token set for bounded_profiles matcher backends

**Status:** done

### Description

A consumer cannot discover which product tokens a `bounded_profiles` matcher
backend accepts, and passing an unaccepted one fails without ever reaching the
caller's attention. Surfaced by sitemapr SITE-fsawklnl.

### Why

`robots_engine_contract_v1()$matcher_capability$<backend>` publishes
`token_policy`, `matcher_semantics` and a prose `note`. For the two
`bounded_profiles` backends (`yandex`, `bing`) the note says the backend is
bounded to "its supported Yandex/Bing vendor profiles only" — but the SET of
accepted tokens is published nowhere, on the contract or off it.

That makes the axis unvalidatable at construction time by any consumer, and the
failure mode is quiet on the Yandex side: an unaccepted token is not an error,
every row comes back `matcher_status = "not_evaluated"`, `reason =
"unsupported_product_token"`, `error_class =
"robots_unsupported_product_token"`, `url_decision = NA`. A caller who does not
inspect those columns sees a clean evaluation in which nothing was decided —
which reads like a transport problem, not a config mistake.

**Downstream cost, already paid.** sitemapr's `yandex` engine preset carried
`"YandexBot"` from the day it was written. It rendered every URL of a sitemap
indeterminate, and nothing caught it, because sitemapr's own findings path was
Google-bounded until SITE-fsawklnl and no non-Google context was ever exercised
end to end. sitemapr now pins each preset token with a behavioral test that
evaluates a mocked robots.txt per backend and asserts `matcher_status ==
"evaluated"` — a workaround for a set this package should publish.

### Verified accepted sets (probed 2026-08-25 against the vendored profiles)

Both backends accept exactly two tokens, ASCII-case-insensitively, with no
aliases. Sources: `src/vendor/robotstxtbing/src/policy.cpp:72`
(`is_supported_profile_token`), `src/vendor/robotstxtyandex/src/`.

| backend | accepted | rejected (sample) |
|---|---|---|
| `yandex` | `Yandex`, `YandexAdditionalBot` | `YandexBot`, `YandexAdditional`, `YandexImages`, `YandexMobileBot`, `YandexAccessibilityBot`, `YandexComBot`, `Yandex/1.0`, `*` |
| `bing` | `bingbot`, `adidxbot` | `Bingbot/2.0`, `msnbot`, `BingPreview`, `bing`, `*` |

**The accepted tokens within a backend are NOT interchangeable.** Probed:

    body "User-agent: Yandex\nDisallow: /private", target /private
      Yandex               -> disallow (rule_disallow)
      YandexAdditionalBot  -> allow    (default_allow)

    body "User-agent: bingbot\nDisallow: /private", target /private
      bingbot              -> disallow (rule_disallow)
      adidxbot             -> allow    (default_allow)

    body "User-agent: *\nDisallow: /private", target /private
      Yandex, bingbot      -> disallow
      YandexAdditionalBot, adidxbot -> allow (wildcard not honoured)

So the pattern is vendor-neutral, not a Yandex quirk. Two selection modes cover
both vendors:

- `exact_else_wildcard` — merge all exactly-named groups; only if none exist,
  merge wildcard groups. (`Yandex`, `bingbot`)
- `exact_only` — merge exactly-named groups; never fall back to wildcard.
  (`YandexAdditionalBot`, `adidxbot`)

A bare character vector of accepted tokens would publish the members of each
pair as equivalent when they demonstrably are not, so the published shape has to
carry selection behaviour, not just membership.

### The two backends do not share a failure vocabulary

The prose above describes the Yandex shape. Bing differs and is louder:

| backend | `matcher_status` | `reason` | `error_class` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `yandex` | `not_evaluated` | `unsupported_product_token` | `robots_unsupported_product_token` |
| `bing` | `unsupported_profile` | `unsupported_profile` | `robots_unsupported_profile` |

`R/match-yandex-v1.R:136-142`, `R/match-bing-v1.R:142,155`. Anything published
or raised must accommodate both without pretending the vocabularies are the
same.

### Namespace problem underneath all of this

Bare `Yandex` is not a crawler name. It appears nowhere in Yandex's reverse-DNS
robot verification list — every real crawler identity there is suffixed
(`YandexBot`, `YandexImages`, …). `Yandex` exists only as a robots.txt
`User-agent:` group label.

RFC 9309 treats the product token as one namespace spanning both the HTTP
`User-Agent` header and the robots.txt `User-agent:` line. Yandex violates that.
The argument name `robots_product_token` therefore invites a caller to pass the
crawler identity — which is exactly how sitemapr failed.
`man/robots_evaluate_text_v1.Rd:47` already states the argument is
group-selection only and never sent as a header, but the framing is too easy to
skim past.

### Decision (settled 2026-08-25; see comments for the Codex consultation)

**Mirror the set in R, gated by semantic conformance tests, and publish it as a
profile table — not a token vector. Add an exported construction-time resolver.**

Rejected: querying the native layer. No registered `.Call` entry point
enumerates supported crawlers today, so it needs a new binding per vendored
profile library, and a native token enumeration alone would still leave the
selection-behaviour mapping mirrored in R. Revisit if the profile sets grow,
gain aliases, change independently of package releases, or if a vendored library
starts exposing a structured capability descriptor that includes selection
behaviour.

Native `contract_info()` field names (`bingbot_profile_revision`,
`adidxbot_profile_revision`) are identity metadata and must not be parsed as a
token enumeration.

### Scope

In scope: publishing the accepted profiles per backend as consumer-readable data
on the engine contract, the schema revision bumps, an exported resolver that
fails fast at configuration-construction time, and the conformance tests that
keep the published data honest.

Out of scope, explicitly:

- Changing which tokens a backend accepts, or accepting more of them.
- Generalizing a bounded backend to arbitrary tokens (the `bounded_profiles`
  boundary is the point; see the existing `note`).
- Turning an unaccepted token into an error inside `robots_evaluate_url_v1()`.
  The per-row status is the correct shape for a batch API and does not change;
  this issue is about letting a caller check FIRST.
- Renaming `robots_product_token` (breaking).

### Acceptance criteria

**Published data**

- Each `bounded_profiles` backend's `matcher_capability` entry gains
  `product_token_role = "matcher_profile_selector"`,
  `product_token_comparison = "ascii_case_insensitive_exact"`, and
  `supported_profiles`, a data frame with columns `profile_id`,
  `accepted_token`, `group_label`, `group_selection`, `profile_revision`.
- `group_selection` is one of `exact_else_wildcard` / `exact_only`, and both
  values are defined normatively in the contract docs.
- Case-folding is published as that precise enum, not a bare
  `case_sensitive = FALSE`, which would leave Unicode and locale behaviour
  ambiguous. Both cores do ASCII-only exact comparison with no trimming, prefix
  or suffix matching, or aliasing.
- For `yandex` on the v0.2.0 vendored profile the accepted tokens are exactly
  `Yandex` (`exact_else_wildcard`) and `YandexAdditionalBot` (`exact_only`).
- For `bing` they are exactly `bingbot` (`exact_else_wildcard`) and `adidxbot`
  (`exact_only`).
- A backend whose `token_policy` is `arbitrary_valid` (`google`) or `rfc9309` is
  unaffected: it publishes no profile table, and its existing capability fields
  are unchanged.
- A backend whose `matcher_availability` is `capability_unavailable` still
  publishes its capability entry; whether it publishes a profile table is stated
  explicitly in the contract docs either way.
- If a convenience token vector is published at all, it is DERIVED from
  `supported_profiles$accepted_token` — never a second maintained source.

**Schema**

- Both `robots_engine_contract_v1()` and `robots_engine_contract_v2()` advance
  their `schema_revision`. They share `engine_backend_capability_v1()`
  (`R/engine-contract-v1.R:301,365`), so the fields appear in both outputs
  whether or not both are bumped; advancing only v1 while v2 changes silently
  would make v2 negotiation unreliable.
- `contract_id` values are unchanged. The addition is additive: no existing
  field changes type or meaning, so consumers pinned to the current schema keep
  working.

**Resolver**

- An exported, vectorized `robots_resolve_matcher_profile_v1(matcher_backend,
  robots_product_token)` resolves a token case-insensitively per the published
  comparison mode and returns the canonical profile row including
  `accepted_token` and `group_selection`.
- It errors on an unsupported bounded token with a stable condition class, and
  the message names the accepted selectors for that backend and states plainly
  that e.g. `"YandexBot"` is a crawler identity, not a matcher-profile selector.
- The batch evaluation API is unchanged by its existence.
- Rationale to preserve: profile support is a matcher capability independent of
  whether a given row ever reaches the matcher. An `allow_all` policy can return
  a decision despite a nonsensical bounded token, so results-inspection can
  never be the guard — validation belongs at configuration construction.

**Tests**

- Conformance tests assert SEMANTICS, not just status, for every published
  profile on both backends: its exact group is selected; the sibling profile's
  group is not; wildcard fallback is applied or not exactly as
  `group_selection` declares; lowercase and uppercase selectors resolve
  identically; and representative near misses (affixed, whitespace-bearing,
  `*`, real crawler identities) remain unsupported.
- The tests force a supplied-body `use_rules` path. An `allow_all`, transport,
  or other policy short-circuit never invokes the matcher and so cannot validate
  profile support.
- Known limit, recorded deliberately: these tests prove the published table has
  no false POSITIVES. They cannot detect a token newly accepted natively but
  omitted from R, nor accidental broadening where every token starts evaluating.
  False positives are the dangerous direction for the sitemapr failure mode; an
  unpublished-but-accepted token is a conservative false negative.

**Docs and messaging**

- The first sentence of the `robots_product_token` documentation changes from
  "used for group selection" to state that it is a matcher-profile selector or
  group label and NOT an HTTP User-Agent crawler identity.
- Unsupported-token `error_message` values list the accepted selectors for the
  backend. This does not change the per-row status model.
- NEWS announces the addition with both token sets spelled out, since the
  surprising values are the whole point.

### Verification

- `robots_engine_contract_v1()$matcher_capability$yandex$supported_profiles`
  shows both rows, contains `Yandex` and `YandexAdditionalBot`, and does not
  contain `YandexBot`.
- `robots_resolve_matcher_profile_v1("yandex", "YandexBot")` errors with a
  message naming `Yandex` and `YandexAdditionalBot`.
- The conformance tests fail when a published token is changed to `YandexBot`,
  and when a `group_selection` value is flipped.
- The package's own check/verify gate passes.
- Cross-repo: sitemapr can replace its behavioral preset-token test with a
  resolver call at preset-construction time. Mirrors SITE-fsawklnl; the
  sitemapr-side memory is `bounded-profile-token-trap`.


### Comments

#### 2026-08-08 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Filed from sitemapr SITE-fsawklnl (merged, sitemapr main f1ef383), which hit this gap in production: the yandex engine preset carried 'YandexBot' and rendered every URL of a sitemap indeterminate. sitemapr's workaround is a behavioral test that evaluates each preset token against a mocked robots.txt per backend and asserts matcher_status == 'evaluated', skipping capability_unavailable backends. That test can become a membership check against the published set once this lands.

#### 2026-08-25 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Correction to the description table, from a direct probe of the vendored yandex-0.1.0 profile (pkgload::load_all on main, 2026-08-25).

The table says only the umbrella token is accepted and the acceptance criteria say the published set for yandex is "exactly Yandex". Both are FALSE. YandexAdditionalBot is also accepted, case-insensitively:

  body "User-agent: * / Disallow: /private", target /private
    Yandex / yandex / YANDEX              evaluated, rule_disallow
    YandexAdditionalBot                   evaluated, default_allow
    yandexadditionalbot / YANDEXADDITIONALBOT  evaluated (case-folded)
    YandexBot, YandexAdditional, YandexImages, YandexMobileBot,
    YandexAccessibilityBot, YandexComBot, Yandex/1.0, *
