The repo already carried this evidence: the committed corpus is 119 Yandex + 21 YandexAdditionalBot records (test-yandex-corpus-novczgii.R:49). The description was written from an incomplete probe.

SEMANTIC POINT the ACs do not yet handle. The two accepted tokens are not interchangeable, so a bare character vector publishes a false equivalence:

  body "User-agent: Yandex / Disallow: /private"
    Yandex               -> disallow (rule_disallow)
    YandexAdditionalBot  -> allow    (default_allow)

YandexAdditionalBot obeys neither "User-agent: *" nor "User-agent: Yandex" - only a group naming it directly. Matches Yandex vendor behaviour for the Additional family. Whatever shape the published set takes has to carry that, or a consumer validating membership still gets a wrong answer about what a token will do.

TERMINOLOGY, raised by the user against yandex.com/support/webmaster/en/robot-workings/check-yandex-robots.html: bare "Yandex" is NOT a bot name and appears nowhere on that reverse-DNS verification list - every real crawler identity there is suffixed (YandexBot, YandexImages, ...). "Yandex" exists only as a robots.txt User-agent group label. RFC 9309 treats the product token as one namespace spanning the HTTP User-Agent header and the robots.txt User-agent line; Yandex breaks that, and the arg name robots_product_token invites callers to pass the crawler identity - which is exactly the sitemapr failure. man/robots_evaluate_text_v1.Rd:47 already states the arg is group-selection only and never sent as a header; that distinction should be part of what this issue publishes, not just the token list.

NO code changed under this id. Description table and ACs need fixing before implementation.

#### 2026-08-25 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Codex consultation (codex-cli 0.149.1, read-only sandbox) on the open (a)-vs-(b) decision and the data shape. Every factual claim below was independently verified against source and by probe before recording; none taken on trust.

RECOMMENDATION: (b) mirror in R — but publish a PROFILE TABLE, not a token vector, and add an exported strict resolver. The contract table alone will not prevent the next sitemapr-class failure.

WHY (b): the profile sets are frozen and tiny (2 tokens per backend), single-sourced in R already. (a) becomes right if sets grow, gain aliases, change independently of package releases, or if a native library exposes a structured capability descriptor including SELECTION BEHAVIOUR — a bare native token enumeration would still leave the behaviour mapping mirrored in R, so it buys less than it looks.

HOLE IN THE PROPOSED CONFORMANCE TEST: "every published token evaluates" only proves the R table has no false POSITIVES. It cannot detect a token newly accepted natively but omitted from R, changed case-folding, changed group-selection while status stays evaluated, or accidental broadening where everything evaluates. Not fatal — false positives are the dangerous direction for the sitemapr failure mode, and an unpublished-but-accepted token is a conservative false negative. But the test must probe SEMANTICS (exact group selected, other profile NOT selected, wildcard applied or not as declared, case variants identical, near-misses/affixed/whitespace/`*`/crawler-identities rejected) and must force a supplied-body use_rules path, since allow_all or a transport short-circuit never invokes the matcher.

VERIFIED FACTS ADDED BY THIS CONSULTATION

1. BING accepted set is NOT unknown — it is exactly `bingbot` + `adidxbot`, ASCII-case-insensitive, no aliases (src/vendor/robotstxtbing/src/policy.cpp:72 is_supported_profile_token). Probe confirms: bingbot/BingBot/BINGBOT/adidxbot/AdIdxBot evaluated; Bingbot/2.0, msnbot, BingPreview, *, bing all rejected. My previous comment said Bing was unprobed; it no longer is.

2. THE TWO BACKENDS DO NOT SHARE A FAILURE VOCABULARY. Yandex: native `unsupported_crawler` -> matcher_status `not_evaluated`, reason `unsupported_product_token`, error_class `robots_unsupported_product_token` (R/match-yandex-v1.R:136-142). Bing: native `unsupported_profile` -> matcher_status `unsupported_profile` (its OWN v2 status, not not_evaluated), error_class `robots_unsupported_profile` (R/match-bing-v1.R:142,155). The issue description generalises the Yandex shape to both. Note Bing is arguably the LOUDER of the two for exactly this reason.

3. THE exact_only WRINKLE IS SYMMETRIC ACROSS VENDORS, not a Yandex quirk. Probed under `User-agent: bingbot / Disallow: /private`: bingbot -> disallow, adidxbot -> allow (default_allow). Under `User-agent: *`: bingbot -> disallow, adidxbot -> allow. So adidxbot is exact-only exactly as YandexAdditionalBot is. Two enums cover both vendors: exact_else_wildcard (merge exactly-named groups; only if none, merge wildcard) and exact_only (never wildcard). Sources: robotstxtyandex/src/crawler_selector.cc:43, robotstxtbing/src/selection.h:21.

4. SCHEMA DECISION THE ISSUE MISSES. robots_engine_contract_v1() (R/engine-contract-v1.R:301) and robots_engine_contract_v2() (:365) both build from the same engine_backend_capability_v1() object. Adding fields there changes BOTH outputs. Advancing only v1 schema_revision while v2 silently changes would make v2 negotiation unreliable — both revisions must advance, keeping their own contract_ids. Alternative is splitting the builders and publishing only via v2, which is worse because evaluation objects embed the v1 contract.

5. Native contract_info() field NAMES (bingbot_profile_revision, adidxbot_profile_revision) are identity metadata, not a supported-token API. Do not parse token enumeration out of field naming — my earlier comment implied that was viable raw material; it is not.

PROPOSED SHAPE (additive, existing three fields untouched, per bounded_profiles backend):
  product_token_role       = "matcher_profile_selector"
  product_token_comparison = "ascii_case_insensitive_exact"
  supported_profiles       = data.frame(profile_id, accepted_token, group_label, group_selection, profile_revision)
Case-folding published as data, as a precise enum — NOT a bare case_sensitive=FALSE, which leaves Unicode/locale ambiguous. Both cores do ASCII-only exact comparison with no trimming, prefix/suffix matching or aliasing. If a convenience token vector is still wanted, DERIVE it from supported_profiles$accepted_token; never maintain two sources.

PREVENTION MECHANISM (the part the issue lacks entirely): an exported, vectorised, fail-fast resolver called at CONFIG-CONSTRUCTION time, e.g. robots_resolve_matcher_profile_v1(matcher_backend, robots_product_token) -> canonical profile row incl. group_selection; errors on an unsupported bounded token with a message that names the accepted selectors and says plainly that e.g. "YandexBot" is a crawler identity, not a profile selector. Batch evaluation API unchanged. Rationale: profile support is a matcher capability independent of whether a row ever reaches the matcher — an allow_all policy can return a decision despite a nonsensical bounded token, so results-inspection can never be the guard. Also: strengthen the robots_product_token doc first sentence from "used for group selection" to "a matcher-profile selector / group label; NOT an HTTP User-Agent crawler identity", and list accepted selectors in unsupported-token error_message. Renaming the argument stays out of scope (breaking).

## ROBO-plkpmoll: Validator: diagnose robots.txt MIME types and declared charset conflicts

**Status:** done

### Description

### Why

Content-Type is retained on fetch rows but not diagnosed. A real robots.txt served as text/html currently has no MIME warning. RFC 9309 section 2.3 specifies text/plain and UTF-8; deployment conformance and crawler acceptance must be distinguished.

### Scope

In: conservative URL-validation diagnostics for missing, malformed or non-text/plain media types, malformed/unsupported charset declarations, and demonstrable header/body conflicts. Preserve the original header and bytes. Explain the difference between declared type, body content and byte validity; use stable codes and justified severities.
Out: automatic transcoding; charset guessing; refusal to parse merely because a header is wrong; assertions that every crawler rejects a MIME mismatch; text-only APIs inventing unavailable HTTP metadata.

### Acceptance criteria

- Correct text/plain with optional UTF-8 charset, case/whitespace variations and parameters is accepted.
- Missing, malformed, conflicting/repeated header values and alternative types are handled explicitly without crashing; compliant headers do not hide HTML or malformed bytes.
- Plain robots rules under text/html and HTML under text/plain retain their distinct findings.
- Header/body contradictions are diagnosed only when the bytes establish them. ASCII alone cannot establish a conflict between UTF-8 and ASCII-compatible encodings. A missing charset is not a UTF-8 violation by itself.
- Existing parsing, acquisition outcomes and matcher decisions remain unchanged; docs and NEWS explain the new codes.

### Verification

Mocked URL responses covering header syntax, body/type disagreements, invalid bytes, ASCII ambiguity and absent metadata; existing content/encoding tests; repository merge gate.

### Dependencies

None. Related completed work: ROBO-nhuirvrd (Content-Type/content flags), ROBO-cthdyvlk (header scope). Standard: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html#section-2.3


### Delivery

Requested by the owner on 2026-11-16 following the robots.txt validator audit. Standalone outcome; no parent or artificial ordering dependency. Do not make this a new 0.4.0 release blocker without an explicit release-scope decision. Preserve raw evidence and distinguish standards conformance, observed crawler behavior and heuristics.

## ROBO-plzvdbjz: DESCRIPTION declares three dead GitHub URLs; blocks the CRAN check

**Status:** done

### Description

`R CMD check --as-cran` checks every URL a package declares. robotstxtr declares
three that resolve to a suspended GitHub account, so they return 404 and the
check will flag them. This blocks robotstxtr's own CRAN submission, and it is
robotstxtr-specific: of the eight packages in the fleet, it is the only one whose
`DESCRIPTION` still names GitHub.

    rurl         0 github references in DESCRIPTION
    pslr         0
    punycoder    0
    sitemapr     0
    pagerankr    0
    seor         0
    raddr        0
    robotstxtr   3

### Measured 2026-09-09

    https://github.com/bart-turczynski/robotstxtr           404
    https://bart-turczynski.github.io/robotstxtr/           404
    https://gitlab.com/bart-turczynski/robotstxtr           200

The GitLab 200 in the same run rules out a general network artifact. `origin` is
already `git@gitlab.com:bart-turczynski/robotstxtr.git` — the code moved, the
declared metadata did not.

### Scope

`DESCRIPTION` is the part that blocks the check:

    URL:        https://github.com/bart-turczynski/robotstxtr,
                https://bart-turczynski.github.io/robotstxtr/
    BugReports: https://github.com/bart-turczynski/robotstxtr/issues

but the same stale self-reference is spread across 13 tracked files, 47
occurrences:

    .zenodo.json  1    README.Rmd  3    _pkgdown.yml            3
    CITATION.cff  2    README.md   3    codemeta.json           6
    DESCRIPTION   2    inst/CITATION 1  design/tracker-snapshot.md 12
    SECURITY-INSIGHTS.yml 13         inst/NOTICE   1
    THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md 2         inst/PROVENANCE 1

Fix `DESCRIPTION` first — it is the only one the check gate reads — then sweep
the rest so the citation, Zenodo and codemeta metadata do not keep publishing
dead links.

**Do not blanket-replace `github` in this repo.** 27 files mention GitHub, and
the difference matters: `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`, `inst/NOTICE` and
`inst/PROVENANCE` cite <https://github.com/google/robotstxt>, the upstream
Apache-2.0 project this package vendors, and `DESCRIPTION`'s own `Description:`
field cites it too. Those must stay. Only `bart-turczynski`-owned references
move.

### The replacement URL for the docs site is not ready

    https://gitlab.com/bart-turczynski/robotstxtr        200   usable
    https://bart-turczynski.gitlab.io/robotstxtr/        403   NOT usable

403, not 404 — the Pages site exists but is not publicly readable. Compare
`https://bart-turczynski.gitlab.io/rurl/` and `.../pslr/`, both 200 in the same
run, so this is a robotstxtr Pages visibility setting rather than the fleet
convention being wrong. Swapping the `github.io` URL for the `gitlab.io` one
without fixing that trades a 404 for a 403 and the check still flags it. Either
make the Pages site public first, or drop the docs URL from `URL:` until it is.

### What `BugReports:` should become, and one thing not to chase

`https://gitlab.com/bart-turczynski/robotstxtr/-/issues` returns 404 to a
logged-out client. That is not a misconfiguration and is not worth investigating:
`https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues` returns 404 to the same
anonymous request. It is GitLab's site-wide anti-scraping behavior. Every other
package in the fleet already declares its `/-/issues` URL and passes; pslr's
`cran-comments.md` pre-empts the resulting NOTE. Follow that precedent rather
than treating this one as a defect to fix.

### Acceptance

- `DESCRIPTION` `URL:` and `BugReports:` name only URLs that resolve, verified by
  request and not by inspection.
- `R CMD check --as-cran` reports no unreachable-URL finding.
- The remaining 12 files carry GitLab self-references; upstream google/robotstxt
  citations are untouched.
- If the `gitlab.io` docs URL is declared, the Pages site returns 200 anonymously.


### Comments

Absorbed into ROBO-bgcloodt (M4 — Repoint package metadata URLs to GitLab). **No code changed under this id.**

The two issues were near-duplicates filed from different angles: this one from the CRAN-blocker side, M4 from the GitHub-to-GitLab migration side. M4 is the broader of the two — it also covers codemeta.json, CITATION.cff, .zenodo.json and the SECURITY-INSIGHTS.yml vulnerability-reporting prose, which this issue did not — and it sits inside the migration epic (ROBO-tiohzehm) where the rest of the sequencing lives. ## ROBO-polznjqh: Yandex backend: upper-case the target's escapes and compare the rule as written (tester, class 11)

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

Yandex's analyzer allows both `/y7/a%3cb` and `/y7/a%3Cb` under `Disallow: /y7/a%3cb` (Y7). Controls: rule `%3C` prohibits both; `%2F` rule prohibits `%2F` and `%2f` targets but not `/`. So Yandex upper-cases the target's escapes, does not decode them, and leaves the rule's case alone, so a lower-case escape in a rule matches nothing. Our backend prohibits the lower-case target.

Out: other classes; served-file (crawler) evidence, which is ROBO-oxfpgdrx.

### Acceptance criteria

The backend answers the observed cases as the tester did, the corpus pins them, and the disagreement doc cites the observation.

### Backend change (2026-11-13)

The backend behavior itself is not changed here: the payloads are frozen vendored releases. It lands in the sibling release (YDX-vgomfspr) and reaches robotstxtr through ROBO-jtsmzesl. ## ROBO-pqsyzudt: Corpus harness: second-pass review minors

**Status:** done

### Description

Second-pass review of the corpus harness (ROBO-qbxsydcf, dev/corpus/) left these minor defects open. None affects a valid run's results; most leave a stale "running" record or a misleading message.

- run.R / README: some refusals still come after create_run_dir() writes a "running" record: a --pkg outside a git work tree (or nonexistent: plain normalizePath error, exit 1) and every compare refusal. Run package_git_facts and the compare checks first.
- harness.R read_corpus_record: rawToChar(magic) and readBin/sha256 sit outside the tryCatch; a NUL in the first bytes or a file that vanishes after the existence check fails the whole chunk as a worker failure instead of marking the file unreadable or vanished. Use identical(magic, charToRaw("BZh")) and move the reads inside.
- modes.R run_and_check: only corpus_harness_worker_failure is caught; any other runner error (e.g. size mode's in-process chunk-0 stage) exits 1 with the record left "running" and no invalid_cause. Catch generically, record, exit 3.
- run.R matches_frozen: compares start hashes without checking both runs planned the same set; a partial run against a full frozen run always reports a mismatch. Compare shared rows or refuse a plan mismatch.
- modes.R mode_compare harness_same: ignores harness_dirty and treats NA on both sides as the same tree. Set FALSE when either run is dirty or a tree is NA.
- harness.R corpus_manifest: in a partial run a planned host dir that vanishes before the start manifest records has_rds = FALSE and the run stays valid. Take the start manifest right after listing; record dir_exists apart from has_rds.
- modes.R run_chunks (workers = 1): every chunk runs under try(), so after a failure the sequential path keeps going for hours on a run already invalid. Stop at the first failure.
- nit: paths$evaluated_bytes repeats one per-file constant on every row; store it once in the files table.
- nit: rule_values duplicates evaluated_text()'s NUL stripping and encoding; call evaluated_text(body).

## ROBO-ptibdnvy: The google ruleset reads a cut robots.txt's first 500 KiB

**Status:** done

### Description

Why: robotstxtr design/adr/0001-safety-level-vs-engine-ruleset.md (accepted 2026-11-05, MR !83, ROBO-xdlzicrq), slice 9, §5: Google parses the first 500 KiB of robots.txt and ignores the rest. A cut 2xx prefix of at least 512,000 bytes holds that whole window. Maintainer 2026-11-05: keep this in ADR 0001 as slice 9.

Scope:
- In: under google, a cut 2xx with `stored_bytes >= 512000` resolves use_rules [documented], matched on its first 512,000 bytes as `match_google_v1()` already reads; engine-profiles.md §7 per the ADR's change 8.
- Out: rfc9309, assumed_rfc9309 and bing, which stay incomplete for a cut file.

## ROBO-pvntbjlb: SSRF guard: WHATWG second look fails open when rurl gives no host

**Status:** done

### Description

Found in the second review of ROBO-dxrljrde.

The WHATWG second look (`ssrf_whatwg_second_look()`) fails open: when rurl's WHATWG parse gives no host, the default verdict (allowed) stands. Spellings that libcurl with libidn2 maps to the metadata host still pass: `http://metadata.google.internal%E3%80%82/`, `http://169.254.169.254%E3%80%82/`, `http://metadata%E3%80%82/`, U+FE52 or U+2024 used as dots, ZWJ/ZWNJ inside a label. Not reproduced end to end (local libcurl has no IDN).

Fix direction: fail closed, as ssrfr does (`parse`). When the WHATWG view gives no host and the raw host is non-ASCII, carries `%`, or the default host has an `xn--` label, block with a fail-closed reason. Also drop the `identical(whatwg, host)` shortcut or run the numeric check on the decoded host (`http://0x7f000001%2e%2e/`, not live). Optional: skip the second parse for plain-ASCII URLs (cost ~0.3 ms per hop).

Root cause is rurl's default host path (no UTS #46 mapping before ACE); see the rurl issue.

## ROBO-pvqrfvol: NUL bytes on the Google backend end the line as upstream does

**Status:** done

### Description

Why
The Google fidelity audit (ROBO-deehqhlc, design/engine-profiles.md §5b class 5) records one class where robotstxtr's Google paths can reach a different decision from Google's open-source engine: a NUL byte in a fetched body. Upstream parses each line as a NUL-terminated C string, so a line ends at its first NUL. robotstxtr's decoder (R/body-decode.R, ROBO-hcqrzikz) removes every NUL and reads on.

Synthesized fixtures (tests/testthat/test-google-fidelity-deehqhlc.R, class 5):
- `User-agent: *` / `\0Disallow: /x`, URL /x: upstream allows (an empty line), robotstxtr disallows on line 2.
- `User-agent: *` / `Disallow: /a\0b`, URLs /a and /ac: upstream disallows (rule /a), robotstxtr allows (rule /ab).

The split goes both ways, so neither reading is the conservative one. It is documented as deliberate (PRD §6.6), but under the `google` ruleset it is the only decision difference from upstream the audit found.

Decision needed
- (A) Keep NUL removal everywhere. The PRD rule stays; the Google path keeps its one documented departure.
- (B) Recommended if Google fidelity is the goal for the `google` ruleset: on the Google backend, end a line at its first NUL as upstream does; keep removal for the other backends. This changes decisions on NUL-bearing files and needs a NEWS bullet and a PRD §6.6 edit.

Either way the validator keeps reporting the NUL. Related: ROBO-igrkabdb (UTF-16 without a BOM, which reaches the matcher through the same NUL removal), ROBO-lvzmmodp.

### Decision (settled)

Option (B). On the `google` backend only, a line ends at its first NUL byte, as Google's open-source parser does (it reads each line as a NUL-terminated C string). rfc9309, yandex and bing keep NUL removal. Reason: fidelity to each engine's real parser comes first, and NUL removal is not the conservative reading (the fixtures split both ways). Needs a NEWS bullet and a PRD §6.6 edit. The validator follows the backend's reading: for `Disallow:\0/private` under google it says the first NUL ends the line, the value is empty so the directive imposes no restriction, and the text after the NUL is ignored. It never announces an overall allow decision. This reverses the ROBO-nrnucnru wording for the google ruleset. Caveat: this gives parity with upstream; exact Googlebot production behavior stays unverified, so describe the guarantee as upstream parity.

Settled 2026-11-11: the maintainer delegated this decision to Claude and Codex (GPT-6.1-Sol, high effort) and accepted their agreement as the answer.

## ROBO-pzgzxkoj: Harden ssrf_classify_ipv6(): dotted-quad spellings of ::1 and :: bypass the pure matcher

**Status:** done

### Description

Found by the ROBO-qzssazvg coverage work (C1), verified directly.

### The defect
ssrf_check() blocks one spelling of an address and allows a bit-for-bit identical one:

  ssrf_check("[::1]")        -> allowed=FALSE  reason=loopback
  ssrf_check("[::0.0.0.1]")  -> allowed=TRUE   reason=NA
  ssrf_check("[::]")         -> allowed=FALSE  reason=unspecified
  ssrf_check("[::0.0.0.0]")  -> allowed=TRUE   reason=NA

::0.0.0.1 is the same 128-bit address as ::1; ::0.0.0.0 is the same as ::.

### Root cause
ssrf_classify_ipv6() special-cases the literal STRINGS "::1" and "::" rather than comparing the expanded address, and ssrf_embedded_ipv4() deliberately skips tail32 <= 1, so the dotted spellings fall through both and reach the default allow.

### Severity: low today, but do not rely on that
NOT exploitable through the real fetch path: rurl canonicalizes http://[::0.0.0.1] to host [::1] before the guard runs (verified). tests/testthat/test-ssrf-quovenef.R now pins that protection explicitly, so a future rurl change cannot silently remove it.

The reason to fix anyway: ROBO-xnsfefvr exists precisely because rurl's URL parsing is changing across versions. Making an upstream library's normalization the SOLE barrier is exactly that coupling. ADR-003 (design/engine-profiles.md) also treats SSRF refusal as a local safety decision that dominates engine policy, which argues the matcher should be correct standalone.

### Fix
Harden ssrf_classify_ipv6() to compare expanded hextets rather than raw strings. The expansion machinery (ssrf_expand_zero_run, ssrf_hextets, ssrf_fold_ipv4_tail) already exists and is now at 100% coverage, so this is contained.

Keep it a focused diff: this changes a security control's behavior and deserves its own review rather than riding along in a coverage PR.

### Parity
sitemapr's copy of the guard has the IDENTICAL gap (verified by running sitemapr:::ssrf_check with the same four inputs). Tracked in sitemapr separately.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-24 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Fixed and merged in PR #57. ssrf_classify_ipv6() now decides the ::1/:: specials on the expanded hextets via a new ssrf_ipv6_special() helper, so every spelling of those 128 bits agrees. [::0.0.0.1] -> loopback, [::0.0.0.0] -> unspecified, plus compressed/partially-compressed/fully-written/dotted-tail forms.

Kept the tail32 > 1 exclusion in ssrf_embedded_ipv4() deliberately: those are the loopback/unspecified specials, not embedded IPv4, so loosening it would have swapped one wrong classification for another. The fix belongs in the classifier.

No over-blocking — ipv4-mapped, nat64, link-local, cloud-metadata and ipv4-compatible all unchanged; a real public address still passes; malformed literals still return without throwing. R/ssrf.R stays at 100% coverage; full suite 3959 pass (+18). Both protection layers (rurl canonicalization and the matcher itself) are now asserted independently so neither can regress silently behind the other. NEWS entry added.

sitemapr parity still open as SITE-vovtwvuh.

## ROBO-qbxsydcf: Corpus harness: re-runnable private scan of real robots.txt files (validate, evaluate, size)

**Status:** done

### Description

### Why

Validator checks were calibrated against the maintainer's private corpus of real robots.txt files on 2026-11-09 with throwaway scripts. Nothing was durable or re-runnable, the shipped code was never re-run, and no matcher decision was checked on real files. Every later audit (validator check, refactor equivalence, engine audit, library comparison) needs one repeatable scan.

### Privacy rule (applies to every corpus issue)

The corpus belongs to an embargoed study. Corpus files, corpus-derived paths and examples, and corpus figures never go into commits, MR text, commit messages, fp issues or comments (this tracker syncs to a cloud workspace), or logs kept in the repo. Committed code is generic; outputs stay in the private store. Public conclusions are stated with synthesized fixtures only.

### Scope

In:
- `dev/corpus/` (already in `.Rbuildignore`): a generic R harness. Input directory from `ROBOTSTXTR_CORPUS`; output only under `ROBOTSTXTR_CORPUS_OUT/<run-id>/` (refuse to run if unset or inside a git work tree). Each run writes a run record: robotstxtr git SHA, installed-package versions, corpus manifest hash, mode, parameters.
- Manifest mode: sha256 per input file, written to the private store, so a run can name the exact frozen snapshot.
- `validate` mode: `robots_validate_text()` per body; per-file codes and severities.
- `evaluate` mode: every engine/ruleset/matcher combination the v1 facade supports, over a deterministic path set: (a) paths taken from each file's own rules, (b) a fixed synthetic list (`$`, `*`, percent-escapes in both cases, `%2F`, letter case, `index.html`, non-ASCII, empty path, query strings), (c) a seeded random synthetic set independent of the parser. Tokens: `*`, Googlebot, Googlebot-Image, Yandex, bingbot, plus one unknown token.
- `size` mode: bodies around the 512,000-byte boundary (just below, at, just above) under each ruleset, from real bodies when present and from synthetic cuts through a rule line and through a percent-escape always.
- A comparison helper: two runs on the same manifest, identical()-level diff of the result tables.

Out: any change to package code; interpreting results (later issues).

### Lead, before dispatch

Create the private store outside every repo, set both env vars for the run, and copy the 2026-11-09 calibration outputs (now in the gitignored `_scratch/corpus-calib-2026-11-09/`) into it.

### Acceptance criteria

- All modes run on the full snapshot; run time and memory recorded in the private run record.
- Two runs on one manifest and one SHA compare identical.
- A pre-refactor baseline `evaluate` run of current main is stored and named, for the matcher-seam slices.
- Tests in `tests/testthat/` cover the harness's path generator and refusal rules on synthetic inputs only (skip when the env vars are unset).
- The MR diff and messages pass a reviewer allowlist check: only code, synthetic fixtures and docs.

### Verification

Pre-push gate; reviewer reads the staged-file list against the allowlist; the lead checks the run record.

### Dependencies

None.

## ROBO-qquftxcx: html_body misses a truncated minified HTML page

**Status:** done

### Description

Found in the review of ROBO-ccfsanhq (MR !112), recorded there as a minor and not fixed.

`html_body` (R/robots_validate.R, R/content-check.R) keys on HTML markers near the start of the body. A minified HTML page that is cut before those markers (a truncated fetch, or a page whose first bytes are inline script or style) is not flagged, so the validator reports it as a robots.txt with unknown lines instead.

Done when: a synthesized example.com fixture for that shape is pinned (first as the known gap), and the check either flags it or the edge-case catalog records why it can't without false positives on real robots.txt bodies.

## ROBO-quovenef: Add SSRF guard to the fetch policy (block private/loopback/link-local; re-check across redirects)

**Status:** done

### Description

### Problem

The deterministic fetch policy in `R/fetch-policy.R` (used by `robots_fetch()` and `allowed_by_robots_url()`) has **no SSRF protection**. It builds a request and drives a manual redirect loop to any host, including private/internal addresses. The loop rejects non-HTTP(S) targets and HTTPS→HTTP downgrades, caps redirects, and streams a byte limit — but it never blocks resolution to private/loopback/link-local/reserved ranges.

### Why it matters

robots.txt origins come from caller-supplied URLs (`allowed_by_robots_url()`) and, downstream, from **untrusted content** in consumers such as sitemapr (URLs listed inside a fetched sitemap). A hostile input can aim a robots.txt fetch at an internal address — the classic target being a cloud metadata endpoint at `169.254.169.254`. That is a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vector.

### Scope

- Block resolution to private / loopback / link-local / reserved ranges (IPv4 **and** IPv6).
- Re-apply the guard at **every redirect hop**, not just the initial origin — the manual redirect loop in `fetch-policy.R` is the natural insertion point (mirror how a redirect to a non-HTTP(S) or downgrade target is already rejected there).
- Prefer mapping a blocked target to a **distinct fetch_outcome** (e.g. `blocked`/`ssrf_blocked`) rather than a generic `network_error`, so decisions and error metadata stay explicit and testable.
- Resolve-then-guard-then-connect; document any TOCTOU / httr2-curl constraints where a fully race-free check isn't achievable.

### Prior art

sitemapr already implements exactly this guard (its ADR-003 network-safety policy + `R/ssrf.R`). Use that as the reference for the range list and the redirect re-check shape.

### Tests (offline)

Mocked resolution / local hosts covering: loopback, the link-local metadata IP, private IPv4 + IPv6 ranges, and a redirect that jumps from a public host to a private IP. No live network.

### Motivation

Unblocks sitemapr Layer E robots check (SITE, E.5), which wants to reuse this fetch path wholesale rather than reimplement robots.txt fetching. Without the guard, sitemapr would ship a fetch path that bypasses its own ADR-003 posture. SSRF-safe robots.txt fetching benefits every robotstxtr consumer, so the capability belongs here, not in a per-consumer workaround.

### Comments

#### 2026-07-15 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Implemented on branch feature/ssrf-guard-robo-quovenef. Ported sitemapr's ADR-003 structural SSRF matcher to R/ssrf.R (pure, no-network; identical reason codes + range matrix), added robots_ssrf_check(url) rurl wrapper, and wired one guard check at the top of perform_fetch's redirect loop so it covers the initial origin AND every redirect target before any socket opens. New ssrf_blocked fetch outcome threaded through fetch_error_meta + allowed_by_robots_url fail-outcomes (-> fetch_unknown/NA, never a silent allow). 10 new tests (31 assertions): pure-matcher cases + initial-origin-blocked + redirect-to-private-blocked + url-decision mapping. R7 loopback harness overrides the guard binding test-scoped only. Full verify.sh green (0 errors/0 warnings; pre-existing New-submission/Remotes NOTE only). NOT merged; PR opening for review.

#### 2026-07-15 — 142225707+bart-turczynski@users.noreply.github.com

Merged to main (c913e88) via PR #23. Ported sitemapr's ADR-003 SSRF matcher verbatim into R/ssrf.R (identical reason codes + IPv4/IPv6 range matrix + embedding-bypass decoder); one guard call at the top of perform_fetch()'s loop covers the initial origin and every redirect hop before any socket; new ssrf_blocked fetch_outcome -> fetch_unknown/NA. Added a caller opt-out ssrf_guard=TRUE (default on) on robots_fetch()/allowed_by_robots_url(), validated via validate_ssrf_guard(). Verify gate green (0/0, 1 pre-existing NOTE). ## ROBO-qxalfvpb: Inspect robots.txt agents with syntax, identity and source provenance

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

The news-ai-access corpus contains 6,822 literal User-agent values, 4,464 interpreted product tokens and large inherited blocklists. A token count is not a count of verified crawler identities. Reusable inspection, registry enrichment and source attribution belong with robotstxtr; news-ai-access should consume the tooling and report its own observations.

### Scope

Deliver a deterministic, offline inspection/enrichment layer composed of three independently useful outcomes: a public declaration inventory; versioned bot identity/category annotations; and block-level upstream-source attribution. The parser and evaluator remain authoritative for computed permissions. Identity aliases, categories, syntax validity and provenance are annotations, not alternate matching rules.

Out: news-publisher prevalence estimates, new live corpus collection, making model calls during normal parsing, changing vendored matcher semantics, or expanding the 0.4.0 release gate. The separate validator-message issue ROBO-txnzyugl retains its existing scope.

### Acceptance criteria

- All three child deliverables are complete, documented and work offline from frozen inputs.
- A caller can trace every annotation to a raw line, a versioned rule or source record, and an evidence level; malformed and unknown values remain available.
- The package does not depend on this study's corpus layout or credentials. Updating external collections is an explicit maintenance operation, never an ordinary parsing side effect.
- Runtime evaluation never depends on an LLM or on inferred canonical bot identities.

### Verification

Each child supplies focused fixtures and the package gate. A documented example joins the three outputs without network access and demonstrates unchanged URL decisions.

### Dependencies

Composition: ROBO-lfxjkycf (public inventory), ROBO-wruetsib (registry enrichment), and ROBO-cdsyatry (block-source attribution). The latter two depend on the inventory and can otherwise proceed independently. Existing token-cut diagnostic work is related, not duplicated. No new prerequisite for the current CRAN release.




## ROBO-qxcwxtbm: Validator: offer opt-in suspicious Unicode and possible text-corruption advisories

**Status:** done

### Description

### Why

Valid UTF-8 can still contain replacement characters, invisible formatting characters or plausible mojibake. The audit found U+200B and U+FFFD inside a rule value produce valid with no findings. These characters may be intentional, so blanket validity errors would be wrong. Mixed UTF-8/Latin-1 that is actually malformed already receives invalid_utf8.

### Scope

In: an explicitly opt-in advisory check for narrowly defined suspicious Unicode/text-corruption indicators in active rules, with escaped evidence and cautious wording. Document confidence/limitations and deliberate-path examples. Define the optional API within existing validator conventions.
Out: automatic repair/normalization; claiming the original encoding or intended text is known; marking all non-ASCII paths invalid; heuristically classifying every accented string as mojibake; duplicating Bing/Yandex engine compatibility warnings.

### Acceptance criteria

- Default validation behavior is unchanged. Opt-in findings are clearly advisory and never claim a character is unintended merely because it is invisible or U+FFFD.
- Pin intended Unicode paths, literal U+FFFD/U+200B, plausible corruption examples and comment-only occurrences. Define a conservative supported indicator set and test its false-positive controls.
- Explain that some mixed encodings yield malformed UTF-8 (existing checks) while valid UTF-8 alone cannot prove or disprove corruption.
- Preserve raw bytes and matching behavior; stable codes, positions, bounded diagnostic volume and documented optional API.

### Verification

Focused default-versus-opt-in tests, raw/character input and mocked URL parity; existing Unicode diagnostics; merge gate.

### Dependencies

None. Related independent engine warnings: ROBO-wrlaufai and ROBO-ovgfyowt. This check must not inherit either engine's affected-character set.


### Delivery

Requested by the owner on 2026-11-16 following the robots.txt validator audit. Standalone outcome; no parent or artificial ordering dependency. Do not make this a new 0.4.0 release blocker without an explicit release-scope decision. Preserve raw evidence and distinguish standards conformance, observed crawler behavior and heuristics.

## ROBO-rdxgnqhw: Validator: suggest safe consolidation of groups with identical effective rules

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

Separate groups often repeat exactly the same rule set for different crawlers. Consecutive User-agent lines can share one set of rules (RFC 9309 section 2.2.1). The owner requested an informational consolidation suggestion on 2026-11-16.

Example: ClaudeBot, cohere-training-data-crawler, Diffbot and FacebookBot each have Disallow: / plus Allow: /creativegroup/ and Allow: /advertising/. They can share one group. DataForSeoBot and europarchive.org have no exceptions and must remain a different group.

### Scope

In: a conservative informational suggestion naming separate groups with identical effective rules that could safely share consecutive User-agent lines. Give relevant lines/tokens and a concise suggested representation or explanation. Valid original files remain valid; this is optional cleanup.
Out: automatic rewriting; merging groups with different exceptions; assuming textual equality alone proves equivalence; modifying matcher behavior; guessing unsupported crawler behavior.

### Acceptance criteria

- Stable info code, bounded output and no repeated suggestion for every pair of a large group set.
- Account for repeated groups for the same crawler, wildcard/specific selection, extra directives, empty values, differing group-boundary behavior and parser normalization. Suggest only consolidation whose behavior is established to be preserved under the stated profile; withhold when uncertain.
- Adjacent User-agent lines in a suggested group have no directive interposed. Do not combine the blocked-only crawlers with the allow-exception group in the example.
- Existing duplicate_rule and user_agent_repeated_group checks retain their meanings; coordinate findings without treating a repeated group as invalid syntax.
- Cover the owner example, distinct rule sets, already-stacked agents, repeated crawler groups and unsupported-directive counterexamples. Preserve byte evidence; update help and NEWS.

### Verification

Focused text and mocked URL validator fixtures; positive and negative consolidation cases demonstrating behavior preservation; existing group diagnostics; repository merge gate.

### Dependencies

None. Related completed ROBO-vnhirero (repeated groups), ROBO-xexjgecr (duplicate rules). No new release blocker. Standard: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html#section-2.2.1

## ROBO-rnjfbhvn: Validator: flag rule patterns with a dot segment that URL parsers may remove

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

Most URL handling removes `.` and `..` path segments before a request: RFC 3986 §5.2.4 when
resolving a link, and WHATWG URL parsing, which also treats `%2e` as a dot. A pattern such as
`Disallow: /a/./b` then matches only clients that send the path unnormalized.

TESTED 2026-11-17: `Disallow: /a/./b` gets no diagnostic today, and `/a/b` → allow on Google,
Bing and Yandex. For `/latam/../account/x`, curl and Node `fetch` request `/account/x`, and Node
does the same for `/latam/%2e%2e/account/x`. Python `urllib` and Go `net/http` send the URL as
written, but resolving an `href` (Python `urljoin`, rurl `resolve_url()`, WHATWG) removes literal
dots.

### Scope

In: a warning (working name `rule_dot_segment`) for an Allow or Disallow pattern with a literal
`.` or `..` path segment, bounded on both sides: between two `/`, before `?`, or last before a
final `$`. Message: "Some URL parsers remove dot segments before requesting, so this pattern may
never match." Initial scope skips any pattern with a `*` before the dot segment, since `*` can
reach into the query (`/*/../x` matches `/?q=/../x`).

Out: unanchored terminal dots (`/a/.` matches `/a/.well-known`; `/a/..` matches `/a/..foo`);
dots inside a segment (`/file.html`, `/a..b`); encoded `%2e` segments, which raise a separate
question (parser normalization vs. each matcher's percent-encoding handling) for a follow-up
once the evaluator normalization decision is made; rewriting patterns; evaluator normalization.

### Acceptance criteria

- Fires on `/a/./b`, `/a/../b`, `/a/.$`, `/a/..$`, `/a/..?q=x`.
- Silent on `/a/.`, `/a/..`, `/a/..foo`, `/file.html`, `/a..b/`, `/.well-known/`, `/?q=/../z`,
  `/*/../x`, `/a/..$x` (an inner `$` is literal), `/a/%2e/b`.
- One row per rule line; docs table, `design/linter-set.md`, NEWS one line.

### Verification

Focused fixtures for each case above. Merge gate.

### Dependencies

None. Related: ROBO-bnvdmdjr (same root cause, URL side). Reviewed
with GPT-6.1-Sol (medium) on 2026-11-17.




## ROBO-roypaoox: Validator: flag P and P/ rule pairs, and bare-versus-slash URL decision splits

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

A rule pattern matches by prefix (RFC 9309 §2.2.2): `/search` matches every path that starts
with `/search`, including `/search/` and `/searchlight`. A trailing `/` restricts matching to
URLs that begin with `P/`, so `Disallow: /x/` does not match `/x` itself. Authors mix the two
forms, and the decision for `/x` versus `/x/` is often not what the file seems to say.

Observed on https://www.washingtonpost.com/robots.txt (fetched 2026-11-17). Decisions are from
the Google backend at 188c0a6:

- **Both forms in one group.** `*` has `Disallow: /comments/` (line 86) and
  `Disallow: /comments` (line 87). The validator is silent: `duplicate_rule` checks exact
  repeats only, and ROBO-xexjgecr chose not to flag a Disallow covered by a shorter one in
  general.
- **Bare URL blocked, slash URL allowed.** The AI groups (lines 177-180 and 14 others) have
  `Disallow: /` and `Allow: /creativegroup/`. `/creativegroup` → disallow L178, and
  `/creativegroup/` → allow L179. The server answers `/creativegroup` with a 301 to
  `/creativegroup/`, and a crawler cannot discover that redirect by fetching the blocked
  source URL.
- **Bare URL allowed, slash URL blocked.** `*` has `Disallow: /newsletter/` (line 68):
  `/newsletter` → allow, `/newsletter/` → disallow L68.

The maintainer asked for this check on 2026-11-17: flag the mix of trailing-slash and bare
lines, and catch "directory home blocked but children allowed, or the reverse". The broader
"bare prefix reaches siblings" part (`/search` → `/searchlight`) is split into its own issue
because of its noise risk.

### Scope

Two facets, both info:

1. **`slash_pair`.** In one crawler's applicable rules, the same type with both `P` and `P/`,
   where P is literal (no `*`, no `$`, not `/`). The code is anchored on the later line, which
   names the earlier one. The message is descriptive: "`P` also matches every path `P/`
   matches". It does not call either line redundant, since prefix inclusion does not establish
   redundancy under longest-match precedence.
2. **`slash_split`.** For each literal candidate rule `P/`, compare the crawler's effective
   decision for the bare URL `P` and the slash URL `P/`. Report only when the two differ.
   - Patterns containing `*` or `$` are excluded as candidates; all applicable rules still take
     part in the decisions.
   - The facet speaks about those two URLs only. A deeper rule can change `P/x`, so the message
     never says "children".
   - Directions:
     - bare URL blocked, slash URL allowed: one row per affected rule;
     - bare URL allowed, slash URL blocked: one aggregated row per group, listing up to five
       patterns plus a count.
   - The message may say that a server redirect between `P` and `P/` changes what a crawler
     reaches, without claiming that either direction is harmless.

Group selection: rules are merged per crawler the way the matcher selects them (repeated
groups, and a line stacking several agents), and every row keeps the original line numbers.

Out:
- Fetching the site.
- Root patterns (`/`), and candidates containing a query (`?`) or percent-encoding. These are
  left for a later version and documented as such.
- Rewrite suggestions beyond naming `P`, `P/` and `P$` with what each matches.

### Acceptance criteria

- Codes and names are settled in the MR. One code with a facet field is acceptable.
- The three WaPo reductions fire as described.
- These patterns alone produce no candidate row: `/x$`, `/x*`, a pattern with inner `*`, and a
  `P` / `P/` pair whose lines apply to different crawlers. They may still change another
  candidate's decisions, and fixtures cover that.
- In the full-block fixture (`Disallow: /`, `Allow: /creativegroup/`), adding
  `Allow: /creativegroup$` or `Allow: /creativegroup` silences the bare-blocked row.
- Fixtures with a deeper override (`Disallow: /x/`, `Allow: /x/y`) and with conflicting
  Allow/Disallow at equal length.
- `wildcard_rules_not_inherited`, `duplicate_rule` and the ROBO-cufxicmz warning keep their
  meanings, and a line never gets the same text twice.
- Diagnostic table, `design/linter-set.md`, NEWS (one line).

### Verification

Every positive fixture is cross-checked with `robots_evaluate_text_v1()` on the Google backend
for `P` and `P/`; that is the correctness gate. Row counts on pinned copies of the WaPo and
Bloomberg files are recorded in the MR as a noise check. Merge gate.

### Dependencies

None. Related: ROBO-acoqvdfb, ROBO-xexjgecr, ROBO-cufxicmz.


### Comments

#### 2026-11-17 — bartek@turczynski.pl

The bare-prefix facet was split out to ROBO-otomgbge.




## ROBO-rozvglkd: Validator: recognize a compressed body instead of reading it as rules

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

A compressed body handed to the validator is read as rules, and the result is wrong: it says the
file restricts nothing. https://www.forbes.com/robots.txt (fetched 2026-11-18) answers with
`Content-Encoding: gzip` even to `Accept-Encoding: identity`. Its 8,088 gzip bytes, saved
undecoded and passed to `robots_validate_text()`, give 145 diagnostics (`nul_byte`,
`invalid_utf8`, `malformed_line`, `unknown_directive`, `accepted_missing_colon` on almost every
line) and end with `no_rules`: "Document has no Allow or Disallow rules, so it places no
restrictions on crawling." The decoded file (33,649 bytes) has about 1,100 rules. No diagnostic
says the bytes are compressed.

A live `robots_fetch()` / `robots_validate_url()` of the same URL is correct today: ssrfr sends
`Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate` when libcurl has zlib (`accept_encoding_value()`), and libcurl
decodes the body. Two ways still reach the validator with raw compressed bytes:

1. `robots_validate_text()` on a body saved by a client that did not decode it (plain `curl`
   without `--compressed` does this).
2. A fetch on a libcurl without zlib: ssrfr then sends `identity`, and a server like Forbes sends
   gzip anyway. The fetch output keeps `content_type` but not `Content-Encoding`, so the mismatch
   is visible nowhere.

### Scope

In:
1. Detect a compression signature at the start of the body: gzip `1f 8b`, zlib `78` followed by
   `01`, `5e`, `9c` or `da`, zstd `28 b5 2f fd`. One error (working name `compressed_body`) names
   the format and says the bytes were not read as rules. It replaces the per-line diagnostics and
   `no_rules`, the way a body that is not robots.txt is handled.
2. Fetched documents record the response's `Content-Encoding` and the `Accept-Encoding` that was
   sent, so a server that ignored `identity` is visible.

Out: decompressing the body and validating the result (Googlebot supports gzip, so this would
match crawler behavior, but it touches the size limit, which ROBO-bowvkbks applies to decoded
bytes, and decompression-bomb limits; a separate issue if wanted). Brotli, which has no
signature. Changing how matchers read such a body.

### Acceptance criteria

- The Forbes gzip bytes give exactly one `compressed_body` error and no `no_rules`,
  `nul_byte`, `invalid_utf8` or `malformed_line` rows.
- A plain-text file that happens to start with bytes like `x` + `^` is not flagged: the zlib
  check also verifies the header checksum (CMF*256+FLG divisible by 31) and is limited to a body
  that is not valid UTF-8 text.
- Fetched rows carry `content_encoding` (NA when absent) and the sent `Accept-Encoding`.
- Docs entry for the new code; NEWS one line.

### Verification

Synthetic fixtures built in the test from a small robots.txt: gzip written through `gzfile()`,
zlib from `memCompress(type = "gzip")` (which emits a zlib stream, not gzip), and a hand-written
zstd header; a negative fixture of text starting with `x^`; a local-server
fetch that sends `Content-Encoding: gzip`. Merge gate.

### Dependencies

None. Related: ROBO-syoccfej (compare fetch variants), ROBO-bowvkbks (size limit on decoded
bytes).




## ROBO-rrzsktxc: Validator: flag unexpected ASCII control bytes inside rule patterns

**Status:** done

### Description

### Why

The audit reproduced User-agent: * followed by Disallow: /private plus byte 0x01 as validation_status valid with no diagnostics. Well-formed UTF-8 is not sufficient to establish rule syntax validity. RFC 9309 section 2.2 excludes these control bytes from path patterns.

### Scope

In: a stable line-specific diagnostic for unexpected ASCII control bytes in active Allow/Disallow values, with escaped byte evidence and a precise explanation. Define the exact set from the grammar and actual parser treatment.
Out: broad rejection of non-ASCII characters; changing matchers; treating LF/CR line boundaries as embedded controls; a speculative crawler-wide matching verdict; replacing existing NUL/whitespace diagnostics.

### Acceptance criteria

- Reproduce and diagnose 0x01 in a rule value; exercise the relevant control set and positions with ordinary-character controls.
- Respect comment cuts, parser trimming, line boundaries and line-buffer limits. Comment-only bytes do not receive an active-rule warning.
- Define severity and interaction with nul_byte, rule_cut_by_nul and rule_inner_whitespace without redundant findings for an already-owned hazard.
- Do not accidentally flag DEL merely by relying on its control-character name: RFC 9309's literal %x24-7F range includes 0x7F. Any DEL advisory requires a separately justified explanation.
- Raw and fetched input preserve exact bytes; help, catalog and NEWS document code and scope.

### Verification

Focused rule/comment/boundary fixtures, existing NUL/whitespace tests and merge gate.

### Dependencies

None. Grammar: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309.html#section-2.2


### Delivery

Requested by the owner on 2026-11-16 following the robots.txt validator audit. Standalone outcome; no parent or artificial ordering dependency. Do not make this a new 0.4.0 release blocker without an explicit release-scope decision. Preserve raw evidence and distinguish standards conformance, observed crawler behavior and heuristics.

## ROBO-rswdwrnp: Validator: flag a % that does not start a valid percent-escape, such as an unfilled placeholder

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

A `%` in a rule that does not start a two-hex-digit escape matches no correctly encoded URL,
since a URL writes a literal `%` as `%25`. https://www.shopify.com/robots.txt (fetched
2026-11-18) has `Disallow: /*hashid=%subscriber_hash%`, a mailing-template merge tag that was
never filled in. The validator says nothing.

Checked with the Google backend on 2026-11-18: the rule disallows only the literal
`/x?hashid=%subscriber_hash%`; `/x?hashid=%25subscriber_hash%25` and `/x?hashid=abc` are allowed.
So the rule blocks neither the encoded placeholder nor any real hash.

### Scope

In: a warning (working name `rule_invalid_percent_escape`) for a rule value holding a `%` not
followed by two hex digits. The message says the rule matches only URLs that carry the raw `%`,
which correctly encoded URLs never do, and suggests `%25` when a literal `%` was meant. A value
shaped like a template placeholder (`%name%`, `{{name}}`, `*|NAME|*`) says it looks like an
unfilled placeholder.

Out: rewriting the rule; changing matching.

### Acceptance criteria

- The Shopify line warns; `%2F`, `%2f` (already `rule_lowercase_escape`) and `%25` do not.
- A trailing `%` and `%` followed by one hex digit warn.
- `{{name}}` and `*|NAME|*` are named as placeholders only in the message, never as a separate
  code. Docs entry; NEWS one line.

### Verification

Synthetic fixtures for each shape above, each cross-checked with `robots_evaluate_text_v1()` on
the Google backend (raw and `%25`-encoded target URLs). Merge gate.

### Dependencies

None.

## ROBO-sdltipng: M3 — macOS CI job on the self-hosted mac-shell runner

**Status:** in-progress

### Description

Gate (fleet groom ROBO-lsbdefbm, 2026-09-27): needs the author (installing gitlab-runner, the registration token) and waits on SEOR-hhtzaknn, which decides where fleet CI runs; the fleet already runs Docker runners on this Mac. Moved out of ROBO-tiohzehm so the migration epic can close without it.

Register a self-hosted GitLab runner on the author's Mac so macOS coverage
survives the migration. GitLab.com hosted macOS runners are Premium/Ultimate
only (verified 2026-08-28), and a self-hosted runner is free, has no compute-minute
ceiling, and tests real hardware rather than a rented VM.

Requires the author: installing `gitlab-runner`, obtaining a runner registration
token from the project's CI/CD settings, and deciding whether the runner is
project-scoped or shared across robotstxtr/rurl/pslr/punycoder.

Tag the runner (e.g. `macos`, `self-hosted`) and gate the macOS matrix entry on
that tag so pipelines still pass when the Mac is offline — an unavailable
personal runner must not turn the pipeline red. Use `allow_failure` or a manual
trigger rather than letting a sleeping laptop block a release.

DONE WHEN: a macOS R CMD check runs on the self-hosted runner, and a pipeline
started while the runner is offline does not fail because of it.

PROMOTED to high and now on the critical path, scope widened. This was macOS-only; it is now the route to having ANY CI at all. ## ROBO-sniltuap: Validator: invalid_utf8 is a lineless error even when only a comment holds the byte

**Status:** done

### Description

### Problem

A Latin-1 byte inside a comment makes `robots_validate_text()` report `invalid_utf8` at severity error with no line number, although the byte changes no rule and the matcher decision is unaffected.

Found by the edge-case catalog (ROBO-mxermwed, 2026-11-09). Fixture(s): `enc-latin1-comment`, in tests/testthat/fixtures/edge-cases/ (manifest.csv) and design/edge-case-catalog.md; the current behavior is pinned in tests/testthat/test-edge-cases-mxermwed.R under a `# known gap:` comment, so a fix turns that block red and updates it.

### Scope

In: anchor `invalid_utf8` on the line(s) holding the invalid bytes, and lower its severity when they are only in comments.

Out: matcher behavior changes. A fix that would change a documented engine policy goes to the maintainer as a [USER] decision first.

### Acceptance criteria

The fixture's known-gap block is replaced by an assertion of the new diagnostic, the catalog row is updated, and the validator code table (roxygen of robots_validate_text) documents any new code.

## ROBO-strnxkgu: [PARKED] SF2 — Parser-family discriminator spike (~10 cases, GUI tester, no infrastructure)

**Status:** todo | **Parent:** cbbyzfvflluniwyrplqtytozumblaeiu

### Description

Parked 2026-09-27 by the maintainer (fleet groom ROBO-lsbdefbm): a conformance study (analysis and vendor contact), not package code. Start only on an instruction naming this issue.

Timebox: ~1 hour. Goal: decide whether the full harness is worth building at all.

Use Screaming Frog's **Custom robots.txt tester** (Configuration > robots.txt > Custom), which reports the *matched line*, not just allow/deny — the only way to check rule attribution, which is what our corpora record in `matched_rule`. No local server, no CLI, no corpus infrastructure.

One fixture body, ~10 request targets chosen so each answer discriminates between Google's matcher and typical alternatives:

1. longest-match vs first-match precedence
2. Allow/Disallow tie-break at equal length (Google: least restrictive wins)
3. `$` end-anchor support
4. `*` mid-path wildcard support
5. empty `Disallow:` = allow all
6. path value with missing leading slash
7. UA group selection: exact token vs substring match
8. two groups with the same UA — merged or first-wins
9. percent-encoded vs literal path (e.g. `/a%2Fb` vs `/a/b`)
10. malformed line recovery (missing colon / typo'd directive name)

Run the set twice: default SF user-agent, then UA set to Googlebot — the UA setting selects the robots group, so cases 7-8 are meaningless without both.

Outcome is a three-way verdict recorded as a comment on the parent:
- **Google-equivalent** → study is a short null-result note, close it out cheap
- **crawler-commons-shaped** → switch to diffing against that open implementation, drop the black-box approach
- **its own thing** → proceed to SF3/SF4 and build the harness

Note the exact SF version and capture date.

## ROBO-syoccfej: Audit: compare robots.txt responses across explicitly selected fetch variants

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

One successful fetch cannot expose a CDN/WAF returning different robots.txt bodies or statuses by HTTP User-Agent, selected origin variant or time. Existing validation correctly evaluates a single acquired response, but has no explicit comparison report.

### Scope

In: an opt-in audit that compares explicitly requested fetch identities, repeated observations and HTTP/HTTPS or hostname variants, using existing acquisition and safety policy. Report differences in status/outcome, final URL/redirects, body hash/bytes and content metadata with provenance.
Out: silently expanding every validation into multiple requests; origin discovery; bypassing safety; impersonation claims from a user-agent string; inferring that separate origins ought to have identical policy; scheduling recurring monitoring; inventing access decisions for failed fetches.

### Acceptance criteria

- Default validators remain single-fetch-per-origin. Extra observations are explicitly selected and bounded, with fetch time, request identity and original origin attached.
- Distinguish HTTP User-Agent identity from the robots group product token. A spoofed header does not prove what verified Googlebot/Bingbot/Yandexbot receives.
- Scheme, host and port variants retain their separate robots scope. Differences are evidence, not automatically configuration errors.
- Separate transient acquisition differences from changed body content; retain raw evidence and make comparison deterministic on supplied/mock observations.
- Define/document the audit API and request-budget controls before implementation; existing SSRF, redirect and size limits apply to every fetch.

### Verification

Mocked same/different body and status matrices, explicit variant selection, repeated fetches, refused targets and no-extra-requests default tests; merge gate.

### Dependencies

None. Existing ROBO-oxfpgdrx concerns live crawler evidence and is related, not replaced. Origin scope reference: https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec


### Delivery

Requested by the owner on 2026-11-16 following the robots.txt validator audit. Standalone outcome; no parent or artificial ordering dependency. Do not make this a new 0.4.0 release blocker without an explicit release-scope decision. Preserve raw evidence and distinguish standards conformance, observed crawler behavior and heuristics.


### Comments

#### 2026-11-17 — bartek@turczynski.pl

Held for the owner (burndown-v2 2026-11-17). Recommended by Claude and Codex (gpt-6.1-sol, high) together; needs the owner's approval before dispatch: one unit with the scout's design (new robots_compare_fetches(variants, max_requests)), plus: max_requests is a hard budget over every outbound request incl. redirect hops and repeats, checked before each request (acquire.R already fetches hop by hop, so it is enforceable); bodies compared byte for byte with report-local equivalence labels, no hash dependency; a truncated body never counts as equal. Owner: approve the API and 0.4.0 scope.

## ROBO-temlykwj: [PARKED] Report AI vendor token coverage for a robots.txt (named, fallback, retired)

**Status:** todo

### Description

### Why

The question publishers ask is per vendor: for each documented vendor token, what permissions
does this robots.txt express under the selected matcher? robots.txt answers per token, and so
does the package today. https://www.washingtonpost.com/robots.txt (fetched 2026-11-17) shows the gap:

- It names `ClaudeBot` (blocked, two Allow exceptions) and the older `anthropic-ai` and
  `Claude-Web`, which Anthropic's current crawler documentation does not list. Their retirement
  needs a dated source. It does not name `Claude-SearchBot` or `Claude-User`, which fall back to `*` and
  are allowed (tested with the Google backend).
- It names no OpenAI token. `GPTBot`, `OAI-SearchBot` and `ChatGPT-User` all fall back to `*`.
- It does not name `Google-Extended`.
- It blocks `PerplexityBot`; `Perplexity-User` falls back to `*`.
- It names `meta-externalfetcher`, which Meta documents as possibly bypassing robots.txt for
  user-initiated fetches. OpenAI says robots.txt may not apply to `ChatGPT-User`, and Perplexity
  says `Perplexity-User` generally ignores it. The report states what the file expresses, not
  what a vendor does.
- `Google-Extended` is a usage-control token with no crawler of its own, so the registry needs
  a control-token role next to training, search and user fetch.

Two more news files fetched the same day show the same gap from other angles:
- https://www.newyorker.com/robots.txt blocks 41 tokens in one group (lines 54-95), including
  `Claude-SearchBot`, `Claude-User`, `Google-Extended` and `Perplexity-User`. It names no OpenAI
  token, so `GPTBot` and `OAI-SearchBot` are allowed via `*`.
- https://www.theguardian.com/robots.txt states in comments that LLM use is not permitted
  (lines 3-7), and blocks 37 tokens (lines 65-102). `GPTBot`, `OAI-SearchBot` and
  `Google-Extended` are not among them and fall back to `*`.

Whether those omissions are deliberate (licensing deals) is outside the package. The report
makes them visible.

The maintainer has said a pseudo-class for AI bots is likely (2026-11-17). This would be its
first consumer.

### Why it waits

It needs a maintained registry of vendor, token, role (training, search, user fetch) and status
(current or retired), with sources and dates. Deciding where that registry lives (robotstxtr,
agent-view or news-ai-access) and who updates it is the maintainer's call.

### Scope

In: a report over one robots.txt. For each registry token: the vendor and role; literal
mentions; the effective matching groups; whether evaluation uses specific rules, `*` rules or no
applicable rules; and the decision for `/` and for sample paths. A token's status (current or
retired) is shown as a sourced annotation, separately from its computed permissions. Built on `robots_evaluate_text_v1()`, Google backend, as an application choice. The
vendors' own parsers are not claimed: agent-view holds the evidence on how each one reads
robots.txt.

Out: the registry's data collection; any claim about whether a vendor complies.

### Acceptance criteria

Written in full when unparked. Invariants recorded now:
- Literal mentions and effective matching are reported separately.
- Fixtures cover repeated matching groups, case differences, cut agent values, and a specific
  group whose rules do not match the requested path, each checked against the evaluator.
- A root block with Allow exceptions is reported path by path, never as a blanket "blocked".
- A retired token keeps its computed decision beside its retirement annotation.
- Acceptance uses a pinned copy of the WaPo file and a pinned registry revision, never a live
  fetch.

### Dependencies

Release gate: registry ownership and maintenance agreed. Implementation needs a versioned
registry input. Related: agent-view research (`research/openai.md`, `claude-server.md`); news-ai-access.

## ROBO-tiohzehm: Migrate off GitHub to GitLab as the sole forge

**Status:** done

### Description

Migrate robotstxtr off GitHub onto GitLab as the sole forge. The
`bart-turczynski` GitHub account is suspended; appeals have gone unanswered, so
GitHub is treated as permanently unavailable rather than temporarily down.

### Why this is urgent, not cosmetic

Verified 2026-08-28: **robotstxtr is currently uninstallable by anyone but the
author.**

- `DESCRIPTION:32` requires `rurl (>= 2.2.1)`.
- CRAN serves `rurl 1.2.0`.
- The R-universe staging repo `https://bart-turczynski.r-universe.dev` returns
  200 for `/src/contrib/PACKAGES` but **no longer lists `rurl` at all**; only
  `pslr` and `punycoder` remain, both still pointing at suspended
  `github.com/bart-turczynski/...` URLs.
- The local gate passes only because this machine has `rurl 3.0.0` installed.

Root cause is the same suspension: r-universe requires the registry repo
(`<name>.r-universe.dev`) to live on **GitHub**. The packages it lists may be on
any git host, but the registry may not. With the account suspended r-universe
cannot read the registry, and `rurl` has already aged out. `pslr` and
`punycoder` are expected to follow.

Consequence: "drop GitHub" and "keep an r-universe staging repo" are mutually
exclusive. Decision taken — drop the staging repo (see DECISIONS below).

### Verified platform facts (GitLab.com, checked 2026-08-28)

| capability | GitLab.com Free | GitHub today |
|---|---|---|
| Linux runners | yes, cost factor 1 | yes |
| Windows runners | **yes, Free tier, cost factor 1** (Beta) | yes, 2x |
| macOS runners | **no — Premium/Ultimate only**, cost factor 6 (Beta) | yes, 10x |
| monthly budget | **400 compute minutes** | effectively unlimited (public repo) |

Windows gets cheaper, which matters because Windows is the historically flaky
platform here (ROBO-yasmzyhl). macOS is the real loss. 400 minutes/month will
not carry the existing 6-entry `full-check.yml` matrix.

### Anonymous-reachability finding (measured with a known-good peer)

    200  https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab
    404  https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues     <- PUBLIC project, still 404
    302  https://gitlab.com/bart-turczynski/robotstxtr     <- private, login redirect
    302  https://gitlab.com/bart-turczynski/robotstxtr/-/issues

The `/-/issues` 404 is GitLab site-wide anti-scraping, NOT a project defect —
it reproduces on a known-public peer in the same run. But CRAN's URL check is an
anonymous client, so a `BugReports:` pointing at `/-/issues` is likely to be
flagged. Decide deliberately; do not discover this at submission.

### DECISIONS (approved by the author 2026-08-28)

1. **macOS coverage** — register a **self-hosted runner on the author's Mac**.
   Free, unlimited minutes, and gives real macOS coverage rather than a rented
   VM. Applying to GitLab for Open Source (Ultimate + 0.5 cost factor) is a
   follow-up, not a blocker.
2. **R-universe staging** — **retire it.** GitLab CI installs the sibling
   packages directly from their GitLab git URLs. This is the only option that
   actually delivers "no GitHub", and `rurl`, `pslr` and `punycoder` are all
   already on GitLab.
3. **Project visibility** — make `robotstxtr`, `rurl`, `pslr` and `punycoder`
   **public**, together. Required for CRAN URL checks, for GitLab Pages, and for
   decision 2 to work at all. Piecemeal leaves the dependency chain broken.

Pre-flip secret audit (2026-08-28): zero hits across the full history of all
four repositories for `glpat-`, `ghp_`, `github_pat_`, `gho_`, `AKIA`, `sk-`,
`xox[baprs]-`, PEM private-key headers, or an inline `CODECOV_TOKEN`. rurl's
`tools/oracle/*-credentials-fragments.R` are WHATWG URL **userinfo** test-vector
oracles, not credentials. `.env.example` files are intended to be committed.

### Scope

312 GitHub references across 36 tracked files (excluding `inst/vendor/`, which
legitimately cites `github.com/google/robotstxt` upstream and must NOT be
rewritten), plus 8 workflow files totalling 712 lines.

Out of scope for this epic: CRAN submission (ROBO-ufxrxxga remains blocked on
rurl reaching CRAN, and this migration does not change that).


### Comments

## ROBO-tipzbglv: Text inputs with undeclared encoding are mangled under LC_ALL=C

**Status:** done

### Description

### Why

Under `LC_ALL=C`, a supplied robots.txt body passed as a character string with non-ASCII bytes and no declared encoding (Encoding "unknown", as `rawToChar()` or `readLines()` without `encoding=` gives) is altered before matching: each non-ASCII byte becomes a `<xx>` escape, so the body grows and rules change. The same call in a UTF-8 locale reads the bytes as written. The C locale is common in containers and CI. Found when the gate's C locale leg failed the ROBO-etlkvljs tests.

Reproduction (synthesized):

```r
b <- rawToChar(c(charToRaw("User-agent: *\nDisallow: /caf"),
                 as.raw(c(0xc3, 0xa9)), charToRaw("\n")))
x <- robots_evaluate_text_v1(b, "http://example.com/caf%C3%A9", "bot",
                             "google", "google")
x$evidence$stored_bytes  # 31 in en_US.UTF-8, 37 under LC_ALL=C
x$results$url_decision   # "disallow" in en_US.UTF-8, "allow" under LC_ALL=C
```

### Scope

In: find where the text entry points convert the string (likely `enc2utf8()`/`iconv()` from native, or a `useBytes = FALSE` call) and take the string's bytes as written when its encoding is "unknown", treating it as UTF-8 as the docs assume; check `allowed_by_robots_text()` and `robots_validate_text()` too. Pin the reproduction under LC_ALL=C (the gate has a C locale leg).
Out: strings declared latin1 (separate question).

### Acceptance criteria

- The reproduction gives the same bytes and decision in both locales, for every text entry point.

**Not done unattended.** It makes the author's own machine start executing
robotstxtr's pipeline — which compiles the vendored C++ matcher via cpp11 and

reconfigures infrastructure shared with another project rather than landing a
code slice. Epic decision 1 already approves self-hosted runners in principle;

first time. That is the actual DONE-WHEN clause here ("a pipeline runs green on
an MR"), and it has never been reachable until now.

blocker is what I can move; the merge decision is not mine.

#### 2026-09-10 — bartek@turczynski.pl

MR !2 IS MERGED, 2026-09-10. **robotstxtr now has CI on `main` for the first
time.** The fleet's highest-leverage pin is out.

    5fa1eb9 + 8d313a6  ->  merge commit b534a0d  into protected main
    not squashed; both original SHAs verified ancestors of main
    source branch removed on both sides; local deleted with `git branch -d`

    git show origin/main:.gitlab-ci.yml   -> PRESENT, 252 lines

The merge also deleted `.github/workflows/verify.yml` and moved the MR template
to `.gitlab/merge_request_templates/Default.md`.

### It did not merge as it stood — the check job was broken

The MR was `mergeable`, but its head pipeline was **failed**, and the previous
handover recorded only the former. Two separate causes, in sequence:

**1. The old failure was not a code failure.** Pipeline 2799393298 (2026-08-28)
had all seven jobs die in under a second with `ci_quota_exceeded` — the shared
namespace 400-minute budget, spent before the local runner existed. Nothing ran.

Note the raddr !39 remedy does **not** work here. robotstxtr `workflow:rules`
send a branch pipeline to `never` when the branch has an open MR, and `api` is
not a listed source, so `POST /pipeline -f ref=<branch>` is filtered out. The
working call is the MR-pipeline endpoint:

    glab api --method POST projects/bart-turczynski%2Frobotstxtr/merge_requests/2/pipelines

That runs on project runner 56078730 (`seor-local-docker`, untagged, online),
which does not draw on the exhausted shared quota.

**2. That run then exposed a real defect in the port.** Six jobs green, `check`
dead at 40s in `before_script`:

    Error in loadVignetteBuilder(pkgdir, TRUE, lib.loc = ...) :
      vignette builder 'knitr' not found

`deps::.` installs **hard dependencies only**. robotstxtr declares
`VignetteBuilder: knitr`, ships `vignettes/introduction.Rmd`, and keeps knitr,
rmarkdown and testthat in `Suggests`. So `--as-cran` could not build the
vignette — and could not have run the suite either. **Fixing only the vignette
builder would have moved the failure one job later, into the tests.**
`coverage` carried the identical defect: covr runs the testthat suite, which
needs testthat, httpuv, jsonlite, callr, oysteR and rosv, every one a Suggests.

Fixed in `8d313a6`: both jobs install the local package soft dependencies with
`pak::local_install_deps(dependencies = TRUE, upgrade = FALSE)`. Scoped to the
local package deliberately — a blanket `dependencies = TRUE` on the existing
vector would also install the Suggests of the packages named in it, and **rurl
suggests pkgdown**, pulling a documentation toolchain into a check job that has
no use for it and cutting against this pipeline compute-budget design. rurl
stays in a separate first call so it is installed before the local solve runs:
CRAN serves 1.2.0, below the declared `rurl (>= 2.2.1)` floor, so a solve that
reached CRAN for it would fail.

### Verification

    glab ci lint                    -> valid
    local pre-push gate on 8d313a6  -> 0 errors | 0 warnings | 1 note
    MR pipeline 2838356532          -> ALL SEVEN GREEN

    lint 50s | readme 67s | docs 56s | vendor-fidelity:yandex 5s
    vendor-fidelity:bing 8s | check 110s | coverage 76s

The one note from the local gate is entirely the **GitHub URL 404s** already
tracked as M4 (`ROBO-bgcloodt`) — `URL:`/`BugReports:` in DESCRIPTION,
